The 3.6 bytes/token constant is an assumption — no tokenizer was available and I would not npm install one — but the conclusion is robust across 3.0-4.0 B/tok.]

THE ROUND TRIP IS NOT UNCLAIMED, AND ITS REVEALED DEMAND IS 846x SMALLER THAN PACKING'S. PLAN §6 calls the round trip 'the unclaimed part' and 'the highest-leverage user ask in the entire demand sweep'. It is claimed: llm-code-format v3.1.0 (published 2025-09-20, zero dependencies, TypeScript) already does 'From source code to Markdown to LLMs and back again', exposes parseMarkdownFiles and formatMarkdownFiles plus a streaming parser, and recognises nine LLM output conventions. It gets 387 downloads/month. repomix gets 327,543. That is 846:1. This is the markdown-it-decorate pattern the brief already warns about — a correct design that nobody installs — and it is now measured for OUR feature rather than an analogy. Corroborating: repomix issue #226 (unpack) has 0 reactions and 6 comments after 19 months while #71 (split the file back up) has 8 reactions, 12 comments, a merged PR, and was still being asked for on 2025-09-08. The single-file property that is our premise is the property its closest neighbours' users keep asking to have removed.

THE HUMAN LANE IS DEAD ON ITS OWN FORUM, AND THE ONE ENCOURAGING NUMBER IS CURIOSITY, NOT DEMAND. forum.obsidian.md t/81878 'How do I export an entire Vault to a Single File?' — created 2024-05-15, 9,010 views, 1 like, 3 posts, in 26 months. t/96068 'Export Vault into a single text file?' — 2025-02-04, 849 views, 1 like, 4 posts. For contrast, 'Share Note plugin - share individual notes' has 172 posts. 9,010 views says people look; 1 like and 3 posts say nobody wanted it enough to reply. Any positioning of the container as a human workspace-sharing feature is unsupported. Note this also constrains D4: the durable escape-hatch export should be a plain zip of plain files, because that is what a departing human actually wants, and the zip's disqualifying properties (opaque diff, 120x git cost) do not apply to a one-shot export.

MY OWN FIRST BOUNDARY-REPAIR MEASUREMENT FLATTERED THE DESIGN AND WAS WRONG BY 99 PERCENTAGE POINTS. The line-diff rebase reported 200/200 recovery within a median-0-line window under clean delimiter deletion. Under the destruction models that actually occur it collapsed: 119/120 wrong on merge-across, 119/120 wrong on elision, 120/120 wrong on reorder. This is the same reward function the previous 18-area run exhibited, reproduced inside this one area within a single hour, and it means the prior prototype described in the brief ('retaining the pre-edit pack, diffing, rebasing stored spans, verifying against digest') was almost certainly validated against the benign case only. Anyone who re-derives that prototype's numbers should assume they are the benign-case numbers until a hostile fixture proves otherwise.

THE 'AGENTIC CLIs ARE EATING THE USE CASE' THREAT IS REFUTED, WHICH IS A NEGATIVE FOR OUR DIFFERENTIATION RATHER THAN A POSITIVE FOR OUR DEMAND. PLAN §6 carries it as threat 1 on the strength of a single HN comment. repomix npm downloads went 119,678 in 2025-07 to 327,053 in 2026-07 — 2.73x year on year, with 2026-07 the highest month in the package's history. The packing market is healthy and growing fast, which means the incumbent is not weakening, is at 27,551 stars, ships a skill and an MCP server, and already implements the fence-collision defense we thought was ours. We would be entering a growing market against a strong, actively-maintained incumbent whose only structural gap is a reverse operation that a zero-dependency library already fills at 387 downloads/month.
unclaimed: A container whose UNPACK IS TRANSACTIONAL AND CLASSIFIED — every file emerges tagged clean / edited / reframed / framing-damaged by dual authority (declared byte count vs fence scan), with an all-or-nothing write. Searched: npm registry for 'unpack repomix', 'markdown container unpack', 'apply llm file blocks', 'split concatenated files' (6 results each, nothing relevant beyond repomix itself and unrelated packages); repomix's own 1,430-entry tree for unpack|apply|reverse (only outputSplit.ts); llm-code-format's README (it parses nine formats and re-serialises, but has no manifest, no digests, no byte counts, and therefore cannot distinguish an edit from a framing error).

GIT-NATIVE ATTRIBUTION OF A PACKED CONTAINER: a diff driver whose hunk header names the contained source file, so `git diff`, `git blame -L` and code review work on the container without any tool. Verified working locally; searched repomix, gitingest, stitchmd and llm-code-format for any .gitattributes / xfuncname shipping — none of the four ships one, because none of the four expects its output to be committed.

BOUNDARY-DAMAGE LOCALISATION AS A FIRST-CLASS DIAGNOSTIC — 'the boundary between A and B was destroyed; it is near line X; within 10 lines with 78% confidence; here are the two candidate splits' — rather than either silent repair or a bare parse error. No existing tool detects boundary damage at all, because no existing tool has a manifest to compare against; repomix issue #226's whole thread is about how to parse the return, never about how to detect that the return is malformed.

AUTOMATIC CARRIER ESCALATION AS A DECLARED, VERIFIABLE PROPERTY: default to a renderable carrier and escalate to the fence when, and only when, the contained bytes require it, with the choice recorded in the manifest and re-verified on read. repomix computes a fence run but does not record it, does not verify it on read (it has no reader), and does not choose between carriers; aider's choose_fence picks from a fixed candidate list and can fail outright — 'Unable to find a fencing strategy! Falling back to:' is a real code path in aider/coders/base_coder.py:630.

A CONTAINER THAT NESTS. Every prior art flattens: tar, zip, cpio, shar, MIME, TextBundle, repomix. The fence carrier nests for free because run length is a nesting counter, verified byte-identical to three levels. Nobody has shipped this because nobody else's delimiter is length-parameterised.
result.design:
DECISION: SINGLE FILE. Ship `.md`, not `.zip`. Evidence, not taste: 120x lower git storage per edit (263 B vs 31,590 B), a reviewable text diff vs 'Binary files differ', 15.4% smaller after gzip (7,874,098 vs 9,310,058), index at the head (0.49%) instead of the tail (98.8%) so it streams and a model can read it, 5x faster to produce at 500 MB scale, and +0.892% uncompressed vs tar's +3.4%. Zip wins exactly one thing, random access (2.94 ms vs 38.48 ms), which neither lane needs. Ship a zip too, but as a DIFFERENT PRODUCT: the D4 escape-hatch export, one-shot, never versioned, plain files, no manifest.

CARRIER — overturns PLAN §5. The delimiter is a backtick fence, run N = max(4, max line-initial backtick run over every contained byte + 1), declared in the manifest and RE-DERIVED AND CROSS-CHECKED on read. Not the HTML comment: it silently loses a boundary whenever a contained file ends inside an open fence (0.369% of real files, so 98.2% of vault-scale packs fail). Prior art is repomix's calculateMarkdownDelimiter; adopt it, credit it.

DELIMITER != LABEL. The fence is the machine boundary; a visible `#### \`<path>\`` line immediately above it is the human label and renders as an anchored heading. If a model mangles the label nothing is lost, because the manifest is the authority. This also fixes the fence carrier's one real cost — the container stops rendering (285/288 chars inside <pre><code>) — by giving a human a navigable outline of file names even though bodies show as monospace.

SPLIT CONTRACT. Open: `<F>text fm:file <i> <json-quoted-path>` at column 0. Close: `<F>` alone at column 0. Manifest: YAML frontmatter, `fmpack: 1`, `fence: N`, `root:`, then ONE LINE PER FILE `- {i, bytes, sha256, path}` — one line per file is worth 47x on diff size and is non-negotiable. Paths: relative, POSIX separators, NFC, JSON-quoted (55.2% of real paths contain spaces), no `..`, no leading `/` or drive letter, no control characters; reject non-canonical, duplicate, and case-folded-duplicate paths (APFS is case-insensitive). Ordering: manifest order == physical order == index order, dense 0..n-1. Trailing newline: git's own `\ No newline at end of file` sentinel (26.6% of real files need it) and `\ Empty file` for zero-byte files (4 in the corpus). NESTING IS ALLOWED — delete PLAN §5's refusal; it works free and byte-exact to three levels.

FAILURE MODES, because a container without one is a data-loss bug. E-codes refuse the entire unpack and write nothing: E-NOHEADER, E-UNTERMINATED-MANIFEST, E-EMPTY-MANIFEST, E-COUNT-MISMATCH, E-INDEX-NOT-DENSE, E-INDEX-RANGE, E-PATH-DISAGREE, E-ABSOLUTE-PATH, E-TRAVERSAL, E-NONCANONICAL, E-DUP-PATH, E-CASE-OR-NORM-COLLISION, E-CTRL-IN-PATH, E-UNCLOSED-FINAL-FENCE (truncation), E-RUN-UNDERDECLARED (a contained body holds a run >= the declared fence — the hole my own verifier had). W-codes unpack but quarantine the file: W-EDITED, W-REFRAMED, W-FRAMING-DAMAGED. The write is transactional: verify everything, then write, never partial.

REJOIN CONTRACT — DUAL AUTHORITY, which resolves the git-fast-import tension the brief raises. Byte count is the fast path and the tamper detector; the fence is the human-editable frame. Agreement => `clean`. Digest matches the byte-count slice only => `framing-damaged`. Digest matches the fence slice only => `reframed` (a human edited the file and the count is stale — accept it and rewrite the manifest). Neither => `edited`. Proven per file by digest: 1084/1084 byte-identical on the pinned corpus.

INJECTION — closed by construction, not by escaping. Never transform the payload (PLAN §3 already forbids it, and it is right). The run length IS the capability: a correct reader pinned to the declared run recovers 3 files with 0 forged paths from an attack file, while a naive `\`{3,}` scanner accepts `../../../.ssh/authorized_keys`. So the spec must mandate the pinned run and forbid any-fence scanning, and pair it with the path validation above. The only residual is a bounded DoS: one file with a 100-backtick line inflates the fence for the whole pack by about 2*N bytes per file — 217 KB across 1084 files, negligible.

EDIT-MAPPING — the actually-unclaimed part, and simpler than the prototype. When boundaries survive, mapping is O(1): read `fm:file <i>` and the offset inside the fence. No diff, no rebase, no span store. The prior prototype's diff-and-rebase solved a problem the delimiter already solves; demote it to the fallback. Per-file digests then classify every file, and only `edited` files get written. Offsets INSIDE an edited file map by a line diff of that file's body against its pre-edit body — 1.9 ms median, and per-file rather than per-container, which matters because difflib on a whole 25 MB container is not viable.

BOUNDARY DESTRUCTION — REFUSE AND LOCALISE, NEVER REPAIR. Detection is certain and cheap (delimiter count vs manifest length, dense-index check, path agreement). Repair is not: exact only when at least one neighbour is unedited (303/400 at p=0.5), and the realistic merge-across case mis-locates 119/120 times. Emit instead: 'the boundary between A and B was destroyed; the manifest byte count puts it near line X (within 10 lines, 78%); here are the two candidate splits; confirm.'

PREVENTION BEATS REPAIR, AND THIS IS THE PRODUCT DECISION. The container is a READ format. Never hand a model a pack and ask for the pack back. Ask for per-file whole-file listings in aider's shape — path line, fence, full body, fence — which is the format models are most reliably well-formed in (median 99.6% vs 94.2% for diffs) and which is structurally identical to one entry of our own container, so one scanner serves both. The container's manifest then VALIDATES the return: every returned path must be in the manifest, every unreturned file is unchanged by definition, and a returned file whose digest equals its pre-edit digest is a no-op. This is independently where the repomix maintainer landed in #226 and where aider already is.

POSITIONING: MACHINES, BOUNDED. Do not ship 'pack my vault'. Ship 'pack this selection' with a token budget, a default of roughly 30 average files per 200K, and a hard refusal above the target model's window with the described index offered instead. The index is 110x cheaper and is what the founder's 'one reference, one marker' line actually describes.
result.measurement:
THE ONE THING I COULD NOT MEASURE, AND IT IS THE THING THAT SETTLES THE AREA: do frontier models preserve container delimiters when asked to edit a multi-file pack? Everything about the write path hinges on it and no proxy answers it. Aider's leaderboard measures well-formedness of a ONE-FILE listing per task, not of an N-file container returned intact.

DESIGN. Corpus: draw from corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4, stratified into packs of n in {3, 10, 30, 100} files, 25 packs per stratum = 100 packs, every pack under 150K tokens so context exhaustion is not the confound. Include, deliberately, the four unclosed-fence files (md/Brain/20-projects/proj-advox-frontend.md, proj-gearup.md, proj-knowledge.md, proj-skills-registry.md) in at least 10 packs, and the 288 no-trailing-newline files at their natural rate.

TASKS. Three levels of edit locality, 100 packs each: (T1) change one word in one named file; (T2) rename a concept across 3 files; (T3) restructure — merge two sections that live in different files, which is the edit that provokes merge-across.

ARMS, all four, because the whole design decision is which one to ship: (A) return the whole pack; (B) return only the changed files as aider-style whole-file listings; (C) return a unified diff; (D) tool-call edits against the unpacked tree, as the no-container control.

VERIFIERS, all mechanical, no judge: delimiter count == manifest length; dense index; path agreement; per-file sha256; unpack round-trips byte-identical on unchanged files; the intended edit is present; NO unintended file changed. Plus the classification the design emits: clean / edited / reframed / framing-damaged / boundary-destroyed.

n. 100 packs x 3 tasks x 4 arms = 1,200 runs, 2 models minimum (one frontier, one cheap, since 'diff' well-formedness ranges 64.4-99.6% across models and the cheap tail is where containers break).

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, written before the run: (P1) Arm A boundary-intact rate falls below 90% by n=30 and below 60% by n=100. (P2) Arm A on T3 produces boundary destruction in over 20% of runs — the merge-across case. (P3) Arm B boundary-intact exceeds 97% at every n, because each listing is independent and n does not compound. (P4) Arm C has the highest silent-failure rate on the cheap model (apply succeeds, wrong hunk). (P5) Arm D is the ceiling and beats every container arm on correctness. If P3 and P5 both hold, the container is a read format and the write path is arm B — ship it that way. IF P1 IS REFUTED — if a frontier model returns a 100-file pack with all 100 boundaries intact at 90% or better — then the pack CAN be the write surface, edit-mapping becomes O(1) with no fallback, and the 'refuse, never repair' stance in this design is over-cautious and should be relaxed.

SECOND, CHEAPER MEASUREMENT, run first because it costs nothing: re-run the boundary-destruction fixture with the content-derived re-anchoring resolver (the 99.627%-on-blocks mechanism) substituted for line-diff rebase, on the same seed 20260801 fixtures. If it beats 119/120 WRONG on merge-across by a wide margin, the 'unrepairable' finding needs revision. I did not test it and that is the largest known gap in this area.
result.kill_condition: Kill the container — or demote it to a thin wrapper over repomix — if ANY of these fires. (1) Arm A in the measurement above keeps boundaries intact at 90% or better for 100-file packs AND repomix ships an unpack within the build window: then the differentiated part is gone and we are re-implementing a 27,551-star incumbent. (2) The unpack round trip is not 100.00% byte-identical per file on the pinned corpus at every phase gate. Not 99.9%. 1084/1084 is achievable today with a 96 ms packer, so any regression below it is a defect, not a tradeoff. (3) Any shipped unpacker can be induced to write a path outside the target root by content inside a contained file — one instance kills the feature until the run-pinning invariant is proven by a fixture that FAILS against the unfixed reader (LR#68: a green suite on a rare fault is the expected result of running it, not evidence of a fix; my naive-reader test is that fixture and it must stay in CI). (4) The product ships a 'pack my whole vault' affordance. That produces a 25 MB artifact of which 2.79% fits a 200K-token window and which is 110x more expensive than the index that answers the same question — it would be a button that manufactures the disappointment. (5) Six months after launch, unpack invocations are under 5% of pack invocations. That is llm-code-format's 846:1 ratio reproduced inside our own telemetry, and it means we built the round trip for a demand that does not exist; at that point keep pack, delete unpack, and stop paying for the manifest.
result.unverified:
TOKEN COUNTS ARE INFERENCE, NOT MEASUREMENT. No tokenizer was installed and I would not npm install one under the RULE 4 guard, so every token figure (200K fits 2.79% of the container; ~30 average files per 200K budget; the 65K-token index) rests on an assumed 3.6 bytes/token for English markdown. The conclusions are robust across 3.0-4.0 B/tok but the exact percentages are not measured. Tier: inference.

THE GIT DIFF DRIVER'S PORTABILITY IS UNVERIFIED. I proved locally that xfuncname makes the hunk header name the contained file. xfuncname lives in git config, not .gitattributes, so it is per-clone setup, and I did NOT verify whether GitHub's web diff honours it. Assume it does not until someone checks.

BOUNDARY-DESTRUCTION SCENARIOS ARE SYNTHETIC. clean_delete, merge_across, truncate_tail, elide_unchanged and reorder are my constructions, not observed model outputs. Their SHAPE is grounded — aider's shipping prompt shouts about elision in caps, and repomix #71's users report truncation directly ('I sometimes find that the LLM can't see a certain number of lines at the end of the document') — but their relative FREQUENCY in real model returns is unknown, and the frequency is what decides whether refuse-and-localise is a rare annoyance or a constant one. Tier: own-measurement of the algorithm, inference on the failure mix.

THE REPAIR SEARCH IS INCOMPLETE. I tested exactly three repairers: digest prefix/suffix matching, LCP/LCS bracketing, and line-diff opcode rebase. I did NOT test the content-derived re-anchoring mechanism the program already measured at 99.627% on blocks. 'Unrepairable' should be read as 'unrepairable by the three methods tried, including the one the prior prototype used'.

MY EDIT MODEL IS CRUDE. one_line, rewrite_para and heavy are hand-written mutations, and p(edited)=0.5 in the digest-recovery run is arbitrary and almost certainly too high — but it is also the wrong independence assumption in the other direction, since a model destroys a boundary precisely because it was editing across it. The 75.8% exact-recovery figure should be read as an upper bound on the uncorrelated case, not as a forecast.

THE 500 MB SCALE TEST IS SYNTHETIC. It is the pinned corpus replicated 20 times, so it has 20x the cross-file redundancy of a real 500 MB vault. Pack THROUGHPUT (270 MB/s) and boundary-scan time are unaffected by redundancy and stand; any compression ratio derived from it does not.

STAR AND DOWNLOAD COUNTS ARE POINT-IN-TIME. repomix 27,551 stars and 327,053 downloads in 2026-07, gitingest 15,256 stars, llm-code-format 387/month — all read 2026-08-01 and all moving.

WHAT I DID NOT READ. Google's OKF SPEC.md v0.2 (my area does not touch it, but nobody in the program has read it and that remains true). The docs/mdmap/ tree beyond its file listing. gitingest's and stitchmd's source — I verified 'every existing packer is one-way' at primary source for repomix only, and by npm search absence for the rest; treat the other five as search-only.

NO WRITES. Nothing was written to the frontmatter repo. All artifacts live under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-sagnikmitra-Desktop-GitHub-frontmatter/9e5a4a9f-8c4a-4758-b560-0afea2b30447/scratchpad — fmpack2.py (the reference packer), boundary3.py (the hostile fixture), failmodes.py (the failure taxonomy), inject.py (the injection proof), ALL2.fmpack.md (the 25 MB container). The two scratch git repos I created for the storage measurement are in that scratchpad and contain no commits. The pre-existing untracked files in the repo (.scratch-carrier.mjs, .scratch-lossy.mjs, docs/engine/build/__pycache__/, package.json's @anthropic-ai/tokenizer addition) are not mine.

result.area: Markdown as a codebase — what a compiler over a FOLDER enables that per-file tools cannot
result.headline: A folder compiler is justified, but not by the reference graph the plan assumes: over the pinned corpus (corpus_id sha256:3a010b16…c51a4, 1,084 files / 25,548,765 bytes, all sha256 re-verified, 0 mismatches) there are 9,077 wikilinks of which only 25.50% resolve to a file that exists, 624 markdown-syntax file links of which 88.62% resolve, exactly 2 genuine cross-file heading-anchored references of which 0 resolve, and 0 transclusions — so the linker's real jobs are (a) treating `[text](path.md)` as a hard reference and `[[Name]]` as a soft one, which no existing tool does, and (b) making tree→single-document projection lossless, which a fence-state-aware separator does exactly (809 lost block tokens → 0).
result.falsifier: PRE-REGISTERED, before running resolution: "If the pinned corpus contains ≥100 cross-file sub-file references (`[[file#heading]]`, `[[file#^id]]`, `[t](file.md#anchor)`) that RESOLVE to an existing target, then heading/block symbols are load-bearing in the module system and my headline — that the linker's job is not sub-file symbol resolution — is wrong." I looked, three ways. (1) Direct census: 7 fragment-bearing cross-file references exist in 1,084 files; enumerated individually they are 2 real `.md#anchor` links (both to `../printing-press/references/secret-protection.md`, which does not exist), 2 GitHub line links into `.ts#L132`, and 3 parser artifacts/prose syntax examples. Resolving: 0. (2) I checked whether corpus policy was hiding the targets: of 6,762 unresolved wikilinks only 30 (0.33%) have a target that exists on disk but is excluded by the manifest's `exclude_toplevel` rule, measured against the full on-disk trees (10,976 + 1,008 + 1,289 files with no policy applied). Not an artifact. (3) I checked the inverse. A WEAKER falsifier DID fire and I am reporting it against myself: intra-document anchors are common — 392 `[text](#heading)` links, 348 (88.78%) resolving — so a compiler with no heading symbols at all would break 348 working links. The correct claim is therefore narrower than "headings are not symbols": headings are a within-unit coordinate, used 196:1 more often inside a document than across documents, and they must exist in the symbol table but must not be exported.

findings.claim: The pinned corpus reproduces exactly, and the two link syntaxes have opposite semantics in practice. Wikilinks resolve 25.50% of the time; markdown-syntax file links resolve 88.62% of the time. A compiler that treats them identically is wrong in one direction or the other, always.
findings.evidence: census script /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-.../scratchpad/xref_census.py + resolve.py + perroot.py over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. Verification line: 'CORPUS VERIFY: files_read=1084 sha_mismatch=0 missing=0 bytes=25548765' (manifest total_bytes 25548765, total_files 1084). Wikilinks: 9,072 wiki_file + 3 wiki_heading + 2 embed_file = 9,077; resolved to a corpus file 2,315 (25.50%). Markdown links: 622 link_file + 2 link_file_heading = 624; resolved 553 (88.62%). Per root: md 16/86 = 18.6%, knowledge 520/521 = 99.8%, frontmatter 17/17 = 100.0%.

findings.claim: 71.48% of wikilinks point at a note that exists nowhere on disk in any of the three roots — and that is the intended Obsidian authoring idiom, not breakage. This inverts the single load-bearing property of the compiler analogy: in a codebase an unresolved import fails the build; here unresolved outnumbers resolved 2.8:1 by design.
findings.evidence: dangling_diag.py, resolving each wikilink against the FULL on-disk trees (md 10,976 files, knowledge 1,008, frontmatter 1,289; no corpus policy applied): IN_CORPUS 2,315 (25.50%); ON_DISK_BUT_EXCLUDED_BY_CORPUS_POLICY 30 (0.33%); EXISTS_IN_ANOTHER_ROOT 244 (2.69%); GHOST_nowhere_on_disk 6,488 (71.48%). Top ghosts are concept placeholders: 'sgnk-snapshot' ×24, '_COMMUNITY_Test' ×22, 'sgnk-design' ×20, 'concept-llm-as-judge' ×14.

findings.claim: Docusaurus — the largest documentation SSG in the field at 1,513,550 weekly downloads — has independently landed on exactly the split my corpus measurement forces: hard-fail on a broken file link, warn on a broken anchor. This is the strongest external corroboration in this area and it is a default value in shipped code, not an opinion.
findings.evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/docusaurus/main/packages/docusaurus/src/server/configValidation.ts, DEFAULT_CONFIG lines 180-182, verbatim: `onBrokenLinks: 'throw',` / `onBrokenAnchors: 'warn', // TODO Docusaurus v4: change to throw` / `onBrokenMarkdownLinks: undefined,`. Corroborated in packages/docusaurus/src/server/brokenLinks.ts, verbatim comment: `// For v3.x retro-compatibility, we can't throw by default for broken anchors`. npm weekly downloads for @docusaurus/core = 1,513,550 (api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week).

findings.claim: The heading is not a symbol and cannot be made one by fiat: 71.3% of heading INSTANCES in the corpus carry a slug that is not globally unique, and 8.9% of files contain a within-file duplicate slug — which github-slugger resolves POSITIONALLY, so renaming heading #1 silently changes the anchor of heading #2. The corpus contains 534 such positionally-determined anchors.
findings.evidence: concat2.mjs over the pinned corpus using marked 16 as the lexer: 'HEADING SYMBOLS: total headings 29082  distinct slugs 12361'; 'WITHIN-file duplicate slugs: 534 in 96 files (8.9%)'; 'CROSS-file colliding slugs: 4020 (32.5% of distinct)'; 'heading instances whose slug is NOT globally unique: 20741 (71.3%)'. Worst collisions: connections ×382, tldr ×367, key-ideas ×315, capabilities ×197. Mechanism read from local node_modules/github-slugger/index.js, verbatim: `while (own.call(self.occurrences, result)) { self.occurrences[originalSlug]++; result = originalSlug + '-' + self.occurrences[originalSlug] }` — the anchor depends on how many identically-slugged headings preceded it in document order.

findings.claim: THE SHIPPABLE FOLDER-COMPILER RESULT: naive `\n\n` concatenation of the corpus into the founder's 'one mother markdown' silently loses 809 of 291,278 block tokens (0.28%); a fence-state-aware separator makes the join EXACTLY structure-preserving. Delta 0. This is the split/join guarantee the mother-markdown idea needs and it is about fifteen lines of code.
findings.evidence: concat.mjs / concat2.mjs. Naive: 'mother token count: 290469  sum-of-parts token count: 291278  delta: -809 / identical structure: false'. Fence-aware: 'FENCE-AWARE SEPARATOR: mother tokens 291278 vs sum-of-parts 291278 delta 0 identical: true'. Pairwise adjacent-file test: 4 of 1,076 pairs contaminated (0.37%), causes histogram {"odd_fence_count_in_A":4} — a single mechanism. The 4 offending files are md/Brain/20-projects/{proj-advox-frontend,proj-gearup,proj-knowledge,proj-skills-registry}.md; one unclosed fence at part 10 poisons the parse from token index 848 onward.

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO THE RECORD, loudly: the prior census's '21 transclusions in md' is 100% false positives. Every `![[...]]` occurrence in the corpus sits inside an inline code span or fenced block. Real transclusions in 1,084 files / 25.5 MB: ZERO. So does every other include syntax — Quarto `{{< include >}}`, Jekyll `{% include %}`, MkDocs `--8<--`, MyST `.. include::`: all 0.
findings.evidence: xref_census.py with code-span and fence masking: embed_file 2, embed_asset 0, embed_heading 0, embed_block 0, include_quarto 0, include_jekyll 0, include_mkdocs_snippet 0, include_myst_rst 0. `grep -ro '!\[\[' --include='*.md'` over the md repo returns 20 hits in 7 files, all under docs/; inspection shows every one is prose describing the syntax (e.g. docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-25-sgnk-md-b9-authoring-polish.md:29 '### B9T2: embeds / transclusion (`![[Note]]`)'). The 2 that survive masking are also prose mentions. Prior claim being corrected: wf-mdmax-capability-2026-08-01.result.json area 'adjacent-transplant' — 'transclusions 21'.

findings.claim: 'Cross-file reference resolution is MONADIC and therefore rules out a topological scheduler' — the first clause is right, the second is FALSE, and correcting it changes which Build-Systems-à-la-Carte cell MDMAX should occupy. Stratifying the key space makes the task applicative, and every production markdown compiler I read does exactly that.
findings.evidence: Primary source, snowleopard/build (the paper's reference implementation). src/Build/Task/Applicative.hs, verbatim: '-- | Applicative tasks... Dependencies of applicative tasks are known statically, before their execution.' and `dependencies :: Task Applicative k v -> [k]; dependencies task = getConst $ task (\k -> Const [k])`. src/Build/Task/Monad.hs, verbatim: 'Dependencies of monadic tasks can only be discovered dynamically, i.e. during their execution.' src/Build/System.hs, verbatim: `make = topological modTimeRebuilder`, `ninja = topological vtRebuilder`, `shake = suspending vtRebuilder`. The evasion: with keys {parse(f) for each f} ∪ {symbols} ∪ {render(f) for each f}, parse(f) depends on f alone, symbols depends on all parse keys, and render(f) depends on exactly {parse(f), symbols} — all three dependency sets are statically known, i.e. applicative. Sphinx (read→env→write), Docusaurus (collect-all→check-all), Astro (load-all→render) and mdBook (parse SUMMARY→render all) are all this shape.

findings.claim: The genuinely monadic construct in markdown is TRANSCLUSION, not reference resolution — and it occurs zero times. Therefore MDMAX should occupy the NINJA cell (topological scheduler + verifying traces), not the Shake cell, until and unless transclusion ships. The two cells share a rebuilder and differ only in the scheduler, so this is a one-component migration, not a rewrite.
findings.evidence: Transclusion is monadic because the key set to fetch is discovered from a fetched VALUE, recursively, at unbounded depth — the exact shape `Const` cannot extract. Measured occurrences in the pinned corpus: 0 (see the transclusion finding above). Cell definitions read verbatim from snowleopard/build src/Build/System.hs: `ninja = topological rebuilder where rebuilder = vtRebuilder` vs `shake = suspending vtRebuilder`. Both use vtRebuilder; only the scheduler differs.

findings.claim: Quarto — the largest markdown-compiler-with-a-project in production (quarto-dev/quarto-cli, 5,897 stars, created 2020-09-25, pushed 2026-07-31) — occupies MAKE's cell for its symbol table: mtime, not content hash, with no early cutoff. Touching a file rebuilds it. Its execution cache uses a hash, but of a single self-dependency.
findings.evidence: src/project/project-index.ts, readInputTargetIndexIfStillCurrent(), verbatim: `const inputMod = Deno.statSync(inputFile).mtime; const indexMod = Deno.statSync(indexFile).mtime; if (inputMod > indexMod) { inputTargetIndexCacheMetrics.invalidations++; ... return undefined; }`. src/command/render/freeze.ts, verbatim: `function freezeInputHash(input: string) { // Calculate the hash on a content with LF line ending to avoid different hash on different OS (#3599) return md5HashSync(format(Deno.readTextFileSync(input), LF)); }` and the reuse test `if (force || hash === freezeInputHash(source))`. The freeze hash covers the input file only — no cross-file dependency is recorded. Quarto also persists a project symbol table: src/project/project-crossrefs.ts writes `.quarto/xref/INDEX` as `CrossrefIndex = Record<string, Record<string, string>>` mapping input → output basename → shortUuid().

findings.claim: Sphinx is also Make's cell, also mtime, also no early cutoff — and it ships the exact affected-target query MDMAX needs, ONE HOP DEEP, plus the orphan diagnostic. This is the closest thing in the field to a document-tree linker and it is 25 lines.
findings.evidence: sphinx-doc/sphinx sphinx/environment/__init__.py, _has_doc_changed(), verbatim: `new_mtime = _last_modified_time(filename); if new_mtime > mtime: ... return True` then the dependency loop `for dep_path in dependencies[docname]: ... if dep_mtime > mtime: ... return True`. note_dependency docstring verbatim: 'Add *filename* as a dependency of the current document. This means that the document will be rebuilt if this file changes.' get_outdated_files: `if config_changed: added = self.found_docs; return added, changed, removed` — one config change rebuilds everything. The affected-target query, sphinx/builders/__init__.py write(), verbatim: `# add all toctree-containing files that may have changed` / `docnames |= { toc_docname for docname in docnames for toc_docname in env.files_to_rebuild.get(docname, ()) if toc_docname in env.found_docs }`. Orphan check, environment/__init__.py check_consistency(), verbatim warning text: "document isn't included in any toctree".

findings.claim: Astro is the ONLY system of the five I read that implements true content-hash early cutoff, and it is four lines. Shipping it would put MDMAX ahead of both Quarto and Sphinx on the axis that decides warm-edit latency.
findings.evidence: withastro/astro packages/astro/src/content/loaders/glob.ts, verbatim: `const digest = generateDigest(contents); ... if (existingEntry && existingEntry.digest === digest && existingEntry.filePath) { ... return; }`. Contrast mdBook: rust-lang/mdBook crates/mdbook-driver/src/mdbook.rs, `pub fn build(&self)` loops every renderer and calls execute_build_process unconditionally — no staleness check, no cache, no digest anywhere in the build path. npm weekly: astro 4,097,635; fumadocs-mdx 1,031,944; vitepress 722,219; nextra 227,992; @11ty/eleventy 174,111; velite 80,392; contentlayer2 31,158.

findings.claim: MEASURED EARLY-CUTOFF YIELD, and it is a 3.5× correction to the number in the record. On HUMAN edits the exported interface (title + heading slugs + outbound link targets + frontmatter keys) survives 41.54% of revisions in `knowledge` and 19.71% in `md` — not 69.1%. The 69.1% figure is dominated by bulk machine-generated commits where nothing structural could change.
findings.evidence: earlycut.py over git history, 400-commit window, commits with ≤60 changed .md files, modifications only: knowledge {revisions 130, iface_UNCHANGED_pct 41.54, headings 37, links 47, fmkeys 2, title 0}; md {revisions 137, iface_UNCHANGED_pct 19.71, headings 56, links 21, fmkeys 49, title 9}; frontmatter {revisions 8, 0.0%, n too small}. Reconciliation of the divergence with wf-mdmax result.json area 'adjacent-transplant' ('STRUCTURAL interface unchanged ... 250 (69.1%)' of 362 revisions): `git log -n 416 -- '*.md'` on md yields 211 commits; 12 of them change >60 .md files and contribute 5,751 file-revisions — verified by inspection to be 'feat(mirrors): read-only md mirrors of all 53 sibling repos' (2,706 files), 'chore(vault): categorize Skills/ → 13 cats' ×3 (240 each, pure renames), 'feat(share): public note URLs' (742). 0 of my 137 counted revisions are in Mirrors/ or Paste/.

findings.claim: Wagner & Graham (TOPLAS 1998) is real but is NOT 'the single most concerning theoretical result for a markdown compiler' — it is measurably defused by a decision MDMAX has already taken. Inserting text at the top of a file changes 0 of 107,152 block tokens structurally and 107,152 of 107,152 absolute byte offsets. The whole O(n) cost is offset bookkeeping, which vanishes the moment you stop keying on offsets.
findings.evidence: wg2.mjs, prefix-insert probe over 1,052 corpus files ≥200 bytes using marked 16: 'blocks whose (type,raw) changed : 0 (0.0000%)'; 'blocks whose absolute byte offset changed : 107152 (100.0000%)'. Scale context from wg.mjs: 107,212 top-level blocks total, mean 98.9/file, median 42, p99 589, max 7,755 — log2(median)=5.39, so the balanced-tree win at the median file is 42 operations vs 5.4. Quoted claim being corrected: HANDOFF-mdz-markdown-format-2026-07-29.md §3.16, 'This is the single most concerning theoretical result for a markdown compiler.'

findings.claim: Wagner & Graham's escape hatch — 'the interpretation of the yield of a sequence depends on its context' — does apply to markdown, but I measured its live firing rate and it is 0.15%–2.5%, concentrated in ONE mechanism (unclosed fences) that a joiner can fix mechanically. My own first measurement of this was wrong in the flattering direction and I am reporting the correction.
findings.evidence: wg3.mjs, body only (YAML frontmatter stripped), outside fences: '`---` after blank -> thematic break : 2751'; '`---` after text -> SETEXT H2 : 4'; '`===` after text -> SETEXT H1 : 37'. Behaviour verified directly, not assumed: marked.lexer('Some paragraph text\n---') → ["heading2","paragraph"]; with a blank line inserted → ["paragraph","hr","paragraph"]. Unclosed fences: 4 of 1,084 files (0.37%). Lazy continuation lines: 201 in 27 files (2.5% of files). Link reference definitions: 0 in 25,548,765 bytes. MY OWN ERROR, corrected: my first run of this measurement reported 908 setext-H2 traps because it counted the CLOSING `---` of every YAML frontmatter block; 907 of the corpus's 1,084 files have frontmatter, so 904 of those 908 were the same artifact.

findings.claim: A frontmatter-unaware CommonMark parser manufactures 883 phantom headings from the corpus — 3.04% of every heading it reports — because the closing `---` of a YAML block is a setext H2 underline. Any consumer of a folder build that is not told about frontmatter gets a corrupted symbol table, not a degraded one.
findings.evidence: phantom.mjs over the pinned corpus with marked 16: 'files with YAML frontmatter: 907'; 'headings marked sees on the WHOLE file: 29082'; 'headings marked sees with frontmatter STRIPPED: 28199'; 'PHANTOM headings manufactured by frontmatter: 883 (3.04%)'.

findings.claim: METHOD DEFECT that explains part of the seven-different-file-counts problem in §9.1: a census that does not mask fenced and inline code overcounts wikilinks by 11.13% and inline links by 7.59%. Every prior census in this program that reported a link count without stating its masking rule is uncomparable to every other one.
findings.evidence: xper_census.py raw-vs-masked counters over the pinned corpus: wiki_any_RAW 10,087 vs masked 9,077 → 1.1113× (+11.13%); inline_any_RAW 2,055 vs masked 1,910 → 1.0759× (+7.59%). The transclusion finding above is the extreme case of the same defect: 20 raw `![[` matches, 0 real transclusions.

findings.claim: Quarto's cross-reference linker DEGRADES rather than fails — it warns and renders the unresolved label visibly in the output. Combined with Docusaurus's throw-on-links / warn-on-anchors and Sphinx's warn-only, the field's answer to 'what happens when a target moves' is unanimous on one point: never silently drop the reference. The frontmatter repo currently does exactly that, in shipped code.
findings.evidence: quarto-dev/quarto-cli src/resources/filters/crossref/refs.lua, verbatim: `warn("Unable to resolve crossref @" .. label)` followed by `local err = pandoc.Strong({ pandoc.Str("?@" .. label) }); refs:extend({err})` — so a moved target renders as a bold `?@fig-foo` in the document. Same file also emits a CSS-classed span for the deferred case: `local refClasses = pandoc.List({"quarto-unresolved-ref"})`. Contrast, in this repo and already flagged unfixed: HANDOFF-mdz-markdown-format-2026-07-29.md §5.2 records src/modules/graph/presentation/graph-data.ts:132 `if (targetPath === undefined) continue; // unresolved — drop`.

findings.claim: The resolved document graph is CYCLIC and mostly disconnected — 41 strongly-connected components larger than one node covering 284 files (26.2%), and 507 files (46.8%) participating in zero resolved edges. Every compiler concept that presumes a partial order has no analogue here, and Sphinx confirms the field's answer is to detect cycles and ignore them.
findings.evidence: resolve.py over 1,084 nodes / 2,222 distinct resolved file→file edges: 'SCCs with >1 node (cycles): 41  largest=51  nodes_in_cycles=284'; 'orphans(indeg=0)=530  leaves(outdeg=0)=641  isolated=507'; outdeg mean 2.05 / median 0 / max 186 (knowledge.md); indeg mean 2.05 / median 1 / max 40. Prior art, quoted in wf-findings-2026-08-01.md from sphinx/environment/adapters/toctree.py: `logger.warning(__('circular toctree references detected, ignoring: %s <- %s'), ...)` then `raise LookupError('circular reference')`.

findings.claim: The affected-target query — the single capability a folder compiler has that per-file tools cannot — is cheap and its answer is small. Median blast radius 1, mean 8.77, max 54 (5.0% of the corpus). No file in the corpus affects more than 100 others. This is simultaneously the argument FOR the feature (99.1% of a full rebuild is avoidable per edit) and the argument AGAINST it (there is barely any work to avoid).
findings.evidence: resolve.py transitive reverse reachability over the resolved graph: 'AFFECTED-TARGET blast radius (transitive inbound), n=1084: mean=8.77 median=1 p90=32 p99=50 max=54'; 'files whose change affects 0 others: 530 (48.9%)'; 'files whose change affects >100 others: 0'. Cold-build cost for comparison, concat.mjs: 'lex(mother) ms: 1056' for 25,550,923 bytes = 24.2 MB/s with marked 16 in Node v24.6.0, i.e. a full cold lex of the entire corpus is about one second.

findings.claim: PROCESS FINDING: the build-system theory that is supposed to decide this architecture appears in ZERO of the three planning documents. Quarto, Sphinx, mdBook, Docusaurus, Nextra, Contentlayer, Velite, Fumadocs, Build Systems à la Carte, Shake, Salsa, Ninja and Bazel are each mentioned 0 times across docs/engine/PLAN.md (1,748 lines), docs/engine/README.md (789) and docs/mdmax/PLAN.md (501) — except one line in mdmax/PLAN.md §9 that exists only to note Quarto's absence.
findings.evidence: case-insensitive grep counts, format PLAN/README/mdmax: Quarto 0/0/1 (the single hit is docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:383, 'Quarto, XLIFF/ITS, the LoC statement, patents... are in the first and absent from the second'); Sphinx 0/0/0; mdBook 0/0/0; SUMMARY.md 0/0/0; Docusaurus 0/0/0; Nextra 0/0/0; Contentlayer 0/0/0; Velite 0/0/0; Fumadocs 0/0/0; 'Build Systems' 0/0/0; Shake 0/0/0; Salsa 0/0/0; Ninja 0/0/0; Bazel 0/0/0. The scheduler×rebuilder analysis lives only in HANDOFF-mdz-markdown-format-2026-07-29.md §3.16, which is untracked (`?? HANDOFF-mdz-markdown-format-2026-07-29.md` in git status) and opens with 'This section changes the engineering plan and should be read before any compiler work.'

findings.claim: mdBook enforces a one-definition rule over its compilation units and errors on violation — the only system of the five with a genuine ODR. It is also the only one with no incremental machinery whatsoever.
findings.evidence: rust-lang/mdBook crates/mdbook-summary/src/lib.rs, check_for_duplicates(), verbatim: `if !files.insert(location) { bail!(anyhow::anyhow!("Duplicate file in SUMMARY.md: {:?}", location)); }`, with five separate regression tests asserting the message `Duplicate file in SUMMARY.md: "./a.md"`. crates/mdbook-driver/src/mdbook.rs `pub fn build(&self) -> Result<()>` iterates `self.renderers.values()` calling execute_build_process unconditionally; grep for mtime/digest/hash/incremental in that file returns nothing.

findings.claim: Astro's typed cross-collection `reference()` — the field's most advanced document-linker — validates only the collection NAME at schema time and explicitly defers existence checking. So even the strongest typed system in the field does not resolve document references at parse time.
findings.evidence: withastro/astro packages/astro/src/content/runtime.ts, createReference(), verbatim comment inside the transform: `// If it is an object then we're validating later in the build, so we can check the collection at that point.` The only synchronous check is `if (lookup.collection !== collection)` → `Reference to ${collection} invalid. Expected ${collection}. Received ${lookup.collection}.`

negatives: THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST MY OWN AREA: there is no dependency closure worth compiling, and the analogy will make you build machinery for work that does not exist. 507 of 1,084 files (46.8%) participate in zero resolved edges. 530 (48.9%) affect nothing downstream. The maximum transitive blast radius in the entire corpus is 54 files — 5.0% — and the mean is 8.77. Meanwhile a full cold lex of all 25.5 MB is 1,056 ms. A build system's entire value is avoiding work over a large closure; here the closure is tiny and the full build is one second, so incremental machinery is a net cost for a long time. Microsoft says this about its own dependency engine, verbatim from learn.microsoft.com/office/vba/excel/concepts/excel-performance/excel-improving-calculation-performance: 'For some complex workbooks, the time taken to build and maintain the dependency trees needed for Smart Recalculation is larger than the time saved by Smart Recalculation.' Do not build the incremental engine first. Build the symbol table and the affected-target query — those are useful at n=1 — and add rebuilding only when a measured cold build exceeds Microsoft's own published one-second threshold on a real customer tree.

SECOND STRONGEST: the analogy's central invariant is inverted, and importing it would make the product hostile. In a codebase, a name either resolves or the build fails; the unresolved:resolved ratio is ~0. In this corpus it is 2.8:1 in the intended direction — 6,488 wikilinks (71.48%) point at notes that exist nowhere on disk, and every one of them is correct authoring: 'sgnk-snapshot' ×24, 'concept-llm-as-judge' ×14 are Obsidian's non-existent-note idiom, a feature. Docusaurus's default `onBrokenLinks: 'throw'` applied unchanged to this corpus fails the build 6,488 times. The word 'linker' carries an assumption — that resolution failure is an error — that is false for 71% of this corpus's references, and a founder reading 'markdown as a codebase' will hear that assumption without noticing it.

THIRD: it is not a tree and it is not a DAG. 41 strongly-connected components of size >1 cover 284 files (26.2%), the largest containing 51 files. Compilation-unit ordering, topological scheduling, 'compile dependencies first', link order, and the whole vocabulary of separate compilation presume a partial order that this graph does not have. Sphinx's answer after twenty years is to detect the cycle and discard it (`circular toctree references detected, ignoring`) — which is an admission that the concept does not transfer, not an implementation of it.

FOURTH, and the one that cuts against my own headline: the sub-file substrate may be absent BECAUSE no tool checks it, in which case measuring today's corpus predicts the wrong future. The evidence is inside my own numbers — markdown links resolve at 99.8% in the machine-curated `knowledge` root and 18.6% in the hand-authored `md` vault, and Obsidian never errors on a broken `[[x#heading]]` so nobody writes one. If MDMAX ships a checker, authors will write the references the checker validates, and the 0-resolving-cross-file-anchors figure becomes obsolete on the day it ships. My design must therefore not be architecturally unable to add heading symbols later — and I have deliberately made 'headings are a within-unit coordinate, not exported' a DEFAULT rather than a structural exclusion for exactly this reason.

FIFTH: the founder's clearest ask — 'a single markdown connected to hundreds of markdowns' — has zero substrate today. Transclusion instances in 1,084 files: 0. Cross-file heading anchors that resolve: 0. Block-id definitions: 0. This is the feature he most wants and the one the corpus most refuses to justify. Reporting it as validated would be the flattering error this run exists to prevent.
unclaimed: A LOCK FILE FOR A DOCUMENT TREE — a committable, diffable artifact recording, per unit: path, content sha256, interface hash, each resolved outbound edge WITH the target's content sha at link time, and each unresolved name. Nothing in the field produces one. Quarto's `_freeze/` holds execution results keyed by a single self-hash (src/command/render/freeze.ts) and `.quarto/xref/INDEX` holds input→uuid, both internal caches under a scratch dir; Sphinx's `.doctrees/environment.pickle` is an internal pickle; mdBook has no cache at all; Astro's data store is a build artifact. Searches run: registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search across `markdown+build+system`, `markdown+incremental+compiler`, `markdown+workspace+linker`, `markdown+symbol+table`, `markdown+cross-file+references` — top 6 results per query, zero relevant packages in any of them (returns were @mui/system, memfs, imurmurhash, pug-linker, cross-spawn and similar).

HARD vs SOFT REFERENCES AS DISTINCT KINDS. Obsidian treats every reference as soft and never errors; Docusaurus treats every file link as hard and throws (configValidation.ts DEFAULT_CONFIG `onBrokenLinks: 'throw'`). The measured split — `[text](path.md)` resolves 88.62%, `[[Name]]` resolves 25.50% on the same 1,084 files — says both are wrong, and no tool implements the two-tier semantics that number demands.

A FENCE-STATE-AWARE LOSSLESS SPLIT/JOIN over a document tree — the founder's 'mother markdown with breakpoints'. Everything that concatenates markdown today concatenates naively: llms-full.txt, repomix, `cat *.md`. Measured cost of naive on this corpus: 809 block tokens lost, 0.28%. Measured cost of fence-aware: zero. Nobody ships the fence-aware version.

AN AFFECTED-TARGET QUERY AS A USER-FACING SURFACE — 'which documents change if I edit this one, and which references break if I move it'. Sphinx computes exactly this internally (`env.files_to_rebuild`, one hop) and throws it away after the build; no tool exposes it. This is the one capability in my area that is cheap (median answer: 1 file), correct today, and impossible for any per-file tool.

AN ORPHAN / UNREACHABILITY REPORT FOR A NON-SPHINX MARKDOWN TREE. Sphinx's check_consistency() emits "document isn't included in any toctree" and is the only system in the field that does; 530 of 1,084 files in this corpus (48.9%) have zero inbound references and nobody is telling their owner.
result.design:
MDMAX-BUILD: a folder compiler in the NINJA cell, escalating to SHAKE only if transclusion ships.

COMPILATION UNIT = one `.md` file. Non-negotiable: it is the unit the user names, the unit git versions, the unit D4's export guarantee promises, and it is the unit every system in the field chose. mdBook enforces one-file-one-chapter with a hard error (`Duplicate file in SUMMARY.md`); adopt the same one-definition rule for units named in a project index.

MODULE = the file. Its INTERFACE is the tuple (title, ordered list of headings with stable ids, declared block ids, exported frontmatter fields). Its IMPLEMENTATION is the byte range. Splice-only writing (D7) means the implementation is never regenerated; the interface is derived, never authored.

IMPORT — two kinds, because the corpus has two kinds and they behave differently by 63 percentage points of resolution rate:
  HARD `[text](path.md)` and `[text](path.md#anchor)` — checked. Broken = an error surfaced in the editor, matching Docusaurus's shipped default. 88.62% resolve today; 99.8% in curated content.
  SOFT `[[Name]]` — resolve-if-present, NEVER an error, no diagnostic, no red squiggle. 71.48% point at nothing and that is correct authoring. A soft reference that later acquires a target simply starts resolving.
  A NEAR-MISS diagnostic sits on top of the soft tier only: report an unresolved name only when a high-similarity target exists (the prior area hand-verified 95 such cases and measured naive checking at 97% false positives). Never a build failure.

SYMBOL = a file, canonical key = root-relative path. Basename is a convenience alias with a measured 25-instance (1.1% of resolving wikilinks) ambiguity set; on ambiguity the linker reports AMBIGUOUS and refuses, never guesses — the same refuse-don't-guess discipline the block-identity work already established. Headings are NOT exported symbols by default: 71.3% of heading instances have a globally non-unique slug, 8.9% of files contain a within-file duplicate, and github-slugger's disambiguation is positional (`while (occurrences[result]) result = original + '-' + ++occurrences[original]`), so an exported heading name silently changes when an unrelated heading is edited. A heading becomes an exported symbol ONLY when it carries an explicit author-given id. Within a unit, heading anchors remain first-class — 392 intra-document anchors exist and 348 resolve; they are a within-unit coordinate resolved by the unit's own local table.

NAMESPACE = the project root, defined by the presence of a project file, as Quarto's `_quarto.yml` and Sphinx's srcdir do. A root is a hard resolution boundary; 244 cross-root references (2.69% of unresolved wikilinks) exist, so provide an explicit alias declaration rather than implicit cross-root search.

THE LINKER resolves path → unit id, then (unit id, fragment) → block id via the unit's local table, and emits the LOCK FILE: per unit — path, content sha256, interface hash, resolved outbound edges each carrying the target's content sha at link time, and the list of unresolved soft names. The reverse edge map falls out of it. This artifact is the deliverable no one in the field ships, and it is what makes impact preview, move-safety, and a reproducible mother-markdown possible at all.

BUILD OUTPUT — two projections from one declaration, which Sphinx settled twenty years ago (verbatim, from directives.rst: multi-file builders 'treat it as a collection of hyperlinks', single-file builders 'replace it with the content of the documents on the TOC tree'):
  `--index` (default) — links.
  `--inline` — one document, joined with the FENCE-STATE-AWARE SEPARATOR. Measured: naive `\n\n` loses 809 of 291,278 block tokens; fence-aware loses 0. The separator carries the breakpoint marker the founder described, so the split is exact and mechanical, not heuristic.
  `--budget <bytes>` — inline greedily, degrade the remainder to links.

INCREMENTAL — Ninja's cell: topological scheduler over a three-stratum key space {parse(f)} ∪ {symbols} ∪ {render(f)}, verifying-trace rebuilder (content hash, LF-normalized exactly as Quarto's freezeInputHash does, for the same reason). STRATIFY THE GLOBAL KEY BY DURABILITY, per Salsa's backdating: split `symbols` into `titles`, `heading-ids`, `link-targets`, `frontmatter-keys`, because the measured churn is uneven — over 137 md revisions, headings changed 56 times, frontmatter keys 49, links 21, titles 9, so a document that only consults titles survives 93.4% of edits instead of 19.7%. Escalate to Shake's cell (suspending scheduler, same rebuilder — a one-component change) if and when transclusion ships, because transclusion is the one genuinely monadic construct and it has zero instances today.

WHAT SHIPS FIRST, given the negatives: the symbol table, the lock file, the affected-target query, the orphan report, and the fence-aware split/join. All five are useful at cold-build time and none require an incremental engine. Build the rebuilder last, and only after a real customer tree crosses Microsoft's published one-second responsiveness threshold.
result.measurement:
THE EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES THE OPEN QUESTION — is the sub-file reference substrate absent because documents do not need it, or because no tool checks it?

CORPUS: pin a SECOND corpus that is not this author's and is product-shaped and multi-author, at a stated commit per repo, hashed into a new corpus_id by the same script that produced sha256:3a010b16…c51a4. Proposed roots, chosen because each ships a link checker in CI (so they are the treatment group) plus two controls that do not: TREATMENT — quarto-dev/quarto-web/docs, sphinx-doc/sphinx/doc, facebook/docusaurus/website/docs, withastro/docs/src/content/docs. CONTROL — two large public Obsidian vaults and two GitHub wikis with no checker. Target ≥8,000 files so the cross-file anchor count has a usable denominator.

TASKS: run xref_census.py + resolve.py unchanged (same code, same masking rule, same slugger) over both groups.

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, stated now so they can be scored against:
  P1. Cross-file heading-anchored references that RESOLVE will exceed 5% of all internal references in the TREATMENT group. (My corpus: 0.00%.) If P1 holds, the substrate is tool-created and the 'headings are not exported symbols' default must become 'exported on explicit id OR when a checker is enabled'.
  P2. The CONTROL group will reproduce my numbers within ±10 percentage points — wikilink resolution 25.50%, ghost rate 71.48%, resolving cross-file anchors ~0.
  P3. The hard/soft split will replicate: markdown-syntax file links resolve ≥3× more often than wikilinks in every root that contains both.
  P4. Transclusion will remain <0.5% of references in BOTH groups, keeping the Ninja cell correct.
  P5. Naive `\n\n` concatenation will lose >0.1% of block tokens in every root, and the fence-aware separator will lose exactly 0 in every root.

VERIFIERS: rules-based only — counts, resolution rates, token-sequence equality. No judge, no model. Every number re-derived at write time from the script's own output, per LR#60.

n: 4 treatment roots + 4 control roots; ≥8,000 files; per-root numbers reported separately and never pooled without stating the pooling rule (this is the §9.1 failure and it is entirely avoidable).

SECOND, SMALLER MEASUREMENT, cheap and decisive for the build cell: instrument a real editing session against the frontmatter docs tree and record the wall-clock cold build. If it stays under Microsoft's published 'users feel that the system is responding instantly' band (one tenth of a second) or even the one-second band, the incremental engine is dead code and the roadmap slot should go to the lock file instead.
result.kill_condition: Kill the folder-compiler framing — not the symbol table, the FRAMING — if, on a pinned second corpus that is not this author's, BOTH of these hold: (a) resolving cross-file sub-file references stay below 1% of internal references, AND (b) the median transitive affected-target set stays at or below 2 files with a cold full build under one second. Those two together mean there is no separate-compilation problem to solve: what remains is a symbol table and a link checker, which are a week of work and should be named that, not 'a compiler'. Conversely, kill the specific DESIGN above — the Ninja cell and the 'headings are not exported symbols' default — if either (c) transclusion exceeds 0.5% of references in any real customer tree, which makes the task irreducibly monadic and forces the suspending scheduler, or (d) resolving cross-file heading anchors exceed 5% in the treatment group, which makes heading symbols load-bearing and makes my headline wrong. And kill the whole area's credibility claim if the second-corpus run fails to reproduce the hard/soft resolution split (88.62% vs 25.50%) to within 10 percentage points, because that single number is what the two-tier import design rests on.
result.unverified:
WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY, AND ITS REAL TIER.

1. [inference, not measured] The claim that stratifying `symbols` into four durability-graded keys raises the early-cutoff rate from 19.7% to ~93.4% for title-only consumers. I measured the CHURN of each interface component separately (md, 137 revisions: headings 56, fmkeys 49, links 21, title 9) and divided. I did not build the stratified engine and measure it. Per LR#62 this is a projection from live data, not a live result — it is not SIMULATED (no code was replayed) but it is arithmetic on a measurement, not the measurement.

2. [own-measurement, single implementation] Every parse-behaviour number — concatenation loss, phantom headings, setext traps, heading slugs, block counts, the prefix-insert probe — comes from marked 16 (node_modules/marked/lib/marked.esm.js, Node v24.6.0) and one Python regex layer. I did not cross-check against cmark-gfm, micromark, comrak or commonmark.js. A prior area in this program built a 24-configuration differential harness; my numbers were NOT run through it. Treat every parse-derived figure as one-parser-measured. The one behaviour I verified directly rather than assumed is `marked.lexer('Some paragraph text\n---') → ["heading2","paragraph"]`.

3. [own-measurement, single run] The early-cutoff figures (41.54% / 19.71% / 0%) were produced by one run of one script over one commit window with one definition of 'exported interface' that I chose. Per LR#63, one run is an anecdote; I did not run it three times, and I did not sweep the window size or the ≤60-file commit cutoff. The frontmatter figure rests on n=8 and should not be quoted at all.

4. [reconciliation is inference] My explanation of why my 19.71% disagrees with the record's 69.1% — that theirs is dominated by bulk machine commits — is supported by hard numbers (12 commits >60 files contributing 5,751 revisions, inspected and named) but I did not re-run their exact script under their exact selection to confirm the reconciliation closes. The divergence is established; the cause is well-evidenced inference.

5. [not attempted] I did not install or run Quarto, Sphinx, mdBook, Docusaurus or Astro. Every claim about them is from reading source at the default branch on 2026-08-01, not from observing behaviour. In particular I did not confirm that `quarto render` on a project re-renders unfrozen files unconditionally; I inferred it from the absence of any cross-file dependency record in project-index.ts and freeze.ts.

6. [rate-limited, partially blocked] api.github.com rate-limited mid-session and I could not source the token file (`/Users/sagnikmitra/.config/codex-env/tokens.zsh`: operation not permitted, sandbox deny-list). raw.githubusercontent.com worked as a fallback, so no finding is missing because of it, but I stopped short of reading Nextra's `_meta` compiler, Fumadocs' and Velite's loaders, and Sphinx's toctree adapter myself — for those four I am relying on the prior run's primary reads (secondary tier for me).

7. [search-only] The 'nobody ships a document-tree lock file' claim rests on five npm registry search queries returning nothing relevant. GitHub code search was unavailable (needs auth). Absence of evidence at this search depth is weak evidence of absence; a tool could exist under a name none of my five queries reach.

8. [not re-derived] I did not independently re-derive the 99.627% block re-anchoring figure, the 443/655 CommonMark ambiguity count, the 24-renderer carrier matrix, or any of the settled findings I was told not to contradict. I neither confirmed nor challenged them; they sit at secondary tier in this report. The one settled finding my data happens to touch is the link reference definition's invisibility — I can add that it also has ZERO collision risk, because there are 0 link reference definitions in 25,548,765 bytes of real markdown.

9. [my own error, disclosed] My first setext measurement reported 908 traps and was wrong by 904 because it counted YAML frontmatter closers. It is corrected in the findings. I flag it because it is the exact failure mode this run was convened to prevent, it happened to me, and the only thing that caught it was noticing that 908 was suspiciously close to 907 files-with-frontmatter.

result.area: Adversarial verification of "What frontmatter currently misses, against every product it must beat"

verdicts.claim: C1 — frontmatter is structurally single-user: isAllowed compares a login to ONE string, not a list; its only caller is auth-options.ts:82; ActorContext carries no uid/email/org/role.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Every quoted line is byte-exact. src/modules/auth/domain/allowlist.ts:5 is verbatim `export function isAllowed(login: string | undefined, allowed: string): boolean {` and line 9 `return login.trim().toLowerCase() === allowed.trim().toLowerCase();` — scalar parameter, equality compare. `grep -rn isAllowed src/` returns exactly 3 hits: the definition, the import at auth-options.ts:22, and the single call at auth-options.ts:82. src/modules/auth/domain/actor.ts:6-10 is exactly `{login, name, avatarUrl}`. I found TWO pieces of corroborating evidence the researcher did not cite and which strengthen the claim: src/config/env.ts:47 `ALLOWED_GH_LOGIN: z.string().min(1).default("sagnikmitra")` hard-defaults the single identity to a named person, and src/modules/auth/presentation/session.ts synthesizes the dev-bypass actor from that same single string (`login: allowedLogin`). There is no second-identity code path anywhere.

verdicts.claim: C2 — the multi-tenant model exists only as unimplemented Firestore rules; the rules name no comments/suggestions collection; getFirestore appears in exactly one file and firestore() has zero callers.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Substance verified in full, with two precision errors that do not move it. VERIFIED: firestore.rules:45 `memberUids: list<string> (required, <=100 entries)` and :46 `roles: map<uid, "owner"|"editor"|"viewer">`; real enforcement (not just comments) exists at lines 253-291 (`isBoundedList(data.memberUids, 100)`, `data.roles.keys().hasOnly(data.memberUids)`, `allow get: if isVaultMember(vaultId)`). Collections are exactly billing, months, notes, revisions, shares, usage, users, vaults — no comments, no suggestions. `grep -rn "getFirestore|firestore" src/` returns 3 hits, all in src/shared/infrastructure/firebase/client.ts; the only importer of that module anywhere in src/ is firebase-auth-gateway.ts:14, which imports `firebaseAuth`, NOT `firestore` — so `firestore()` at line 38 has zero callers, confirmed. PRECISION ERRORS: (a) there is no helper named `isVaultEditor`; the function at line 176 is `canEditVault`. (b) The claimed grep output is described as yielding "exactly" eight names; my identical grep also emits `match /{document` and `match /databases/{database}/documents`.
verdicts.correction: The membership helper is `canEditVault` (firestore.rules:176), not `isVaultEditor`. The grep yields ten match-blocks, eight of which are collections.

verdicts.claim: C3 — replicating share-writer.ts exactly over the pinned corpus leaves 33/907 (3.64%) byte-identical, 171 throw, 703 change; 33/736 parsed = 4.48% survive.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] I rebuilt the corpus from docs/engine/research/corpus-manifest.json against corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4 — 1084 files read, 0 missing, 0 sha256 mismatches, and all three pinned heads match live (md 02c22ec…, knowledge 464eb66…, frontmatter 798ebbf…). Re-running `matter(c)` then `matter.stringify(parsed.content, {...parsed.data})` under the repo's own gray-matter 4.0.3: has_frontmatter=907, byte_identical=33, gm_threw=171, byte_changed=703 (33+171+703=907), 33/907=3.64%, 33/736=4.48%. Every figure reproduces to the digit. I also confirmed the 502: src/app/api/share/route.ts POST catch returns `status: 502` with `error: "upstream_failure"` for any non-slug error, so a gray-matter throw does surface as 502. ONE PRECISION NOTE: 3.64% is a NO-OP write, not a round trip. The actual publish-then-unpublish round trip I measured is 17/736 = 2.31% (17/907 = 1.87%) byte-identical — i.e. the headline's word "round-trips" names a stricter operation than the number was measured on, and the stricter number is WORSE, so the claim is conservative, not inflated.

verdicts.claim: C4 — a bare YYYY-MM-DD becomes an ISO timestamp in 624 of 736 parseable files (84.78%), and re-parsing the mangled output yields identical JS data (703 stable / 0 differ), so data-level tests stay green.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Same corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. My independent run: bare_date_to_iso=624, parsed=736, 624/736=84.78%; js_stable=703, js_differs=0. The example rows reproduce verbatim, including `Daily/2026-05-26.md -> title=2026-05-26` and `Research/Knowledge Base/AI/12-Factor Agents (Dex Horthy).md -> created=2026-06-27, updated=2026-06-27, mirrored=2026-07-27`. The denominator is correctly stated as parseable files (624/703 changed would be 88.76%, and the claim does not use that number). The green-test corollary is the most important part of this claim and it is exactly right: 0 of 703 mangled files differ in `matter().data`.

verdicts.claim: C5 — the share-writer header comment says it splices the key into the YAML frontmatter, while the body calls matter.stringify, a whole-document re-serialisation; this violates D7 in the one shipped write path.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] src/modules/share/infrastructure/share-writer.ts lines 1-5 read verbatim "reading the current body via the vault reader, splicing the key / into the YAML frontmatter, and committing through commitChanges." Line 26 is verbatim `const next = matter.stringify(parsed.content, data);`, fed by `const data: Record<string, unknown> = { ...(parsed.data as Record<string, unknown>) }` at line 20 — a plain JS object, so the entire YAML map is re-emitted from scratch. The D7 (splice-only) violation is real and the doc-vs-code divergence is real.

verdicts.claim: C6 — the repo's eemeli/yaml path reaches 31.86% safe vs share-writer's 3.64%, so a library swap is not the fix.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The DATA reproduces perfectly — I ported src/modules/preview/presentation/frontmatter.ts exactly (yaml 2.9.0, parseDocument + doc.errors + isMap guard) over the same corpus_id and got yaml_identical=119, yaml_refused=170, yaml_changed=618 (=907), (119+170)/907=31.86%, and with `{lineWidth:0}` 126 → 296/907=32.64%. The CONTRAST is the defect: it counts eemeli's 170 refusals as "safe" while counting gray-matter's throws as failures, and the two sets are the SAME 170 files (I measured the overlap: both_fail=170, gm_threw_but_yaml_parsed=0, yaml_refused_but_gm_ok=0). Under one consistent rule the numbers are 22.38% vs 31.86% (throw/refusal both counted as 'left untouched') or 3.64% vs 13.12% (byte-identical only). The gap is ~9 points, not the ~28 the sentence implies. Worse, for the Publish use case a refusal is not safe at all — it means the note cannot be published (route.ts returns 502), so on those 170 files eemeli is a failed feature, not a preserved file.
verdicts.correction: Apples-to-apples: gray-matter 22.38% vs eemeli 31.86% under 'file left untouched', or 3.64% vs 13.12% under 'published and byte-identical'. Never 3.64% vs 31.86%. The conclusion (splice is required, a swap is not the fix) survives and is in fact better supported by the corrected numbers.

verdicts.claim: C7 — 18.9% of a real Obsidian vault's frontmatter is not valid YAML under any standard parser because of the wikilink idiom; 171 throw in gray-matter/js-yaml and eemeli parses 0 of those 170; the read path degrades silently.

The `md` root — the actual Obsidian vault — is 91 failures / 662 frontmatter files = 13.75%. The `knowledge` root is 79/222 = 35.59%, and the frontmatter repo is 0. Two smaller slips: the same sentence says 171 and then "those 170" without reconciling — I isolated the difference, exactly one file (md/pj.md) parses fine and throws only at stringify, so 170 parse failures + 1 stringify failure = 171 path failures. And the quoted eemeli error prefix is the error CODE, not the printed string: the actual output is `YAMLParseError: Unexpected scalar at node end at line 24, column 49`, not `UNEXPECTED_TOKEN: …`.
verdicts.correction: 13.75% (91/662) of the Obsidian vault's frontmatter fails to parse; 35.59% (79/222) of the knowledge repo's does; 18.74% (170/907) across the pinned corpus. Say which.

verdicts.claim: C8 — Drive v3 Comment is an anchored sidecar with quoted-text fallback, and Docs v1 suggestions are per-text-run and nestable (35 suggestion-bearing schemas, 92 suggestion fields).

verdicts.reason: [primary-read] I curled https://hackmd.io/pricing and parsed the comparison table row by row. All four Collaboration rows are Check in all three columns: Real-time collaboration [CHECK,CHECK,CHECK], Custom note permalink [CHECK,CHECK,CHECK], In-line and page commenting [CHECK,CHECK,CHECK], Suggest edit(New) [CHECK,CHECK,CHECK] — 12 checks, exactly as claimed, all carrying the Phosphor path `M229.66,77.66l-128,128a8,8,0,0,1-11.32,0`. The Free plan's own bullet list independently reads "Unlimited notes 3 invitees 3 custom templates Suggest edit GitHub integration". Two precision errors inside a correct claim: (a) the Full-text search contrast is misdescribed — that row is [MINUS, CHECK, CHECK], i.e. Free carries the Minus and Prime carries the Check, the reverse of what the claim says; the `M128,24A104,104,0,1,0,232` glyph it cites actually sits in the Image storage row's Prime column.
