'.

verdicts.claim: Pre-registered falsifier was genuinely pursued rather than written to fail.
verdicts.reason: Genuinely pursued, on three pieces of evidence. (1) Branch (a) was worked candidate-by-candidate and the researcher DISCLOSED a near-miss that cuts against itself — the inline link title 'wins all four axes' — then killed it on an availability argument (1,838 CommonMark links vs 142,802 paragraphs) that I independently reproduced exactly. (2) The Unicode Tag block entry is a self-correction in the UN-flattering direction ('my initial "GitHub strips it" reading was a harness artifact'), and it is correct: I sent 9 tag characters through api.github.com/markdown and all 9 survived intact, which is precisely the hazard that forced it onto the DO-NOT-USE list. (3) I tested the one gap I could find — the program's other 24/24-invisible carrier, the [//]: # idiom, which the researcher did not usage-test — and it has 0 occurrences in 0 files, as do CriticMarkup (0) and ::: directives (0); {#id} appears 9 times in 4 files and a term-colon deflist once. So no invisible carrier has non-zero live usage and branch (a) would not have fired for any candidate. The falsifier was real and it survived.

new_defects: Denominator swap in C10: the 13.2% rate uses 77,516 as denominator while the claim states the total as 76,118 (10220/76118 = 13.4%). Numerator/denominator mismatch in C9: numerator from a regex line scan (which found 88,097 items, and 88,390 in my replication) but denominator from the AST (88,434). Immaterial at 0.4%, and the AST-native recomputation lands higher (21.94%) so the claim is safe — but the two should be derived from the same pass.

The A1 'one label per document' rule is correct but rests on a refuted justification. Restate it on the real mechanism: any multi-record tail block is non-byte-stable through remark-stringify (blank-line reflow) regardless of label uniqueness — and note that prettier, unlike remark, PRESERVES the multi-record form, so a repo running both will ping-pong the tail block exactly as C7 describes for the title delimiter.

I tested it: 0 occurrences in 0 files, as are CriticMarkup (0) and ::: directives (0); {#id} appears 9 times in 4 files. result.area: Technical foolproofing — what makes a markdown compiler unbreakable
result.headline: The markdown quadratic that will actually take frontmatter down is not in the scanner and is not adversarial: `mdast-util-from-markdown` is quadratic (k≈1.9 at 25k–100k items, 9.5× per 2× above 100k) on a FLAT bullet list — 196,096 ms on 200,000 items / 6.09 MB — while micromark on the identical bytes is linear (k=1.08, 3,835 ms) and Lezer is 460 ms; so the compiler must consume micromark's event stream or Lezer's tree and never build an mdast tree, and the second-biggest hazard is likewise already shipped and non-adversarial — a strictly quadratic (k=2.00, 9,994 ms on 160 KB) wikilink regex running on the browser main thread in `src/modules/vault/infrastructure/markdown-parser.ts:12`.
result.falsifier: PRE-REGISTERED, three clauses. (1) "The flat-list blowup is an artifact of my generator" — if uniform item text, random item text, ordered lists, and blank-line-separated lists do NOT all show the same exponent, the headline is a measurement artifact. I RAN IT (`falsify.mjs`): uniform k=1.82, random-text k=1.85, ordered k=1.99, blank-line-separated k=1.86, and a PARAGRAPH control on the same byte count k=1.08. Content-independent, list-specific. Headline survives. (2) "The blowup is in micromark, so switching AST layer won't help" — if micromark's exponent tracked mdast's, my prescription is wrong. I RAN IT across 4 sizes: micromark 392/842/1,821/3,835 ms for 20k/50k/100k/200k items (k=1.08); mdast 1,129/5,554/20,626/196,096 ms. 51× gap at 200k. Headline survives. (3) "micromark hard-crashes the process, so no in-process design is safe" — the brief asserts remark "CRASHES THE PROCESS on 20 KB of nested blockquotes". I RAN IT at default stack: micromark parsed 20,480 nested `>` in 257 ms, 100,000 in 8,704 ms, and 200,000 in 28,328 ms, never crashing at any depth. Across 45 hostile cases × 5 parsers, micromark and mdast produced ZERO process aborts. The one process abort (rc≠0, V8 fatal trace) was **marked**, not remark. That clause of the brief is REFUTED and I say so. What I did NOT falsify and must flag: mdast DOES SIGABRT (rc=134, "Allocation failed") on an 11.9 MB / 400,001-paragraph file at every `--max-old-space-size` from 256 up to 2048 MB — so an uncatchable abort exists, just from memory rather than stack.

findings.claim: The worst markdown performance hazard is a FLAT bullet list and it lives in the AST builder, not the tokenizer. Flat `- item N with a few words` lists, no nesting: mdast-util-from-markdown 2.0.3 takes 1,129 / 5,554 / 20,626 / 196,096 ms at 20,000 / 50,000 / 100,000 / 200,000 items (6.09 MB), while micromark 4.0.2 on the same files takes 392 / 842 / 1,821 / 3,835 ms and @lezer/markdown 1.6.3 takes 61 / 133 / 241 / 460 ms. mdast is 51.1× slower than micromark at 200k items and its exponent is k=1.82-1.99 over 25k-100k vs micromark k=1.08.
findings.evidence: Harness $TMPDIR/hostile/run-node.mjs + falsify.mjs, node v24.6.0 darwin arm64. Table:  items/bytes/mdast/micromark/lezer/mdit-py = 20000/588890/1129/392/61/338 · 50000/1488890/5554/842/133/831 · 100000/2988890/20626/1821/241/1723 · 200000/6088890/196096/3835/460/3484 (ms). Control (paragraphs, same byte count) mdast k=1.08.

findings.claim: SHIPPED DEFECT: `WIKILINK_RE = /(!?)\[\[([^\]]+)\]\]/g` in src/modules/vault/infrastructure/markdown-parser.ts:12 is exactly quadratic on unclosed `[[` and runs synchronously on the browser main thread for every file in the vault snapshot. 20,000 `[[` (40 KB) = 627.7 ms; 40,000 (80 KB) = 2,487.6 ms; 80,000 (160 KB) = 9,993.8 ms. Successive ratios 3.96× and 4.02× on 2× input ⇒ k = 1.99 and 2.01. No adversary needed: a half-typed Obsidian vault or pasted ASCII art produces this.
findings.evidence: src/modules/vault/infrastructure/markdown-parser.ts line 12: `const WIKILINK_RE = /(!?)\[\[([^\]]+)\]\]/g;` — timed verbatim in scratchpad/threat.mjs. Same file's `stripCode` regexes measured LINEAR (391 KB tail = 0.7 ms), so this is the only ReDoS in that file.

findings.claim: SHIPPED DEFECT: a 336-byte file freezes the browser tab for ~12 seconds. A 9-level YAML alias bomb in frontmatter is parsed by gray-matter/js-yaml in 1.5 ms (aliases become SHARED references, so the in-memory graph is 81 nodes) and survives `structuredClone` in 0.1 ms — but `JSON.stringify` of the same object materialises the full 9^9 tree: 12,076.4 ms, 827 MB RSS, then `RangeError: Invalid string length`. SnapshotProvider.tsx:78 does exactly `localStorage.setItem(SNAPSHOT_CACHE_KEY, JSON.stringify(snapshot))`, and ParsedNote carries `frontmatter: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>` verbatim. The RangeError is caught; the 12 s synchronous freeze is not, and the catch comment reads "quota exceeded / private mode — skip, not fatal". The `yaml` package (eemeli), also a prod dependency, REFUSES the same input at parse time.
findings.evidence: Measured: `gray-matter parse 1.5ms rss=54MB` · `structuredClone(data) 0.1ms` · `JSON.stringify(data) 12076.4ms rss=827MB ERR RangeError: Invalid string length` · `eemeli YAML.parse 5.1ms ERR ReferenceError: Excessive alias count indicates a resource exhaustion attack`. Source: src/modules/vault/presentation/SnapshotProvider.tsx:78; src/modules/vault/domain/note.ts `readonly frontmatter: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>`. Payload = 336 bytes.

findings.claim: SHIPPED DEFECT, and it is a D7 violation in production: `share-writer.ts` calls `matter.stringify(parsed.content, data)`, regenerating YAML from an object on every Share/Unshare. Over the pinned corpus this changes the frontmatter block on 695 of 737 files with frontmatter (94.3%) — 33 byte-identical, 8 trailing-newline-only — while changing the BODY on 0 of 737. The modal damage is a quoting flip: `up: "[[WithArin Stock Market]]"` → `up: '[[WithArin Stock Market]]'`.
findings.evidence: corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. scratchpad/yamldiff.mjs: {"sRun":737,"sIdentical":33,"sTrailingNlOnly":8,"sBodyChanged":0,"sFmChanged":695}. Source: src/modules/share/infrastructure/share-writer.ts — `const next = matter.stringify(parsed.content, data);`

findings.claim: The product ships TWO YAML frontmatter parsers that return DIFFERENT TYPES for the same field on 84.8% of real files. js-yaml (via gray-matter, used by the vault index) and eemeli/yaml (used by the preview/properties panel) both parse 737 of 907 frontmatter blocks successfully, agree on which 737, and disagree on the VALUE in 625 of them (84.8%) across 973 field occurrences. Every single divergence is one class: js-yaml's YAML-1.1 implicit `!!timestamp` returns a JS `Date`, eemeli's YAML-1.2 core schema returns a `string`.
findings.evidence: corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. scratchpad/yamlkind.mjs: {"bothParsed":737,"filesWithValueDiff":625,"topKinds":[{"kind":"Date() vs string()","files":973,"example":"md/Daily/2026-05-26.md :: title: Date(Tue May 26 2026 05:30:00 GMT) vs string(2026-05-26)"}]} — exactly one kind, no others.

findings.claim: Ordinary Obsidian wikilinks in YAML frontmatter break YAML on 170 of 1,084 pinned-corpus files (15.68%). `entities: [[[Anthropic]], [[Google]], ...]` and `related: [[a]], [[b]]` are illegal YAML flow syntax. Both parsers reject identically (js-yaml 170 errors, eemeli 170 errors, 0 files where only one accepts). Reason histogram: 148 "end of the stream or a document separator is expected", 10 "missed comma between flow collection entries", 6 "can not read a block mapping entry", 6 "incomplete explicit mapping pair". markdown-parser.ts catches this and degrades; share-writer.ts does not, so Share is broken on 15.68% of the corpus.
findings.evidence: corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. scratchpad/offsets.mjs throwReasons block. Sample file: md/Research/Knowledge Base/AI/100 Hours Testing Claude Code vs Antigravity.md line 23: `entities: [[[Anthropic]], [[Google]], [[Claude Code]], ...]`. share-writer.ts has no try/catch around `matter(file.content)`.

findings.claim: THE ISOLATION ARCHITECTURE'S TIME GUARD WORKS AND ITS MEMORY GUARD DOES NOT. `worker.terminate()` interrupts a synchronous, non-yielding parse: across 9 hostile shapes (including an infinite `for(;;)` spin) with a 250 ms budget, every worker was reclaimed at 251.3–255.4 ms wall — max overshoot 5.4 ms (2.2%) — and the main thread survived every time, including the case that hard-aborts the process when run bare. But `resourceLimits.maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 32` did NOT stop a worker from reaching heapUsed = 3,382 MB / rss = 4,030 MB parsing an 11.9 MB file to completion (105× over the declared cap), even though the same limit DOES fire `ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY` on a synthetic `array.push(new Array(10000))` loop. Memory containment is pattern-dependent and must not be relied on.

I built a 12-case delimiter table and found gray-matter and the preview's `FM_RE` disagreeing on BOM-first, trailing space after the opening `---`, the `...` YAML document-end closer, unterminated frontmatter, empty frontmatter, a scalar (non-map) block, tabs, a leading blank line, and a `**---**` closer — and gray-matter with a `...` closer either silently eats the whole body or throws "expected a single document in the stream". Hardening the delimiter grammar would have caught zero real bugs. The synthetic table is a REGRESSION FENCE, not a bug list, and should be built only once the real defects (the Date/string divergence, the 15.68% wikilink-YAML rejection, the share-writer regeneration) are fixed.

MY OWN ReDoS HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG WHERE I WAS MOST CONFIDENT, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST AUDIT-BY-INSPECTION. I predicted `stripCode`'s lazy quantifiers — `/```[\s\S]*?```/g` and `` /`[^`]*`/g `` — would be the quadratic, because a lazy quantifier that fails to close restarts. Measured: 32,000 unmatched fences (125 KB) = 0.4 ms; one opening fence + a 391 KB tail = 0.7 ms; 200,000 unmatched backticks = 1.8 ms. All linear. The one that IS quadratic (`WIKILINK_RE`) looks completely innocuous. Reading regexes for danger is not a method; only `eslint-plugin-redos`/`recheck`-style static analysis plus timed scaling sweeps found it. Budget the tool, not the code review.

THE INCREMENTAL-INVALIDATION RESEARCH (Dubroy & Warth SLE 2017, Wagner & Graham TOPLAS 1998) IS THE MOST-CITED HAZARD IN docs/engine/PLAN.md AND IS THE LEAST WORTH BUILDING FOR. The construct it is about — the link reference definition — occurs 0 times in the entire 25.5 MB pinned corpus, and Lezer's existing `TreeFragment.applyChanges` produced a tree identical to a full reparse on 7 of 7 lookahead cases I could construct, including a mid-document open-fence insertion that collapses 37 blocks. Writing a bespoke examined-vs-consumed invalidation rule would be re-deriving something CodeMirror already gets right, for a construct nobody in this corpus uses. Adopt Lezer's incrementality and write a property test that asserts `incremental == full`; do not write the algorithm.

MOST OF THE HOSTILE CORPUS IS DECORATION. Of 45 generated cases, 5 produced a finding that changes a design decision (flat list, indented list, bracket bomb, blockquote depth, YAML alias bomb). The other 40 — bidi controls, lone surrogates, invalid UTF-8, U+0000, BOM-mid-document, zero-width joiners, huge single lines, unclosed fences, unclosed HTML comments, 1 MB fence info strings, 5,000-column tables, 200,000 refdefs, entity runs — all parsed in under 500 ms across every parser with zero crashes. Shipping the corpus as a CI gate is cheap and correct; spending engineering time hardening against those 40 shapes is not. Rank the corpus by demonstrated blast radius and gate only the top tier in pre-merge CI.

THE 99.627% RE-ANCHORING NUMBER IS NOT THE ROBUSTNESS RISK; THE SHINGLE STAGE'S INPUT DISTRIBUTION IS. I could not find a hostile input that makes re-anchoring return a WRONG answer — the failure mode I could measure is cost, not correctness, and cost is bounded by refusal. Effort spent adversarially attacking the anchor's accuracy is likely wasted; effort spent bounding its candidate-set size is not.

result.design:
"SIX SPECIFICATIONS, EACH ANCHORED TO A MEASUREMENT ABOVE.

=== 1. THE HOSTILE CORPUS (built; 51 files, 56 MB, generator at $TMPDIR/hostile/gen.py) ===
Eight families, each a directory with a manifest recording {shape, generator params, expected class}: H1 pathological nesting (blockquote 20k/100k, indented list, emphasis, brackets, link destinations, raw HTML); H2 quadratic shapes (unclosed shortcut refs, `![`×50k, alternating emphasis, unmatched backticks, 5,000-column table, autolink backtrack, 50k-line setext flip, 200k refdefs); H3 amplification (refdef reuse, YAML 9-level alias bomb, 200k entities); H4 unicode (astral, 20k combining marks, Trojan-Source bidi, lone surrogate, invalid UTF-8, U+0000, mixed line separators, BOM mid-document, zero-width, Bengali NFC exclusion); H5 malformed frontmatter (unterminated, tabs, 50k keys + duplicate, `!!python/object/apply`, 10k-deep flow, not-at-byte-0); H6 huge artifacts (10 MB one line, 2M blank lines, no trailing newline); H7 unclosed constructs (fence swallowing 200k lines, nested fence markers, 1 MB unclosed HTML comment, 1 MB info string, 1,000 tabs); H8 combined. PLUS the three families the brief did not name and that produced the biggest numbers: **flat bullet lists at 20k–200k items**, **indented lists** (2.56 MB → micromark 39,611 ms), and **near-duplicate block sets** (the shingle quadratic). Corpus ships as a package with a `run` script emitting a JSON row per (case, parser, status, ms, rss) and a diff against a checked-in baseline.

=== 2. ISOLATION ARCHITECTURE ===
Runs in a worker: parse, AST/tree build, re-anchor, shingle index build/query, projection, YAML frontmatter parse. Runs on the main thread: nothing that touches untrusted document bytes.
What the worker is: a POOL of `worker_threads` workers (size = hardwareConcurrency−1, min 1), each long-lived, each holding at most one document.
TIME budget — enforced, and MEASURED to work: 250 ms for a keystroke reparse, 2,000 ms for a cold open, 10,000 ms for a batch index. On expiry the parent calls `worker.terminate()` and replaces the worker. Measured overshoot across 9 hostile shapes including an infinite spin loop: max 5.4 ms on a 250 ms budget (2.2%). `terminate()` DOES interrupt synchronous non-yielding JS; this is the load-bearing fact and it holds.
MEMORY budget — NOT enforceable by `resourceLimits`, so enforce it by PRECHECK: reject before parsing if bytes > 4 MB, or lines > 200,000, or (bullet-or-ordered list-marker lines) > 20,000. Constants derived from the measured amplification: mdast costs 119–513 MB of heap per MB of input, so a 4 MB cap bounds peak heap at ~2 GB worst case; the flat-list quadratic crosses 20 s at ~100,000 items. `resourceLimits: {maxOldGenerationSizeMb, stackSizeMb: 4}` is still SET — it fires on some allocation patterns and costs nothing — but is documented as best-effort after a worker declared at 32 MB reached heapUsed 3,382 MB. Hard memory containment, if ever needed, is a child process under a container memory limit, not a worker.
HOW FAILURE SURFACES: never as an exception in a route handler. The worker protocol is `{ok: true, tree} | {ok: false, reason: 'BUDGET_TIME'|'BUDGET_BYTES'|'BUDGET_BLOCKS'|'PARSER_THREW'|'WORKER_DIED', at: {line, col}}`. A route handler renders the document as a plain `<pre>` with a banner naming the reason and the offending offset. The editor keeps the last good tree and marks anchors STALE, never LOST. This matters because a `RangeError` from marked becomes a catchable parent `'error'` event and a V8 fatal becomes `'exit' code 1` — both survivable — but only if the parent is written to expect all four.
NOTE ON PARSER CHOICE, and it is the biggest lever here: **do not build an mdast tree.** Consume micromark's event stream (linear, k=1.08 on the shape that costs mdast 196 s) or Lezer's tree (already in memory because CodeMirror 6 is already a dependency). `mdast-util-from-markdown` is the quadratic. If mdast is needed for interop, produce it lazily per-block, never for the whole document.

=== 3. THE OFFSET MODEL, END TO END ===
ONE UNIT: UTF-16 code units, because CodeMirror, Lezer and mdast all use it natively, str.length is free (0 ms over 25.5 MB) and code-point iteration costs 52 ms.
ONE BOUNDARY POLICY: every offset is a UTF-16 index into the document string as read with `Buffer.from(bytes).toString('utf8')` after BOM stripping and WITHOUT any normalisation. An offset may never fall inside a surrogate pair; a range whose start or end would split one is rejected at construction (`assertBoundary`), not silently rounded. This is the direct fix for LR#68's `awk substr` class.
ONE CONVERSION POINT: a single `OffsetMap` object per open document, built once, holding a `Uint32Array` UTF-16→byte prefix table (4 ms and 5.8 MB for the largest corpus file) plus a lazily-built grapheme-boundary bitset (Intl.Segmenter, 28.6 MB/s, ~3.5 ms per 100 KB doc). Every byte offset entering the system (git blob, HTTP Range, Rust/Go impl, LSP negotiated utf-8) and every grapheme index leaving it (iA Writer annotations, external anchor export) goes through that one object. NO other file in the codebase is permitted to call `Buffer.byteLength`, `TextEncoder`, `codePointAt`, `slice` on a document, or an `Intl.Segmenter`; enforced by an eslint no-restricted-syntax rule.
WHY THIS IS NOT OVER-ENGINEERING: only 71 of 1,084 pinned-corpus files (6.55%) have bytes == UTF-16 == code points == graphemes. 93.4% already diverge. A single file diverges by 533,366 units.
TYPE-LEVEL ENFORCEMENT: branded types `U16Offset`, `ByteOffset`, `GraphemeIndex` so the three cannot be mixed without an explicit `OffsetMap` call. This is the cheapest part of the whole design and it is the one that removes the recurring bug.

=== 4. DIFFERENTIAL TESTING REGIME ===
Tier A, blocking, every PR: CommonMark 0.31.2 spec suite (652 examples) against the reference parser. PASS BAR: 652/652. Measured achievable — micromark is already 652/652. Plus the GFM extension suite (tables, task lists, strikethrough, autolinks) at 100%.
Tier B, blocking, every PR: SELF-DIFFERENTIAL. For all 1,084 pinned-corpus files assert (i) micromark block segmentation == Lezer block segmentation modulo a DOCUMENTED start-offset tolerance, (ii) Lezer incremental reparse == Lezer full reparse for every single-character edit at 100 sampled positions per file, (iii) splice round trip is byte-identical. Current measured baseline for (i): 997/1,080 identical (92.31%), 0 type divergences, 80 start-offset + 3 end-offset. ALLOWED DIVERGENCE, documented as a decision: a block start offset may differ by up to the block's leading-whitespace run when both parsers agree on type and end offset. Everything else fails the build. (ii) currently 7/7 on hand-built cases; the sampled sweep is new work.
Tier C, blocking, every PR: the hostile corpus with budgets asserted — every case must return `ok` or a NAMED budget refusal within 2× the budget, and zero cases may abort the process. Regression-guard the timings as a FLOOR-and-ceiling band, never an equality (LR#66).
Tier D, nightly, non-blocking: fuzzing. Since cmark-gfm is not installed here (`which cmark-gfm` → not found), the achievable oracle today is a three-way vote among micromark, markdown-it-py 4.2.0 and Lezer on generated documents, reporting any 2-1 split. A cmark-gfm oracle requires building it and is the one piece of Tier D worth the build step.
EXPLICITLY OUT: marked as a conformance target. It scores 531/652 (81.4%) on CommonMark 0.31.2 and emits raw `<script>` by default. It is a DEGRADATION TARGET in the certificate matrix with its 121 known divergences enumerated, never a correctness oracle.

=== 5. INCREMENTAL PARSE INVALIDATION ===
The rule, stated as a rule: **do not write one. Adopt Lezer's `TreeFragment.applyChanges` and verify it.** Measured sound on 7 of 7 unbounded-lookahead cases (refdef at EOF for shortcut and collapsed refs, setext underline, opening fence, closing fence, duplicate refdef, mid-document open-fence insertion). Dubroy & Warth's examined-vs-consumed requirement is satisfied by Lezer's design; re-deriving it is work with no measured defect to fix, on a construct (link reference definition) that occurs 0 times in the corpus.
What we DO write is the ANCHOR invalidation rule, which is a different thing and is where the cost actually is:
  - An anchor is invalidated when the block's normalized text hash changes. NOT when its offsets change — 80 of the 83 corpus divergences between our two parsers are offset-only.
  - A single 5-character insertion can change the block identity of 37 of 40 blocks (measured: inserting an opening fence). Therefore the anchor layer must handle MASS invalidation as a normal event, not an error: batch-refuse, mark STALE, and re-resolve lazily on view.
  - Semantic (inline-resolved) indexes key on document version, never on block version — a refdef appended at EOF changes block 1's inline children from `[text]` to `[linkReference, text]` with block 1's bytes unchanged.

=== 6. THREAT MODEL OF THE COMPILER ITSELF ===
RE-ANCHOR: the cost, not the correctness, is attackable. Cap the S3 shingle candidate set at 256 (real-corpus average is 186, so this is a 1.4× headroom) and return AMBIGUOUS when exceeded — refusal is already the design's cheap outcome. Cap per-block token count at 4,096 before shingling. Reject the whole S3 stage when block count > 20,000.
SHINGLE INDEX: posting-list length is the attack parameter and k = 2.00 exactly. Cap any posting list at 512 entries (the real corpus's worst is `"how to use:"` at 2,324, so this cap FIRES on real content and that is correct — those shingles carry no discriminating information). Drop shingles whose posting list exceeds the cap from the index entirely, like a stopword list derived at build time.
SPLICE WRITER: forbid `matter.stringify` and every other YAML re-emitter. The share-writer must splice the `public_slug:` line into the existing frontmatter block by offset, or append it, and never round-trip the YAML — measured, the round trip rewrites 94.3% of frontmatter blocks.
YAML: switch the vault path from gray-matter/js-yaml to eemeli/yaml. It refuses the alias bomb at parse (`ReferenceError: Excessive alias count indicates a resource exhaustion attack`) where js-yaml accepts it, and it is YAML 1.2 core so dates stay strings. Then ban `JSON.stringify` on any object derived from document bytes — use `structuredClone`/IndexedDB (0.1 ms on the bomb) rather than localStorage (12,076 ms and a RangeError). Add a depth-and-node-count guard on the parsed frontmatter object regardless.
REGEX: run `eslint-plugin-redos` over the whole repo in CI; it is the tool that finds `WIKILINK_RE` when inspection does not. Replace `WIKILINK_RE` with an index-scan (`indexOf('[[')` then bounded forward scan) rather than a backtracking regex.
AND THE UNGLAMOROUS ONE: 15.68% of the founders' own corpus has YAML-invalid frontmatter because Obsidian wikilinks are not valid YAML flow syntax. Ship a lenient frontmatter pre-pass that quotes bare `[[...]]` runs before handing the block to YAML, and NEVER let a frontmatter parse failure fail a user action — share-writer currently has no try/catch."
result.measurement:
"THE EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES THE ONE OPEN QUESTION. The open question is: does the budget-and-refuse architecture hold on real user documents, or does it refuse so often that it is unusable? Everything above measures the failure side; nothing measures the false-refusal rate.

CORPUS: the pinned corpus (corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4, 1,084 files / 25,548,765 bytes) as the BENIGN arm, plus the 51-file hostile corpus as the MALIGN arm, plus a third arm nobody has built: 500 documents sampled from AI output (the plan's own 68,798-message measurement says AI markdown is a narrow 9-construct dialect and 48.3% of its list items open with a bold run — AI writes long flat lists, which is precisely the shape that costs mdast 196 s).

TASKS, n = 1,635 documents × 4 parser configurations = 6,540 runs:
  T1 cold parse under a 2,000 ms budget → {ok | BUDGET_TIME | BUDGET_BYTES | BUDGET_BLOCKS | THREW | DIED}
  T2 100 single-character edits per document, incremental reparse under a 250 ms budget
  T3 incremental tree vs full tree byte-equality
  T4 splice round trip byte-equality
  T5 anchor resolve for every block after each edit → {resolved | AMBIGUOUS | LOST}

VERIFIERS, all rules-based (LR#25 — cheapest applicable verifier): spec-suite equality, tree equality, byte equality, budget-status enum. No judge, no model call.

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, stated before the run so they can be wrong:
  P1 BENIGN false-refusal rate on T1 ≤ 0.5% (≤ 6 of 1,084). Basis: the corpus's largest file is 1,466,025 bytes, under the 4 MB cap, and its slowest measured mdast parse was well under 2 s.
  P2 MALIGN refusal rate on T1 ≥ 20% (≥ 11 of 51). Basis: 11 hostile cases exceeded 2 s in the run above.
  P3 AI-OUTPUT refusal rate on T1 between 0% and 3%. This is the risky one. If AI documents routinely carry >20,000 list items the precheck fires on the product's most important input class and the byte-cap constants must move.
  P4 T3 incremental==full on 100.0% of 163,500 edits. Basis: 7/7 on hand-built lookahead cases. Any failure is a Lezer soundness bug and a blocking finding.
  P5 T4 splice byte-identity 100.0% by construction. A single failure means the splice writer is not splice-only.
  P6 T2 p99 latency < 50 ms with micromark/Lezer, and > 250 ms (i.e. budget-refused) with mdast on the AI arm. This is the measurement that either confirms or kills the headline's prescription.

COST: ~40 minutes of wall clock on one machine, no model calls, no network. Every number reproducible from the pinned corpus hash.

SECOND EXPERIMENT, cheaper and more urgent: re-run the exact three shipped-defect measurements after the fixes land — WIKILINK_RE scaling (must be k ≤ 1.05 at 80,000 unclosed `[[`), gray-matter removal (js-yaml must appear 0 times in `src/`), and share-writer splice (`sFmChanged` must be 0 of 737, currently 695). These are one-line assertions with existing harnesses."
result.kill_condition:
"KILL THE HEADLINE'S PRESCRIPTION if micromark's event stream turns out to be insufficient to build the anchor layer — i.e. if reconstructing block boundaries and normalized block text from micromark events requires materialising an mdast-equivalent structure anyway, at which point the 51× advantage evaporates and the honest answer is 'use Lezer for everything'. Test: implement `blocksFromEvents(micromark.events(src))` and assert its output equals `fromMarkdown(src).children.map(n => ({type, start, end}))` on all 1,084 corpus files, then time it. If it is within 2× of mdast's time, the prescription is dead.

KILL THE ISOLATION ARCHITECTURE if `worker.terminate()` fails to reclaim the main thread within 2× budget on ANY input, or if the worker pool's structured-clone cost for a tree exceeds the parse cost (measured today: mdast-transfer of docs/engine/PLAN.md was 71.0 ms total against 35.5 ms parse — i.e. the transfer already costs as much as the parse, and on a document 20× larger it may dominate). If transfer dominates, the answer is a SharedArrayBuffer flat-tree encoding, not a worker with a message boundary, and that is a materially different and more expensive design.

KILL THE UTF-16 OFFSET DECISION if the compiler ever needs to be callable from Rust or Python at a hot boundary. UTF-16 is right because CodeMirror, Lezer and mdast are all UTF-16; the moment a second implementation exists in a language that indexes bytes (Rust) or code points (Python), the single-unit rule becomes a per-call conversion and the 4 ms prefix table becomes a per-request cost. Trigger: the first non-JS MDMAX implementation.

KILL THE WHOLE ROBUSTNESS PROGRAM'S PRIORITY if the measured benign false-refusal rate (P1/P3 above) exceeds 3%. At that point budgets are hurting more users than hostile documents are, and the correct move is to raise every cap until refusal is under 0.5% and accept that a determined attacker can hang one worker — which is survivable, because the main thread is not the worker.

AND THE HONEST STOP CONDITION FOR ME: three of my four highest-value findings (the wikilink quadratic, the YAML Date divergence, the share-writer regeneration) are defects in code that already exists, not in a compiler that does not. If the team fixes those three and finds the fourth (the mdast quadratic) does not reproduce on their machine, this entire area was a code review wearing a research costume and should be re-run as one."
result.effort: "HIGH. ~50 tool calls, ~2 hours wall clock, all measurement, zero model calls. Built: a 51-file / 56 MB hostile corpus with a generator ($TMPDIR/hostile/gen.py), a 5-parser × timeout-isolated driver (drive.py, run-node.mjs, run-py.py), and 11 purpose-built measurement scripts in the scratchpad (corpus.mjs, offsets.mjs, yamldiff.mjs, yamlkind.mjs, twoparsers.mjs, spec.mjs, incremental.mjs, incr2.mjs, shingle.mjs, threat.mjs, units.mjs, worker-test.mjs, worker2.mjs, wmem*.mjs, ratio.mjs, falsify.mjs). Ran ~330 parser invocations across 45 hostile cases × 5 parsers plus 6 scaling sweeps, 3 full passes over the 1,084-file pinned corpus, the 652-example CommonMark 0.31.2 spec suite, and 6 npm registry / raw.githubusercontent queries by curl. Primary sources read: the CommonMark 0.31.2 spec text, four files of the repo's own source, the corpus manifest. Corrected myself twice mid-run in the unflattering direction (the 1.13 GB YAML figure was my harness's JSON.stringify, not gray-matter's parse; and my first read of the worker memory limit was wrong in both directions before I pinned it). RULE 4 observed throughout: no commits, no installs, no writes outside $TMPDIR and the scratchpad."
result.unverified:
"WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY, AND ITS REAL TIER.

1. cmark-gfm and pandoc are NOT installed (`which cmark cmark-gfm pandoc` → not found; no Homebrew formula present). So the CVE-2023-22484 comparison to the C reference implementation, and the 'fuzz against cmark-gfm' element of the differential regime, are UNTESTED. Everything I say about that CVE's shape is measured against JS parsers only. Tier: my numbers are own-measurement; the C-reference comparison is search-only.

2. markdown-it 15.0.0 (JS) is not installed. I used markdown-it-py 4.2.0 (the Python port) as its proxy. Its `maxNesting` default is 100 in both, but the timings are Python-vs-JS and NOT comparable as absolute numbers — only the SHAPE of its scaling is transferable. The brief's claim that 'markdown-it does both in ~12 ms' does NOT reproduce in the port: I measured 41.7 ms on 20k blockquotes and 1,370.5 ms on the 5,000-deep indented list. Tier: inference for markdown-it JS, own-measurement for the port.

3. The 12,076 ms JSON.stringify freeze was measured in Node v24.6.0, not in a browser. It is the same V8 and the same `RangeError: Invalid string length` cap, so I believe it transfers, but I did not run it in Chrome. Tier: own-measurement in Node, inference for the browser.

4. `resourceLimits.maxOldGenerationSizeMb` behaviour is measured on ONE configuration (node v24.6.0, darwin arm64, parent at --max-old-space-size=6000). The mechanism by which a 32 MB cap permitted 3,382 MB of heapUsed is NOT explained — I observed it reproducibly across three caps (32/128/512) and I observed the same option firing correctly on a different allocation pattern, but I did not read V8's near-heap-limit callback code. Do not generalise this to Linux or to other Node majors without re-measuring. Tier: own-measurement, mechanism unexplained.

5. My hostile case H1c (5,000-deep indented list, 25 MB) TIMED OUT rather than completing for micromark, mdast and Lezer at a 10 s budget. I extrapolate from the n=100..1600 sweep that it would take hours; I did not run it to completion. Tier: inference.

6. Hostile case H3b's exponent is measured at 9 alias levels only. I deliberately did not test 10 or 11 levels to avoid OOMing the machine. The claim 'a guaranteed OOM at slightly larger payloads' is inference, not measurement.

7. My shingle hostile-case B (a single 3 MB block) was BADLY DESIGNED — I generated tokens with a modulo-97 vocabulary, so it produced only 97 distinct shingles and proved nothing about a genuinely high-entropy giant block. The 127 ms figure is a tokenization cost, not a shingle-set-size result. That sub-experiment should be re-run.

8. The claim that eslint-plugin-redos would have found WIKILINK_RE is UNTESTED — I did not install or run it (RULE 4: no npm install). Tier: inference from the plugin's stated purpose.

9. The 'prior run found a 45-second scan on a 1.49 MB file' and 'two full runs hung on catastrophic regex backtracking' from my brief: I did not locate or re-run those artifacts. My shingle measurement is a plausible mechanism for the 45 s figure, not a reproduction of it. Tier: search-only for the original, own-measurement for my mechanism.

10. Every corpus number in this report cites corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4 and was produced by re-reading all 1,084 files from disk at the manifest's recorded paths (0 missing). I did NOT re-verify the per-file sha256 hashes against the manifest, so I am asserting the file SET, not the file CONTENT, matches the pin. Tier: own-measurement over the pinned path set; content-hash verification not performed."

result.area: Adversarial verification of "The agent-native document — what changes when the primary author is a machine"

verdicts.claim: Claim 3 / the area headline — the OKF benchmark 'found the bundle cost 5.2% MORE tokens', and (in the falsifier) 'the one measurement of the latter that exists (OKF's) is +5.2%, i.e. a loss.'
verdicts.reason: Every verbatim quote checks out against https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scaccogatto/okf-skills/main/benchmark/results.md (5,811 B): the bold line, the 257,602 / 244,805 totals, the 22/26 vs 20/26 row, the n=1 caveat, and the ADR passage are all exact. But the researcher stopped the quote one sentence early. The source's very next sentence reads, verbatim: "At n=1 per cell that total is inside the noise — Q6 alone swings 28% with both arms reading the same two files — so the honest reading is not \"the bundle costs 5% more\" but **\"no measurable cost saving, in either direction.\"**" The author explicitly refuses the exact reading the researcher then builds a headline and a falsifier conclusion on. verdicts.claim: Claim 5 — 'Concurrent multi-agent writing to one document did not happen once. Not rarely — zero times across 1,200 sessions and 724 written files... The concurrency case that a merge contract, CRDT, or block-level identity would exist to serve has an observed frequency of zero.'
verdicts.reason: The measurement reproduces exactly: 724 distinct written file_paths, 29 (4.0%) touched by more than one session, 0 pairs from different sessions inside 60 minutes; markdown 143 files, 5 (3.5%) multi-session, 0 concurrent. But the '0' is entirely an artifact of the one window the researcher chose and did not vary. Re-running the same data at wider windows: 60 min -> 0 files, 6 h -> 8 files, 24 h -> 12, 168 h -> 13. A reader is given an absolute ('frequency of zero') that is actually a knob setting. Second and larger problem: the sample is one developer's agent sessions on one machine, a population that structurally CANNOT exhibit the multi-author concurrency the mechanism exists to serve. D1 makes frontmatter 'Google Docs for markdown' — a multi-user co-editing product — and no co-editing users appear anywhere in this corpus.
verdicts.correction: Correct form: across 1,200 single-user agent sessions, no two sessions wrote the same file within 60 minutes (8 did within 6 hours). This is evidence that AGENT concurrency on one machine is rare; it is not evidence about human co-editing concurrency, which this corpus cannot observe. The design conclusion 'no concurrency protocol' should be justified on the isolation-plus-409 prior art of claim 6, not on this number.

verdicts.claim: Claim 1 — OKF v0.2 'already specifies the entire agent-native document feature set this area was briefed to design... a live, versioned, conformance-tested Apache-2.0 spec that this program has now decided against three times without reading', with the implication (headline) that 'that market is served'.
verdicts.reason: The inventory is exact and I confirmed every element by primary read of the canonical 37,544-byte SPEC.md: §5.1 sources with resource/id/title/author/usage_count/last_modified plus a usage_window sibling; §5.2 generated{by,at} and verified[{by,at}]; §5.3 the three tiers verbatim; §5.4 status; §5.5 stale_after; §10's attestation sentence word-for-word; §11's 'MUST NOT reject a bundle because of: ... (2) OKF's UNIT is a bundle, not a document: §3, verbatim, 'A bundle is a directory tree of markdown files', with reserved index.md/log.md. frontmatter's unit is one collaborative document. (3) OKF buys the feature set with a carrier this program has already ruled out — §11 conformance rule 1 requires 'Every non-reserved `.md` file in the tree contains a parseable YAML frontmatter block', and the settled finding in this brief is that frontmatter is VISIBLE in 23 of 24 renderer configs. OKF took the branch D6 forbids.
verdicts.correction: OKF has shipped the agent-native FIELD VOCABULARY for a bundle, by mandating a carrier that fails the degradation test MDMAX is built around. 'That market is served' does not follow for a single-document product. The honest read is stronger for the design, not weaker: MDMAX should adopt OKF's vocabulary and check it, which is exactly what design item 4 proposes.

verdicts.claim: The pre-registered falsifier was a genuine attempt to break the researcher's own headline, not one written knowing it would not fire.

verdicts.claim: Claim 3 — corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… DOES NOT REPRODUCE under any of 64 serializations of the manifest's own (path, sha256) list, and has no derivation script, violating the plan's own P2.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] It reproduces exactly on the first try under a natural serialization the researcher's 64-variant sweep evidently never combined. Recipe: for every root, build `root + '/' + path`, pair it with the file's sha256 as `path:sha256`, sort the list, join with '\n', NO trailing newline, sha256 the UTF-8 bytes. Result: `3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4` == declared corpus_id, over n=1084 entries. My sweep of 208 variants found it under two labels ('sorted_rootpath|colon|root=True|term=False' and 'sorted_rootslashpath|colon|root=True|term=False'). The manifest's own totals also reproduce: summed across roots = 1084 files / 25,548,765 bytes, matching declared total_files and total_bytes exactly. And the recipe is stated in prose in the document the researcher read — docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:29 verbatim: 'That id is a hash over the sorted `(path, sha256)` list of 1,084 files / 25,548,765 bytes across `md`, `knowledge` and `frontmatter`.'
verdicts.correction: The sub-claim 'no derivation script exists' is CONFIRMED — `grep -rn 'corpus_id|corpus-manifest' --include='*.py' --include='*.mjs' --include='*.js' --include='*.sh' --include='*.ts'` over the repo returns nothing, so P2 ('No headline without a committed derivation script and its captured output') is genuinely unmet for this artifact. But the headline 'DOES NOT REPRODUCE' is false, and it is load-bearing: it is the compounding clause of N8 ('even with the manifest in hand, the id cannot be recomputed') and it is the exact defect class — an absence proven by an incomplete search — that this run was convened to catch.

verdicts.claim: Claim 4 — 'THE CORPUS THE FLAGSHIP NUMBER RESTS ON IS APPEND-DOMINATED': over the md root at pinned HEAD 02c22ec4, 4,948 of 5,715 .md file-revision pairs (86.6%) delete zero lines; delete/add ratio 0.1861.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The arithmetic essentially replicates — my independent numstat pass with -M rename normalization gives pairs=5,708, zero-del=4,940 (86.5%), pure-del=408 (7.1%), <=2 del=305 (5.3%), >2 del=55 (1.0%), ratio=0.1862 (researcher: 5,715 / 4,948 / 86.6% / 408 / 305 / 54 / 0.1861). But the claim is a statement about 'the corpus the flagship number rests on', and it is computed under a selection that contradicts that corpus's own definition. The manifest's `policy` block excludes top-level `Mirrors` and `Paste` plus nine directory names and all dot-directories. Applying the manifest's OWN policy to the same git history: pairs=2,229, zero-del=1,497 (67.2%), pure-del=388 (17.4%), >2 del=39 (1.7%), ratio=0.4297. That is 3,479 of 5,708 pairs (61%) drawn from directories the pinned corpus explicitly excludes — overwhelmingly the md HEAD commit itself, `02c22ec4 feat(mirrors): read-only md mirrors of all 53 sibling repos`, which is a pure bulk creation event.
verdicts.correction: Under the pinned corpus's own exclusion policy the zero-deletion rate is 67.2%, not 86.6%, and the delete/add ratio is 0.4297, not 0.1861 — 2.3x higher. The researcher disclosed the selection difference (Rule 3 honoured) but then drew a conclusion about the pinned corpus from it anyway.

verdicts.claim: Claim 5 — restricting to multi-revision files gives 1,399 revision pairs, of which 676 (48.3%) still delete zero lines, 408 (29.2%) pure deletions, 284 (20.3%) <=2, 31 (2.2%) substantive rewrites.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The denominator is wrong and the error is provable from the researcher's own buckets. 676+408+284+31 = 1,399 exactly — so the '1,399 revision pairs' population is file-revision RECORDS on multi-revision files, and the 642 file CREATIONS were dropped into the zero-deletion bucket. A creation has no predecessor revision and cannot be a member of a 'consecutive revision pair' population by construction. The correct pair count is Sum(revisions-1) = 770. On those 770 genuine pairs (each file's oldest revision excluded): zero-del=47 (6.1%), pure-del=408 (53.0%), <=2 del=284 (36.9%), >2 del=31 (4.0%). My 408 / 284 / 31 match the researcher's 408 / 284 / 31 EXACTLY — only the zero-deletion count differs (47 vs 676), which is the 629 creations. Under the manifest's exclusion policy: 748 pairs, zero-del 46 (6.1%), unchanged in shape.
verdicts.correction: On genuine consecutive revision pairs the md corpus is DELETION-dominated (53.0% pure deletions), not append-dominated. The zero-deletion rate is 6.1%, not 48.3% — an 8x error, in the direction that flatters the researcher's own headline. This is the report's single largest defect.

verdicts.claim: Claim 6 — 'THE S1 RATE AND THE APPEND RATE AGREEING TO 0.4pp IS NOT A COINCIDENCE': S1 exact-hash resolves 87.0% and my measured zero-deletion rate on the same root is 86.6%, so the flagship 99.627% averages over a stratum where nothing was edited.

Under the pinned corpus's own exclusion policy the file-revision zero-deletion rate is 67.2%; on genuine consecutive revision pairs it is 6.1%. Neither is 87.0%, and the gap is 20pp and 81pp respectively, not 0.4pp. The two quantities were also never comparable: S1's 87.0% is a per-BLOCK-VERSION resolution rate over 41,642 block-versions, the 86.6% is a per-FILE-REVISION edit-shape rate over a population 61% of which the corpus excludes. verdicts.claim: Claim 7 — §1.1a's 12.9%/2.66% multi-candidate stratum blows through kill-gate K3 at 5.3x its 0.5% threshold, and the headline averages it away.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Both quotes are verbatim and correctly located (docs/engine/PLAN.md:140-141; docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:439 'K3 | the range resolver's false-match rate is above ~0.5% hand-audited'). But 'the headline averages it away' is refuted by the source: the 2.66% is stated in bold, and the very next sentence is the plan's response to it — 'Hence DELTA: within 0.05 after context weighting, **return AMBIGUOUS**. Removing that refusal produced 183 extra false matches.' It is the stated justification for the refusal, not a suppressed residual. Arithmetically the 2.66% also cannot be the recommended configuration's rate: the plan reports 0.050% false on anchorable blocks and 'All 14 false matches on anchorable blocks were hand-audited, not sampled' (0.00050 x 28,170 = 14.085). 12.9% of the 32,919 surviving block-versions is 4,247; 2.66% of that is 113 false matches, 8x more than the 14 the plan hand-audits in total. Fourteen total false matches bounds the multi-candidate stratum at <= 14/4,247 = 0.330% (or <= 14/3,634 = 0.385% on the anchorable denominator) — below K3.
verdicts.correction: There IS a real finding here and the researcher missed it: §1.1a is internally inconsistent. 94.94 + 2.66 = 97.60 leaves a 2.40% refusal share, implying DELTA is applied, yet 2.66% of the stratum is ~113 false matches against a hand-audited total of 14. One of those two numbers in §1.1a is wrong. That is worth reporting; 'K3 is already blown' is not, because it requires believing one of them and ignoring the other.

killed: Claim 3 — 'corpus_id DOES NOT REPRODUCE'. It reproduces exactly: sha256 of '\n'.join(sorted('<root>/<path>:<sha256>')), no trailing newline, n=1084 -> 3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. The manifest's total_files (1084) and total_bytes (25,548,765) also reproduce from its own per-root lists. The recipe is stated in prose at docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:29, in the document being audited.

Claim 5 — '1,399 revision pairs, 676 (48.3%) delete zero lines'. 642 of those 1,399 are file CREATIONS with no predecessor revision. True pair count = Sum(revisions-1) = 770; zero-deletion on genuine pairs = 47 (6.1%), pure deletions = 408 (53.0%). The researcher's own 408/284/31 buckets match mine exactly on the 770-pair population, which proves the 629 creations were added only to the zero-deletion bucket. An 8x error in the flattering direction.

Claim 6 — 'the S1 rate and the append rate agreeing to 0.4pp is not a coincidence'. The coincidence dissolves under either correction: 67.2% under the pinned corpus's own exclusion policy, 6.1% on genuine consecutive revision pairs. Neither is 87.0%. The two quantities were never comparable — per-block-version resolution rate vs per-file-revision edit shape.

Claim 8 — 'the true figure is 12/18 = 66.7%, not 100%'. An artifact of matching /headline/i on one JSON field plus killed.startswith('HEADLINE'). Extending the search to the reason/correction fields the report itself quotes from gives 18/18. Four of the five 'never adjudicated' areas carry explicit word-'headline' kills, and PLAN.md:285's two cited examples come from two of those five. N7's evidentiary base goes with it.

Claim 7's 'the headline averages it away' — the plan states the 2.66% stratum in bold and immediately answers it with DELTA; and 14 hand-audited false matches over 28,170 anchorable blocks bounds the stratum at <=0.385%, below K3's 0.5%. A rejected configuration's number was presented as the shipped one.

The N3 ranking (position 3, 'probability MEDIUM-HIGH because 86.6% append-dominance is measured, not speculated') — the measurement that elevates it does not hold on the corpus it is a claim about. N3 may still be right for the reasons the plan itself gives in §9.3 and §9.5; it is not right for the reason offered here.
new_defects: Claim 4's population contradicts the pinned corpus's own `policy` block. The manifest excludes top-level `Mirrors` and `Paste`; 3,479 of 5,708 md pairs (61%) come from excluded directories, overwhelmingly the md HEAD commit 02c22ec4 'feat(mirrors): read-only md mirrors of all 53 sibling repos'. Applying the manifest's policy: 67.2% zero-deletion, ratio 0.4297 — vs the reported 86.6% / 0.1861. The single most obvious check for a claim about the pinned corpus was not run.

Claim 5 is a rate confused with a population: 642 file creations counted as members of a 'consecutive revision pair' corpus. Exactly the 'ratio without its denominator' defect this run was told to hunt.

Claim 3 is an absence proven by an incomplete search and stated as a fact ('MATCH: NONE', 'variants tried: 64'). My 208-variant sweep found it, and the recipe was already written in prose in the plan.

Claim 8 is one string-matching rule presented as an exhaustive adjudication census, on an artifact the report had already parsed. The report's own derived counts (193 killed / 188 new defects) reproduce exactly — so the parse was sound and only the classifier was brittle, which is what makes the error avoidable.

REAL AND UNREPORTED: docs/engine/PLAN.md §1.1a is internally inconsistent. 12.9% of 32,919 block-versions is 4,247; 2.66% of that is ~113 false matches; but the same section states 0.050% false on 28,170 anchorable blocks and 'All 14 false matches on anchorable blocks were hand-audited, not sampled'. 113 vs 14. result.area: Live competitive sweep — what shipped in the last 120 days (2026-04-03 → 2026-08-01), plus a direct read of OKF SPEC.md v0.2
result.headline: The threat is not OKF — it is inkeep/OpenKnowledge (GPL-3.0, 3,239 stars, 14,790 npm dl/wk), which on 2026-07-30 merged a content-derived comment-anchoring system for markdown (exact quote + auto-widened prefix/suffix context, orphan-rather-than-guess, plus bracket-recovery for edited passages) that reached the npm BETA channel at 0.46.0-beta.32 on 2026-08-01T02:38:33Z but is absent from stable 0.45.4; MDMAX §4.1 is therefore no longer an unclaimed capability, only an unclaimed *measured* one, while OKF v0.2 — read in full — contains no block identity, no range anchoring, no splice guarantee and no runtime, and its actual tooling adoption is 52 downloads/week.
result.falsifier: PRE-REGISTERED, before concluding: "My headline is wrong if OpenKnowledge's comment anchoring is (a) not actually content-derived — i.e. it stores plain offsets and re-finds by position — or (b) exists only as an unmerged branch / merged-but-unpublished code, so no user can run it." I looked for both. (a) FAILED to falsify: I read both implementations verbatim (`packages/server/src/comments/anchor.ts`, sha256 9f65280c…, and `packages/app/src/comments/anchor-search.ts`, sha256 754cfe99…). The server file's own header is "Content-addressed anchoring — 'remember the words, not the position.' The durable record is the exact quoted text plus widened context; the position is a fast-path hint only." It is content-derived. (b) PARTIALLY FIRED, and it changed my headline. I downloaded both published tarballs and grepped them: `@inkeep/open-knowledge@0.45.4` (dist-tag `latest`, published 2026-07-31T22:56:04.451Z) contains ZERO files matching "Add Comment", "Send to AI" or "orphaned"; `@inkeep/open-knowledge@0.46.0-beta.32` (published 2026-08-01T02:38:33.569Z) contains all three plus the minified anchor shape `exact:i,prefix:a,suffix:o` and `status:"orphaned"` and `rewritten`. So it is real and published, but BETA-ONLY as of this measurement. I rewrote the headline from "shipped" to "reached beta, absent from stable" accordingly. Second falsifier, on the OKF half: "my claim that OKF does not contest MDMAX's spine is wrong if SPEC.md v0.2 defines identity for text ranges or blocks." I read all 37,544 bytes. It does not: the only keyed identity in the spec is `sources[].id`, a join key for footnote attribution inside frontmatter (§5.1). Not falsified.

findings.claim: OKF SPEC.md v0.2 contains NO block identity, NO range anchoring, NO splice/round-trip guarantee and NO degradation story. The only keyed identity it defines is `sources[].id`, a join key for markdown footnotes pointing into a frontmatter provenance list. The plan's worry that "its §5.1 already ships keyed identity with our own rationale" is true only in the narrow sense that the RATIONALE matches; the OBJECT keyed is a bibliography entry, not a piece of document text. OKF does not contest MDMAX's spine at any point.
findings.evidence: Read in full: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/main/okf/SPEC.md — 37,544 bytes, sha256:5a3311d270bebb16d558010e75064f5b75323f284992641732b1c8097511f948. §5.1 verbatim: "The footnote label is the join key into `sources`; consumers resolve attribution through the matching entry, not by parsing the footnote prose. Labels are keyed rather than positional (`sources[0]`) because agents constantly rewrite these documents: a positional index misattributes silently the moment the list is reordered, whereas a stable `id` survives reordering." Grep of the full spec for block/range/anchor/offset identity: absent.

findings.claim: CORRECTION to the settled record: OKF v0.2 is NOT "acquiring a runtime". It specifies a runtime *interface* (`executor.resource`, `executor.receipt`, `attester.resource`) and then explicitly defers everything that would make it a runtime. Its own README markets the opposite. This materially lowers the OKF threat level and should change §13.5's framing.
findings.evidence: SPEC.md §10 opening: "OKF records the computation and the means to check it; it does not execute anything itself." §12 "Considered and deferred": "The full runtime protocol: receipt and verdict wire formats, and the attestation lifecycle around a run. The attester ABI, portability, and sandboxing… Attestation caching." §1 Non-goals: "Specifying a packaging or invocation standard for the code an executor or attester points at. OKF fixes the interface, not the packaging." okf/README.md: "…so an agent-maintained corpus stays trustable **without any bespoke runtime**."

findings.claim: OKF's real-world runtime adoption is negligible, and the ecosystem's apparent momentum is GitHub-star momentum from Claude-Code skill wrappers, not usage. One of the most-linked OKF quickstarts installs a package that does not exist.

findings.claim: THE FINDING THAT MATTERS. inkeep/OpenKnowledge merged a content-derived comment-anchoring system for markdown on 2026-07-30 whose design is convergent with MDMAX §4.1 to an uncomfortable degree — exact quote as the durable record, prefix/suffix context widened AT CREATE TIME until the triple is unique, context-scored disambiguation of repeated quotes, and explicit refusal (`status:'orphaned'`) rather than a guess. It cites Hypothesis and Semiont as priors. It was NOT known to this program (grep of docs/ for "inkeep" returns nothing).
findings.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/inkeep/open-knowledge/main/packages/server/src/comments/anchor.ts (261 lines, sha256:9f65280cbda7d2a423a889af58f4e0989ade68b2d1674d29b8dd2492b7823acc). Header verbatim: "Content-addressed anchoring — 'remember the words, not the position.' The durable record is the exact quoted text plus widened context; the position is a fast-path hint only. Re-find runs an ordered fallback and fails SAFE (flags orphaned) rather than ever guessing a wrong location. No fuzzy matching." Also: "const DEFAULT_CONTEXT_LEN = 32;" with the comment "Hypothesis uses 32 chars of context for web text; a reasonable markdown default." And `assertAnchorConsistent` header: "Semiont 'reconcile at write time'". PR: github.com/inkeep/open-knowledge/pull/926 "Comments feature (#2944)", closed 2026-07-30.

findings.claim: OpenKnowledge ships a capability MDMAX's published scheme does not describe: recovering a passage whose TEXT ITSELF changed, by bracketing it between its unchanged surroundings, with a bounded growth ceiling and refusal on ambiguity. This is the "someone edited the words I commented on" case, which in frontmatter is the single most common comment lifecycle event.
findings.evidence: anchor-search.ts `findBetweenBrackets`: "Both brackets must match exactly once and in order; whatever sits between them is the passage. Ambiguity or runaway growth declines rather than guesses." Constants: `const MAX_REWRITE_GROWTH = 4; const REWRITE_GROWTH_FLOOR = 64;` and `const ceiling = Math.max(quote.length * MAX_REWRITE_GROWTH, quote.length + REWRITE_GROWTH_FLOOR);`. Result type carries `rewritten?: boolean` meaning "The quote itself changed — the range was recovered from its surrounding context, so the stored `exact` is stale and must be re-captured."

findings.claim: OpenKnowledge's anchoring makes the SAME mistake MDMAX measured as catastrophic — a nearest-position tiebreak — but only after two rounds of refusal, and it has published no false-positive rate at all. This is MDMAX's real differentiator and it is narrower than the plan assumes: not "we have anchoring and they don't", but "we have a fuzzy S3 tier and a measured false rate; they have neither".
findings.evidence: anchor-search.ts, final fallback: "Context couldn't separate them — take the one nearest the last known position… `const hint = context?.start;` … `const dist = Math.abs(hit.start - hint);`". Compare docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.1: "Every position-based tiebreak made it dramatically worse — content-hash plus nearest-position goes 0.00% → 22.20% false." OpenKnowledge publishes no correct/false/refusal numbers; MDMAX publishes 99.627% / 0.050% / 0.323%. Conversely MDMAX's S3 (3-gram shingles, jaccard >= 0.20) has no counterpart: anchor.ts states "No fuzzy matching: the quote is matched exactly; context only disambiguates between multiple exact hits."

findings.claim: OpenKnowledge independently arrived at D2 — comments live OUTSIDE the file, in a machine-local JSON sidecar, never committed. This is convergent validation of a decision the plan reached by argument. But their comments are explicitly SINGLE-PLAYER (a queue for your own agent), which is precisely the slot frontmatter's D1/D3 multiplayer review loop still owns.
findings.evidence: packages/server/src/comments/thread-store.ts header: "Durable comment-thread storage — `<localDir>/comments/`, machine-local and never committed… `<threadId>.meta.json` the whole thread." .changeset/comments-v1.md closing line verbatim: "Comments are stored per-machine next to your content and are not committed — a comment here is a note to your own agent, not a message to a teammate."

findings.claim: markdown-it 15.0.0 shipped 2026-07-30 — two days before this gate — and it hands MDMAX's two surviving carriers a first-class token API with SOURCE LINE RANGES, in a 27,323,922 downloads/week parser, while leaving rendered output byte-identical. This is a direct, unclaimed gift to the splice writer, and the program does not know about it (grep of docs/ for "reference_definition" and "strip_references": zero hits).
findings.evidence:
markdown-it CHANGELOG.md [15.0.0] - 2026-07-30, Added: "Added `reference_definition` tokens. They remain stripped by default for backwards compatibility, #1055." and "Added reference labels to link/image tokens, #938." I ran it (tarball extracted to $TMPDIR, ESM browser bundle, no install into any repo). Default: `m.parse(src).filter(t=>t.type==='reference_definition').length === 0`. After `m.core.ruler.disable('strip_references')`: tokens appear as `RD> {"content":"","meta":{"label":"FM-ANCHOR-1"},"map":[2,3],"markup":"","info":"","attrs":null}` and `RD> {"content":"","meta":{"label":"//"},"map":[4,5],…}`. Render is IDENTICAL in both modes: `"

Hello world.

Second para with a ref link.

\n"`. New core rule list now includes `strip_references=true`.

findings.claim: The pinned corpus is already 73.6% conformant with OKF v0.2's only hard requirement, with zero code written — which makes "OKF as a certificate column" nearly free, and correspondingly makes it a weak moat for anyone. It also already uses two of v0.2's new frontmatter families under different semantics.

Measured: 899/1084 (82.93%) carry a YAML frontmatter block; 798/1084 (73.616%) carry a non-empty `type` (OKF §11 conformance rule 2); 23 files bear a reserved OKF filename (index.md/log.md). `status` appears in 810 files, `sources` in 370, `content_hash` in 365. `type` values present: synthesis 365, skill 184, workflow 184, concept 33, entity 13, map 13.

findings.claim: mdbase (the "typed markdown collections spec" previously named) did not stand still — it is now a 17-chapter spec with a durable runtime profile, a CEL query profile, RFC 6901 JSON Pointer field references, and an executable interoperability testbed. It also explicitly maps to Obsidian Bases, which answers that competitor line too. It is NOT in MDMAX's slot — it is a records/query/workflow database over markdown, with no block identity and no splice guarantee — but its conformance machinery is far ahead of ours.

findings.claim: Obsidian tightened its IN-FILE comment carrier on 2026-07-30, which is a live datapoint against ever putting comments in the .md: the `%%…%%` syntax is Obsidian-only, its parsing rules are still changing seven years in, and it produces visible junk in every other renderer. D2 is corroborated by a competitor's changelog, not just by argument.
findings.evidence: obsidian.md/changelog/2026-07-30-desktop-v1.13.4/ verbatim: "Reading mode no longer interprets %%%% as a non-terminated comment. Comments are always fenced with exactly two % characters." Obsidian desktop-releases.json latestVersion = 1.13.4, released 2026-07-30.

findings.claim: No library competitor emerged on npm for any of MDMAX's six capabilities in the window. Every new package in the adjacent lanes is a context packer with no measurable adoption. The competitive pressure came from an application, not a library — which is a warning about how this sweep was scoped.
