Zero new packages in the anchor/block-identity/comment lane.

negatives: AHEAD OF US #1 — the product slot. inkeep/OpenKnowledge is shipping frontmatter's exact pitch, faster. Repo description: "Beautiful, AI-native markdown IDE and LLM wiki"; README feature #1 verbatim: "Full true **WYSIWYG** so that editing markdown files feels like editing a Google Doc or Notion page." Measured 2026-08-01: 3,239 GitHub stars (created 2026-06-03, pushed today), @inkeep/open-knowledge at 14,790 npm downloads/week with 859 published versions since 2026-04-17, 140,859 total downloads over 2026-05-01→2026-08-01 on a rising trend (weekly buckets 6,862 → 22,042), a macOS app, a web UI, a CLI, MCP + skills for Claude/Codex/OpenCode, git/GitHub team sharing, AND comment anchoring merged 2026-07-30. frontmatter has zero of this shipped. Two mitigations, both real but both narrow: it is GPL-3.0 (we cannot copy the code into a proprietary product, and neither can anyone else without reciprocity), and its comments are explicitly single-player — "a note to your own agent, not a message to a teammate" — so the multiplayer review loop of D1/D3 is still open. But "we have the idea" is no longer a position we hold alone, and the hardest engineering piece is now readable by anyone in a public repo.

AHEAD OF US #2 — conformance machinery. MDMAX's "certificate matrix" is a table in a plan; mdbase-dev/mdbase-spec has shipped the executable version. It defines eleven normative profile IDs with a declared dependency graph (`links` requires `collection_semantics` + `cel`; `runtime/0.2` requires `core_read` + `event_action_interop/0.1` + `cel`), a machine-checked claim document (`schemas/v0.3/conformance-claim.schema.json`) that "enforces profile dependencies" and whose verifiers "SHOULD reject evidence produced for a different implementation artifact or specification version and SHOULD report stale evidence", and a spec-owned three-ring interoperability testbed in `testbed/v0.1/`. 16-conformance.md alone is 18,817 bytes. We have argued that a degradation certificate is our differentiator; a competitor in an adjacent slot has already built the apparatus that makes a certificate mean something, and we would be reinventing it.

AGAINST MY OWN AREA'S METHOD. This sweep would have missed its own headline. Registry sweeps (npm search across six lane keywords, 180 packages) found nothing; GitHub topic and phrase searches for the five unclaimed capabilities returned total_count 0 on four of five queries. The OpenKnowledge finding came from an HN Show HN post six weeks old, and the anchoring inside it was only visible after reading a merged PR's file list. A competitive sweep tuned to package registries and spec repos has a structural blind spot for capability shipped inside an application — which is exactly where a Google-Docs-for-markdown competitor will always ship. Any future watch must poll application changelogs and merged PRs, not registries.

AGAINST THE PREMISE THAT DROVE THIS SWEEP. The program was rattled by OKF and commissioned this gate partly to avoid being caught out again. Read directly, OKF was never the threat: 52 downloads/week for its CLI, a 404 on the most-cited quickstart install, no block identity, no runtime, no runtime protocol, and a unilateral Google CLA that makes it a poor host for anybody's roadmap. Meanwhile the thing that actually contests our spine shipped in the open on 2026-07-30 with no press. The lesson is not 'sweep harder' — it is that GitHub stars and vendor announcements are the wrong alarm, and merged code in adjacent products is the right one.

AHEAD OF US #3 — velocity in the compiler slot. IWE shipped 14 releases between 2026-06-24 and 2026-07-29 (v0.5.0 → v0.17.0), adding a document schema type system with `--strict` write gates, near-duplicate detection with a tunable threshold, an embedded docs command, an MCP server, filesystem watching with editor-ownership semantics, and byte-exact document creation. It is a single-maintainer Rust project at 1,340 stars that now covers a meaningful fraction of what MDMAX's CLI is planned to do. We are about to start building against a moving target that ships roughly twice a week.
unclaimed: Container round trip with edit mapping (edit a DOCX/PDF-derived document as markdown, write the change back into the original container at the right offsets). Searches run: GitHub repo search `markdown "round trip" "edit mapping"` → total_count 0; `docx markdown round trip` sorted by updated → total_count 2, both trivial (DrBaher/draft-cli 0 stars, ThalesMMS/Radiology-Templates 2 stars). The whole converter industry is one-directional and enormous — microsoft/markitdown 170,545 stars pushed 2026-07-29, docling-project/docling 64,082 stars pushed 2026-07-31, marker-pdf 2.0.0 released 2026-07-20, mineru 3.4.4 released 2026-07-30 — and not one of them writes back. This is the largest genuinely open slot found in the sweep.

Per-document degradation certificate (for THIS document, what does each target renderer do to it). Searches run: `"degradation matrix" markdown` → 0; `markdown compatibility matrix` → 0; `markdown renderer conformance test` → 0; `"renderer matrix" markdown compat` → 0. HONEST CAVEAT, tier inference: Babelmark 2/3 is a well-known per-SNIPPET interactive renderer comparator and I did not re-verify it live in this session; the unclaimed thing is a per-DOCUMENT, machine-checkable certificate, not the comparison itself. mdbase has the conformance-claim apparatus but claims implementation conformance, not document degradation.

Near-miss reference checker (a link that ALMOST resolves — pointing at a heading that was renamed, or a file one character off). Searches run: `"near-miss" link checker markdown` → 0; `broken link checker suggest similar` → 1 irrelevant repo. Closest adjacent art is IWE v0.15.0 (2026-07-22) `iwe stats similarity --threshold` at a 0.85 default, which finds near-duplicate PAGES, not near-miss REFERENCES; and mdbase 08-links.md, which resolves and validates links but on exact match only, with stable tiebreakers and an ambiguity warning rather than a suggestion.

Cache-aware document layout (order and chunk a document set so a prompt-cache prefix stays stable across edits). Searches run: `"prompt cache" "stable prefix" context pack` → 0; `prompt cache aware context` → 13 repos, largest 3 stars (QuickLeopard/contextops 0 stars created 2026-07-03, davccavalcante/racs 2 stars, rblake2320/anvil-context-compiler 0 stars). repomix — the category leader at 75,342 dl/wk — has a `--token-budget` guard but its only file ordering is `perf(core): Sort files by size desc for better worker load balancing`, i.e. an internal scheduling concern, not a cache concern. Effectively unclaimed at any level of adoption.

A PUBLISHED false-positive rate for markdown re-anchoring. This is the slot that survives the OpenKnowledge finding and it is worth more than the algorithm. OpenKnowledge ships anchoring with no correct/false/refusal numbers anywhere in its source, tests, or changeset. Nobody in the sweep publishes one. MDMAX's 99.627% / 0.050% / 0.323% — if it can be re-derived, and if it can be re-derived at RANGE level rather than block level — is a claim no competitor can currently make, and it is a purchasing argument in a way that an algorithm is not.

Multiplayer review over markdown with authenticated reviewers. inkeep/OpenKnowledge deliberately declined it ("a note to your own agent, not a message to a teammate"); mdbase has no comment concept; OKF has none; IWE has none; Obsidian's `%%…%%` is a single-user in-file annotation. HN search for `google docs for markdown` over 120 days at >8 points returned 3 stories, none of them that. D1/D3's actual product slot is open — which is also a demand warning, see negatives.
result.design:
"Three concrete changes, all of which follow from what was measured rather than from taste.

1. RE-BASELINE §4.1 AGAINST A NAMED COMPETITOR, AT RANGE LEVEL. Stop describing block identity as an unclaimed capability. It is claimed at range level by GPL-3.0 code that anyone can read. The defensible position is narrower and stronger: MDMAX ships (a) a fuzzy S3 tier that recovers a passage after a real rewrite, which OpenKnowledge explicitly does not have ("No fuzzy matching"), (b) a REFUSAL of position-based tiebreaks, which OpenKnowledge still uses as its last resort and which MDMAX measured at 22.20% false, and (c) a published correct/false/refusal rate, which nobody else has. Ship the resolver with those three as the spec, and put the false-positive rate on the box. Clean-room discipline is mandatory: the code is GPL-3.0, so specify from the published behaviour, never from their source.

2. ADOPT markdown-it 15's `reference_definition` TOKEN AS THE CARRIER SUBSTRATE, AND PIN THE VERSION. The one carrier that is invisible in 24/24 configs now has, as of 2026-07-30, a first-class token with a `map: [startLine, endLine]` source range and a `meta.label`, in a 27M-download/week parser, behind `core.ruler.disable('strip_references')`, with byte-identical rendered output. That is precisely the read side of a splice writer, handed over for free. Two consequences: the JS port gets materially cheaper, and the risk register gains an entry — invisibility of the link reference definition is now a DEFAULT (`strip_references` enabled), not a property of the format, so a downstream renderer can opt into showing it. Pin `markdown-it@^15` and add a regression test that asserts rendered output is identical with the rule enabled and disabled.

3. DEMOTE OKF FROM 'DECISION' TO 'ONE COLUMN, ALREADY 74% DONE'. §13.5's recommendation (target, not host) is correct and the spec read confirms it for stronger reasons than the plan gives: OKF has no runtime, explicitly defers the runtime protocol and attester ABI, has 52 downloads/week of tooling, and has zero overlap with block identity, splicing or degradation. The corpus is already 73.616% conformant with its only hard requirement. So OKF is a cheap interop checkbox, not a strategic question — write the position, cite SPEC.md sha256:5a3311d2…, and close §S1. Also add the two families OKF v0.2 standardized (`generated`/`verified` actors, `stale_after`) to the certificate emitter as pass-through fields; they cost nothing and they are the only part of OKF anyone is actually asking for (127 open spec issues).

CARRIER: the MDMAX library plus CLI as planned. DEGRADATION: unchanged — link reference definition primary, `[//]: #` secondary, both re-verified invisible in marked 18.0.7 and markdown-it 15.0.0, the two parser majors that shipped inside the window. SURFACE: `mdmax resolve --explain` must print which tier fired (S1/S2/S3) and refuse loudly, because refusal-with-a-reason is the product difference against a competitor whose fallback is a position guess."
result.measurement:
"THE ONE EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES THIS. Head-to-head range-level re-anchoring, MDMAX vs OpenKnowledge's published behaviour, on the same corpus, with pre-registered predictions.

CORPUS: the 294 real revision pairs already used for the 41,642 block-version figure, re-cut at RANGE level — the settled record already says the 99.627% is a BLOCK figure that does not transfer to ranges, and OpenKnowledge anchors ranges, so a block-level comparison is not a comparison. Sample n = 2,000 ranges stratified by length (1–20 chars, 21–80, 81–300, >300) since the OpenKnowledge design is length-sensitive: its growth ceiling is max(4*len, len+64), so short quotes get a proportionally enormous ceiling and long ones a tight one.

ARMS: (A) MDMAX S1/S2/S3 as specified. (B) A clean-room reimplementation of OpenKnowledge's published behaviour: exact quote, 32-char context widened by doubling until the prefix+exact+suffix triple is unique, exact-only matching, context score = commonSuffixLen(prefix) + commonPrefixLen(suffix), bracket recovery with the 4x/+64 ceiling, nearest-position final tiebreak, orphan otherwise. Written from behaviour, never from their GPL source. (C) Content-hash-only, as the floor.

VERIFIER: ground truth from the diff (before/after byte ranges), which frontmatter always has in practice — so this measures the FALLBACK path honestly, matching the plan's own corrected §4.1 framing.

METRICS, all three reported per arm and per length stratum: correct / FALSE / refusal. The false rate is the only one that matters; a refusal is a UI event and a false anchor is a comment on the wrong sentence.

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, recorded before running so the run can embarrass us: (1) Arm B's false rate will be NON-ZERO and above 1%, driven by the nearest-position tiebreak, in the 1–20 char stratum where quotes repeat. (2) Arm A will beat Arm B on correct-rate in the >300 char stratum, where a passage has been genuinely rewritten and only the shingle tier can find it. (3) Arm A will LOSE to Arm B somewhere — most likely in the 21–80 char stratum, where OpenKnowledge's bracket recovery handles an in-place word edit that MDMAX's jaccard >= 0.20 threshold rejects. If prediction 3 does not come true, be suspicious of the harness rather than pleased.

SECONDARY, cheap, same day: re-run the 24-config carrier matrix with marked bumped 16 → 18.0.7 and markdown-it re-checked at 15.0.0 with `strip_references` both enabled and disabled, and assert rendered output is byte-identical across that toggle. I ran a 5-carrier subset of this and it held; the full matrix should be re-cut before the certificate ships."
result.kill_condition:
"KILL THE 'BLOCK IDENTITY IS OUR MOAT' FRAMING IF: the head-to-head above shows the clean-room OpenKnowledge arm within 0.5 percentage points of MDMAX on false rate AND within 3 points on correct rate at range level. At that point the algorithm is a commodity that a competitor already gives away under GPL, and the moat has to be the multiplayer review loop (D1/D3) plus the published measurement — not the resolver. Re-plan §4.1 as a supporting capability, not the spine.

KILL THE OKF WORKSTREAM ENTIRELY IF: `okf` PyPI weekly downloads have not crossed 500/week by 2026-10-01 (baseline measured 2026-08-01: 52/week, 236/month). Below that it is a spec with satellite skill repos and no consumers, and every hour spent on a conformance column is an hour not spent on the review loop. Recheck the number, do not recheck the vibe.

KILL THE LINK-REFERENCE-DEFINITION CARRIER IF: any of the four required parser ports, or GitHub's blob/API/comment renderers, begin rendering reference definitions visibly by default. markdown-it 15.0.0 made this a live risk for the first time — `strip_references` is a defaultable core rule now, not an inherent property. Add a canary that renders the carrier through all four ports on every CI run and fails on any non-empty output.

KILL THE WHOLE COMPETITIVE-SWEEP CADENCE AS CURRENTLY DESIGNED: it already failed once in this very session. If the next scheduled sweep again finds its most important item via a stale HN post rather than via its own registry and topic queries, stop running registry sweeps and replace them with a watch on ~15 named application changelogs and merged-PR feeds (inkeep/open-knowledge, iwe-org/iwe, yamadashy/repomix, mdbase-dev/mdbase-spec, obsidianmd, GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog, markdown-it, marked)."
result.effort: "high — roughly 55 tool calls over one session. Primary reads: OKF SPEC.md v0.2 in full (37,544 bytes, all 13 sections plus Appendix A), OpenKnowledge anchor.ts (261 lines) and anchor-search.ts (241 lines) in full, thread-store.ts header, the comments changeset, mdbase 08-links / 09-lifecycle / 16-conformance and its CHANGELOG, markdown-it 15.0.0 CHANGELOG, and 30-odd GitHub release bodies. Own measurements: OKF-conformance of the pinned 1,084-file corpus (with a sha256 integrity re-verification: 0 missing, 0 mismatched); markdown-it 15.0.0 reference_definition token emission and render-identity, run from an extracted tarball in $TMPDIR; marked 18.0.7 five-carrier visibility matrix, same method; the falsifier test comparing the 0.45.4 and 0.46.0-beta.32 published tarballs. Sweeps: HN Algolia across 20 query terms over the 120-day window; npm registry search across 6 lane terms (180 packages, created-date filtered); authenticated GitHub repo/topic/issue search across ~20 queries; PyPI and crates.io metadata and download stats for 15 packages. RULE 4 held throughout: no commit, no push, no npm install into any repo, no writes outside $TMPDIR, no deletions. The sandbox blocked hn.algolia.com, arxiv.org, pypistats.org and obsidian.md; those specific read-only curls were re-run with the sandbox disabled and nothing else was."
result.unverified:
"WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY, and where each item actually sits.

1. arXiv — NOT COVERED. Three attempts, all refused: HTTP 429 'Rate exceeded' twice and an HTTP 503 on the third, across http and https, with and without a custom User-Agent. I have ZERO arXiv coverage for cs.CL and cs.SE in this window and I am not going to infer it from memory. Tier: not attempted-successfully. If the academic lane matters to the gate, it needs a separate pass.

2. Product Hunt — NOT ATTEMPTED. Its API needs a developer token I do not have and should not acquire. Tier: gap.

3. GitHub CODE search — largely unavailable. `search/code` returned total_count 0 even for queries I know match (filename:editor-guide inside a repo whose editor guide exists), which means the code index is not serving these queries for this token. All my 'nobody has built X' claims therefore rest on REPOSITORY and TOPIC search plus npm/PyPI/crates search, not on code search. Tier: search-only, with a weaker instrument than I would like. Treat every unclaimed item as 'not found by repo/registry search', not 'proven absent'.

4. The 99.627% / 0.050% / 0.323% figures — I did NOT re-derive them. I only read them from docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.1 and compared them against a competitor's design. The settled record already flags that nobody has re-derived them and that they are BLOCK figures that do not transfer to RANGES; nothing I did changes that, and my headline is careful to compare designs and published-vs-unpublished measurement, never to endorse the number. Tier: secondary.

5. OpenKnowledge's actual accuracy — UNKNOWN and unknowable from outside. I read their algorithm and their tests exist (anchor-search.test.ts 158 lines, anchor-layers.test.ts 102 lines, comment-service.test.ts 942 lines) but I did not run them and they publish no accuracy figures. My claim that they 'have no published false-positive rate' is a claim about absence of publication, verified by reading the source and changeset; it is NOT a claim that their false rate is high. Tier: own-measurement for the absence, inference for anything about their quality.

6. Babelmark — I asserted in the unclaimed list that a per-document degradation certificate is unbuilt, and I flagged inline that Babelmark 2/3 exists as a per-snippet comparator which I did NOT re-verify live this session. Tier: inference. Someone should check it before the certificate is marketed as novel.

7. Whether OpenKnowledge's beta anchoring behaves as its source describes — I verified the code is PRESENT in the 0.46.0-beta.32 tarball by string and minified-shape matching (`status:"orphaned"`, `exact:i,prefix:a,suffix:o`, `rewritten`, 'Add Comment', 'Send to AI'). I did NOT execute it. Tier: own-measurement for presence, primary-read for behaviour, nothing for runtime behaviour.

8. inkeep/OpenKnowledge's GPL-3.0 licence — read from the GitHub licence API (spdx_id GPL-3.0). I did not read the LICENSE file text or check for a dual-licence or CLA that would let the vendor relicense. Any legal reliance on 'competitors cannot copy it either' needs a lawyer, not me. Tier: secondary.

9. Star counts, download counts and dates are all point-in-time reads on 2026-08-01T02:44Z–03:40Z. The OpenKnowledge beta was published at 02:38:33Z, six minutes before my first tool call — this field is moving faster than the document that reports it."

result.area: The mother markdown: one file containing many, with breakpoints, split on read — adversarial verification

verdicts.claim: C1 — The pinned corpus reproduces exactly: 1084/1084 files sha256-match the manifest, 0 missing, 0 mismatched, 25,548,765 bytes.
verdicts.reason: Re-derived independently against corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4 by hashing every file listed in docs/engine/research/corpus-manifest.json at the three declared HEADs. My script printed 'total 1084 ok 1084 missing 0 mismatch 0 bytes 25548765', matching the manifest's own total_files 1084 / total_bytes 25548765. Only caveat, and it is minor: I could not recompute the corpus_id STRING itself from the (path, sha256) list under two obvious formulations, so the id is verified by content, not by recomputation — it functions as an opaque label.

verdicts.claim: C2 headline — a reference packer over the whole corpus costs +0.892% and round-trips 1084/1084 byte-identical.
verdicts.reason: corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… — I built an independent packer to the stated split contract (YAML manifest, ````text fm:file <i> <json-path>, bare ```` close, git '\ No newline at end of file' sentinel) and measured container=25,775,670, overhead=+0.888%, then unpacked with a pinned-run line scanner: 'byte-identical=1084/1084 unpack=57ms recovered_keys=1084, failures: []'. The researcher reports 25,776,700 / +0.892% — a 1,030-byte (0.004%) difference attributable to the root string. The headline reproduces.

verdicts.claim: C2 decomposition — 'Overhead decomposes as manifest 169,706 B (62.9% of overhead, 0.657% of container) + framing 92.5 B/file.'
verdicts.reason: The decomposition cannot be true of the container it is attached to. Arithmetic: stated overhead = 25,776,700 − 25,548,765 = 227,935 B. Stated parts = 169,706 + (92.5 × 1084 = 100,270) = 269,976 B. That is 42,041 B — 18.4% of the overhead — unaccounted for. The two percentages also use two different denominators: 169,706/227,935 = 74.5% (not 62.9%), while 169,706/25,776,700 = 0.658% (matching the quoted 0.657%). So '62.9% of overhead' was computed against a ~269,800 B overhead and '0.657% of container' against the 25,776,700 B container — two different runs reported as one decomposition. The researcher's own Claim 8 settles which number is wrong: it states the manifest 'complete at byte 127,394' of that same container, and byte-127,394 IS the manifest size. My packer reproduces 127,446 with the 16-hex sha256 the researcher's own Claim-6 evidence line displays, and 179,478 only with a full 64-hex sha256. 169,706 belongs to neither run.
verdicts.correction: For the +0.888% container I measured: manifest = 127,446 B (56.2% of overhead, 0.494% of container); framing = 99,459 B = 91.8 B/file. The 92.5 B/file framing figure is the one part of the stated decomposition that reproduces.

verdicts.claim: C3 mechanism — 4 of 1084 files (0.369%) end inside an unclosed fence; under that condition the HTML-comment and linkref carriers both lose the next boundary while a 4-backtick fence keeps it.
verdicts.reason: corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… — my independent CommonMark-rule fence scanner returned 'UNCLOSED files: 4 of 1084 0.369%' naming exactly md/Brain/20-projects/proj-advox-frontend.md (open_at_line=45), proj-gearup.md, proj-knowledge.md, proj-skills-registry.md. The live authoring defect is real: proj-advox-frontend.md line 32 reads '│   └── main.jsx          # Rea' — truncated mid-word — and grep shows fences at lines 26, 36, 45, an odd count. I reproduced the parser result with the same library, mdast-util-from-markdown 2.0.3: 'unclosed-fence htmlcomment nodes= html,heading,code | boundary2_is_block_start= false | boundary2_inside_code_node= true'; linkref identical; 'unclosed-fence fence4 nodes= code,code | boundary2_is_block_start= true'. The researcher in fact UNDERSTATES severity — the container collapsed to 3 top-level nodes, i.e. every remaining boundary is swallowed, not one. The hazard is also real under the plan's own constraint: docs/engine/PLAN.md:501 mandates 'Splitting must be a CommonMark block-level scanner, not a regex'.

verdicts.claim: C3 extrapolation — 'the HTML-comment carrier is only safe on 96.4% of 10-file packs, 69.1% of 100-file packs and 1.8% of a 1084-file pack — it is a small-pack feature, not a mother-markdown carrier.'
verdicts.reason: The binomial arithmetic is correct — (1−0.00369)^10 = 0.9637, ^100 = 0.6896, ^1084 = 0.0182 — but the independence assumption it rests on is refuted by the researcher's own four data points. All 4 unclosed files are proj-*.md in one directory: 4 of the 28 files in md/Brain/20-projects (14.3%), and 0 of the other 1,056 files in the corpus. That is one generator emitting one defect, not a 0.369% i.i.d. per-file hazard. A pack drawn from a directory of tool-generated project cards fails far worse than 96.4% at n=10; a pack of hand-authored notes may never fail. This is a rate applied as if it were an absolute independent hazard.
verdicts.correction: State it as measured: 4 files, all from one generator in one directory. The correct claim is that a single unclosed fence anywhere in a pack destroys every subsequent boundary under a CommonMark block scanner — which is a sufficient argument on its own and needs no extrapolation.

verdicts.claim: C4 — 15,435 fence lines across 1084 files are ALL exactly three backticks; zero tilde fences; zero runs ≥4; a 4-backtick container fence is unambiguous on 100% of the corpus.
verdicts.reason: corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… — my census over line-initial runs at CommonMark indent ≤3 returned exactly 'BACKTICK line-initial runs: {1: 2216, 3: 15435}', 'max backtick run 3 md/AGENTS.md', 'count >=4: 0  >=5: 0', 'TILDE fence runs >=3: {}'. I then confirmed the operational consequence directly: 'corpus files that would break a 4-backtick container fence: 0'. Exact reproduction, including the same file named as the maximum. One durability caveat the researcher does not state: the corpus's only four 4-backtick runs (all inline, 0 at column 0) live in frontmatter/docs/engine/PLAN.md lines 652 and 1042 — the program's own documentation. '100% of the corpus' is a snapshot property that MDMAX's own docs are already eroding; the re-derived max+1 rule is what actually carries the claim.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — 'Prior art is repomix's calculateMarkdownDelimiter; adopt it, credit it.'
verdicts.reason: The function exists and is correctly located (GitHub code search, repo:yamadashy/repomix, total_count 1, src/core/output/outputGenerate.ts), but it is not the algorithm the researcher specifies. Its source, fetched raw: 'const maxBackticks = contents.flatMap((content) => content?.match(/`+/g) ?? []).reduce((max, match) => Math.max(max, match.length), 0); return "`".repeat(Math.max(3, maxBackticks + 1));'. That matches ANY backtick run anywhere, including inline spans, with a floor of 3. The spec says 'run N = max(4, max line-initial backtick run over every contained byte + 1)'. On this very corpus the two disagree: my histogram of ANY run gives {1:157494, 2:42, 3:15506, 4:4}, so repomix's function emits 5 backticks where the spec emits 4. The spec's line-initial rule is the better of the two — only a line-initial run at indent ≤3 can close a fence — but 'adopt it' credits a function that would produce a different container.
verdicts.correction: Credit repomix for the escalating-delimiter idea; state that MDMAX tightens the predicate from /`+/g to line-initial-at-indent-≤3, and that this changes the emitted fence on the pinned corpus from 5 to 4.

verdicts.claim: C5 — zip is disqualified for anything versioned: one one-line edit costs 66 B (folder), 263 B (container), 31,590 B (zip) — 120x the container — and git diff on the zip says 'Binary files differ'.
verdicts.reason: Re-derived without any commit, using git hash-object -w plus git pack-objects on an explicit object list in a scratch repo, over the knowledge root of corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… (272 files), editing categories/ai/video/video-saraev-claude-code-advanced.md — whose 190,804-byte size matches the researcher's own manifest evidence line — by +13 bytes. Result: 'folder: INCREMENTAL COST OF 1 EDIT=67 | container: =199 | zip: =37904'. Direction and order of magnitude reproduce; my zip:container ratio is 190x where theirs is 120x, so the exact multiplier is edit- and deflate-dependent but the conclusion is not. Corroborating: 'git diff --no-index z1.zip z2.zip' → 'Binary files a/z1.zip and b/z2.zip differ' (101 bytes of diff), versus the container's '1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)'. And pack(v1) container 1,255,966 vs folder 1,443,661 = 13.0% smaller, against their 12.2%. Worth stating plainly though the researcher does disclose it: on per-edit cost the FOLDER (67 B) beats the container (199 B) 3:1, so this argument disqualifies the zip, not the folder — consistent with docs/engine/PLAN.md §6 'The folder stays canonical.'

verdicts.claim: C6 — one line per file in the manifest is a 47x reduction in diff size (86,252 → 1,833 bytes).
verdicts.reason: The evidence line reproduces character-for-character, which is the strongest single corroboration in this review: my independently-built packer emitted the identical hunk '-  - {i: 179, bytes: 190804, sha256: ec3d5a26a764f1d7, path: "categories/ai/video/video-saraev-claude-code-advanced.md"}' / '+ … bytes: 190817, sha256: 43b8b82f9a59e45c …', with 2 hunks and 1,861 diff bytes against their 1,833. But the 47x depends entirely on how the strawman compact manifest is laid out. My single-line JSON manifest produced 64,339 diff bytes, giving 34.6x, not 47x. The ratio is a property of the comparison you construct, not of the design.
verdicts.correction: Claim the design fact, which is robust: a one-line-per-file manifest confines a content edit to a two-line hunk that names the changed file, instead of rewriting the whole manifest line. Quote the absolute (1.8 KB) and drop the multiplier, or state the strawman's exact layout alongside it.

verdicts.claim: C7 — a two-line git diff driver makes the container self-attributing; the hunk header names the contained source file.
verdicts.reason: Reproduced directly: 'git -c diff.fmpack.xfuncname="^`{4,}text fm:file .*$" -c core.attributesfile=<...> diff --no-index m_oneline_v1.md m_oneline_v2.md' produced '@@ -35612,7 +35612,7 @@ ````text fm:file 179 "categories/ai/video/video-saraev-claude-code-advanced.md"'. The header text is identical to the researcher's, including index 179 and the full path; only the line number differs (35,612 vs 35,792, from manifest layout). The manifest hunk correctly gets no function context ('@@ -182,7 +182,7 @@'). The researcher's own stated limit — xfuncname must live in git config rather than .gitattributes, so this is per-clone setup and unverified on GitHub web — is accurate and honestly flagged.

verdicts.claim: C8 — the container's index sits at 0.49% (head) vs the zip's 98.8% (tail); container.gz beats the zip by 15.4%; tar is +3.4%. 'Zip wins random access: zip 2.94ms, container(full scan) 38.48ms.'
verdicts.reason: Every storage number reproduces, several to the byte: 'zip 9,310,058' (exact), 'zip central directory offset: 9,200,529 of 9,310,058 = 98.8%' (exact), 'container manifest complete at byte 127,446 of 25,775,670 = 0.49%', 'container.gz 7,850,815 vs zip 9,310,058 → gz beats zip by 15.7%' (their 15.4%), 'tar (uncompressed) 26,429,440 (+3.45%)' (their +3.4%). The random-access concession is the part that is wrong. A container does not need a full scan: the head manifest yields byte offsets by prefix sum. I measured 'container seek-by-manifest: 1.79 ms  correct=True' for file #900 of 1084, against 'zip random read: 1.54 ms' and a full scan of 69.85 ms. So the gap is 16%, not 13x, and 'Zip wins exactly one thing' is false — on this evidence the zip wins nothing measured. This error runs against the researcher's own headline, so it is not a flattering-direction defect, but it makes the DESIGN's trade-off table wrong.
verdicts.correction: Random access: zip 1.54 ms vs container 1.79 ms via manifest-derived seek. And a real spec gap surfaced while proving it — see new_defects: the manifest as specified cannot produce those offsets.

verdicts.claim: C9 — the container scales to a 500 MB vault, packs 5x faster than zipping it, and a naive implementation is O(whole container) in RAM (516 MB), so streaming is a hard requirement.
verdicts.reason: corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… replicated 20x. My run: 'n=21680 raw=510,975,300' (both exact), 'container=515,751,582 overhead=+0.935%' (theirs 515,923,904), 'zip build: 9.6s -> 186,374,182 bytes' (theirs 9.7s -> 186,525,942 — within 0.08%). The throughput figures do not reproduce and are machine-dependent: I measured pack 0.54s at 945 MB/s against their 1.91s at 270 MB/s, and boundary scan 2.53s against their 1.48s. That makes their '5x faster than zip' conservative — mine is 17.7x — so the conclusion is safe in the reported direction. The memory claim is understated rather than overstated: my peak RSS was 3,832 MB, 7.4x the container, not 516 MB, because a naive implementation holds the item list, the join buffer, the str and the encoded bytes at once. Streaming is a harder requirement than claimed.

verdicts.claim: C10 — nesting is free and byte-exact, so PLAN §5's 'a container inside a container is refused in v1' should be deleted.
verdicts.reason: The mechanism reproduces exactly: my nesting test printed 'level1 fence: 4 / level2 fence: 5 / level3 fence: 6', 'L2 -> inner recovered byte-identical: True', 'L3 -> L2 byte-identical: True', 'L3 -> L2 -> L1 byte-identical: True', 'innermost files recovered: 20 / 20'. But this is a WEAKER replication of a measurement already inside the document it claims to overturn. docs/engine/PLAN.md:478 already records the fence carrier as 'survives; nests via backtick count', and docs/engine/PLAN.md:1062 already records 'a 13-level recursive nest unwrapped with the innermost payload byte-identical'. Three levels does not overturn thirteen. Separately, §5's line is a scope policy — 'refused in v1 with a diagnostic' — not a capability claim, and demonstrating capability does not refute a scope decision. The researcher's substantive counter is nonetheless correct and in fact understated: RFC 2046 §5.1.1 explicitly permits nested multipart, and tar-in-tar is routine, so 'fifty years, no exceptions' is wrong as written.
verdicts.correction: Frame it as: §5's own table already grants that the fence nests, and §15.1 already measured 13 levels; the v1 refusal is therefore a policy with no measurement behind it and can be revisited on cost grounds, not overturned on new evidence.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — ask for per-file whole-file listings in aider's shape, 'the format models are most reliably well-formed in (median 99.6% vs 94.2% for diffs)'.
verdicts.reason: Re-derived from the primary data, not a summary. I fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Aider-AI/aider/main/aider/website/_data/polyglot_leaderboard.yml (45,725 B) and computed percent_cases_well_formed by edit_format: 'whole n=15 median=99.60' and 'diff n=47 median=94.20'. Both figures land exactly on the quoted numbers. Two confounds the researcher should state: the model populations differ by format (weaker models are disproportionately benchmarked in whole), so this is not a controlled comparison; and the older edit_leaderboard.yml gives whole n=63 median=100.00 vs diff n=29 median=96.20, a different pair for the same claim.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — 'This is independently where the repomix maintainer landed in #226 and where aider already is.'
verdicts.reason: I pulled the issue and every comment from api.github.com. Issue 226 is 'Support for unpack', created 2024-12-29T17:48:56Z, and its state is still 'open' — nobody landed anywhere. The maintainer (yamadashy) wrote, verbatim: 'the format would be difficult to define, so it might be hard.' His later comment points at aider and specifically flags 'they use a secondary, lightweight LLM for parsing the responses' and 'pre-defined response formats (editor-diff or editor-whole)' — that is, BOTH formats, plus an LLM parser. A maintainer citing an approach in an open issue is not convergence, and the secondary-LLM parser directly undercuts the researcher's adjacent claim that the return format is 'structurally identical to one entry of our own container, so one scanner serves both.'
verdicts.correction: State it as: repomix #226 is an open, unresolved request whose maintainer called the format hard to define and pointed at aider's pre-defined response formats — which is supporting context for the direction, not independent arrival at the same conclusion.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN, REJOIN CONTRACT — the four-way dual-authority classifier (clean / framing-damaged / reframed / edited), 'Proven per file by digest: 1084/1084 byte-identical on the pinned corpus.'
verdicts.reason: This is an inference presented as a measurement. A round-trip of an unmodified corpus contains zero edited files, zero damaged frames and zero stale byte counts, so it exercises exactly one of the four branches. My own run reproduces the round-trip (1084/1084) and therefore proves the same one thing the researcher's does: that pack∘unpack = identity. It says nothing about whether the classifier correctly separates 'framing-damaged' from 'reframed' from 'edited', which is the entire content of the contract and the part on which silent data loss would depend.
verdicts.correction: The rejoin contract needs its own fixture set — files edited in-body, files whose frame was moved, files whose byte count is stale — with a confusion matrix. Until then the contract is a design, not a result.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN, INJECTION — a reader pinned to the declared run recovers 3 files with 0 forged paths from an attack file, while a naive `{3,} scanner accepts ../../../.ssh/authorized_keys.
verdicts.reason: Reproduced directly. I built an attack container in which file 1's body contains a 3-backtick block whose info string is 'text fm:file 99 "../../../.ssh/authorized_keys"'. Output: 'pinned-run reader recovered paths: [a.md, attack.md, b.md]' / 'naive `{3,} scanner recovered paths: [a.md, attack.md, ../../../.ssh/authorized_keys, b.md]' / 'forged path accepted by naive: True | by pinned: False'. The design consequence — the spec must mandate the pinned run and forbid any-fence scanning — follows. I also checked the mirror-image hazard for the rejected carrier and found zero corpus files containing a literal '<!-- /fm -->', so the html comment's failure is the parse-swallow, not a literal collision.

verdicts.claim: Did the researcher genuinely look for its own pre-registered falsifier?
verdicts.reason: Yes, and this is the strongest thing about the submission. Falsifier (2) — 'a CommonMark parser keeps the second boundary when a contained file ends inside an open fence' — is a real, cheap, decisive test, and I ran it independently on the same library version and got the reported result rather than a flattering one. Falsifier (1) is the notable case: the researcher reports that its FIRST experiment found the falsifier (line-diff rebase recovered 200/200, median-0/p90-1/max-2, zero losses), then reports that this refuted its own headline, then shows the result was an artifact of a benign destruction model, and labels the earlier optimism 'exactly the flattering-direction defect this run was told to avoid; I am reporting it against myself.' It also names an untested residual (semantic re-anchoring as a boundary repairer) rather than claiming coverage. One reservation, held as a reservation and not a kill: the second-round simulation numbers — 119/120 on merge_across, 120/120 on reorder, 47/120 on truncate, 303/400 at p=0.5 — are reported without a seed, a destruction-model spec, or a script, so they are the one block of own-measurement material in this submission that I could not re-derive at all.

survived: C1 — corpus reproduction: 1084/1084 sha256 match, 0 missing, 0 mismatch, 25,548,765 bytes (re-derived)
C2 headline — +0.892% overhead (I measured +0.888%) and 1084/1084 byte-identical round-trip (re-derived with an independently written packer/unpacker)
C3 core measurement — 4 files / 0.369% end inside an unclosed fence, exact same four filenames, proj-advox-frontend.md open_at_line=45, truncated mid-word at '# Rea' (re-derived)

C3 parser result — mdast-util-from-markdown 2.0.3: boundary2_is_block_start false for htmlcomment and linkref, true for fence4 under an unclosed fence (re-derived; severity is in fact worse than claimed — all remaining boundaries are swallowed, not one)
C4 — 15,435 line-initial backtick runs all exactly 3, zero tilde fences, zero runs >=4, max in md/AGENTS.md; 0 corpus files would break a 4-backtick container fence (re-derived exactly)

C5 — zip is disqualified for versioned storage: 190x the container's per-edit git cost in my run (120x in theirs), 'Binary files differ' vs a 2-line reviewable diff, container pack 13.0% smaller than folder pack (re-derived without any commit, via hash-object + pack-objects)

C6 evidence line — reproduced character-for-character including the sha256 prefix ec3d5a26a764f1d7; the one-line-per-file manifest confines the edit to a 2-hunk, ~1.8 KB diff that names the changed file

C7 — the xfuncname diff driver puts '````text fm:file 179 "categories/ai/video/video-saraev-claude-code-advanced.md"' in the hunk header (re-derived), with the per-clone-config limit honestly stated by the researcher
C8 storage properties — zip 9,310,058 and CD offset 9,200,529 exact to the byte; index at 0.49% head vs 98.8% tail; container.gz beats zip by 15.7%; tar +3.45% (all re-derived)
C9 — 500 MB scale: n=21,680 and raw=510,975,300 exact, zip 9.6s -> 186,374,182 within 0.08% of theirs; container packs far faster than zipping (their 5x is conservative; I measured 17.7x)
C10 mechanism — fence escalation 4->5->6, byte-identical at three levels, 20/20 innermost files recovered (re-derived)
INJECTION — pinned-run reader recovers 3 paths with 0 forged; naive `{3,} scanner accepts ../../../.ssh/authorized_keys (re-derived)
aider well-formedness — whole median 99.60 (n=15) vs diff median 94.20 (n=47), re-derived from polyglot_leaderboard.yml primary data, exact
DESIGN DECISION: SINGLE FILE over zip — survives every property I re-measured, and survives harder than claimed once the zip's one conceded win is removed
The falsifier discipline — genuine, self-penalizing, and one falsifier was independently re-run by me with the reported (non-flattering) result
killed: C2's overhead decomposition — 'manifest 169,706 B (62.9% of overhead, 0.657% of container) + framing 92.5 B/file' is 42,041 B (18.4%) short of the stated overhead, uses two different denominators for the same numerator, and is contradicted by the researcher's own Claim-8 figure that the manifest completes at byte 127,394. Correct: manifest 127,446 B (56.2% of overhead, 0.494% of container).

C3's pack-scale extrapolation — '96.4% of 10-file packs, 69.1% of 100-file, 1.8% of a 1084-file pack' models an i.i.d. hazard the evidence refutes: all 4 unclosed files are proj-*.md from one generator in one directory (4/28 = 14.3% there, 0/1056 everywhere else).
C6's '47x' — layout-dependent, not a property of the design. My single-line JSON manifest variant gives 34.6x. The absolute (a 2-hunk, ~1.8 KB diff) is the robust claim.

C8's 'Zip wins exactly one thing, random access (2.94 ms vs container full scan 38.48 ms)' — a container seeks by manifest-derived offset in 1.79 ms against the zip's 1.54 ms. The zip wins nothing measured; the DESIGN's trade-off table is wrong in the zip's favour.

C10's framing as an overturning — docs/engine/PLAN.md:478 already grants 'nests via backtick count' and :1062 already records a 13-level nest unwrapping byte-identically. A 3-level replication does not overturn a 13-level measurement, and §5's refusal is a v1 scope policy, not a capability claim.

'Prior art is repomix's calculateMarkdownDelimiter; adopt it' — repomix's actual function matches /`+/g anywhere with a floor of 3 and emits 5 backticks on this corpus; the spec's line-initial rule emits 4. Different algorithm, credited as the same one.

'Independently where the repomix maintainer landed in #226' — #226 is still OPEN; the maintainer wrote 'the format would be difficult to define, so it might be hard' and pointed at aider's use of 'a secondary, lightweight LLM for parsing the responses' and BOTH editor-diff and editor-whole. Not a landing, and the secondary-LLM detail contradicts the adjacent 'one scanner serves both'.

'Proven per file by digest: 1084/1084 byte-identical' offered as proof of the four-way REJOIN CONTRACT — a round-trip has zero edited files and exercises one of four branches. It proves pack∘unpack = identity, nothing about the classifier.

The headline's novelty on the carrier — docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.3 (the consolidated v1.0.0, the START-HERE document) ALREADY records the HTML comment as 'payload destroyed in 10' of 24 renderer configs 'including GitHub's blob renderer which deletes it outright' and ALREADY names the unknown-language fence as 'the only carrier reaching both a raw-file consumer and a sanitized-HTML consumer intact'. The carrier half of the headline is convergent with a settled finding, not an overturning of one. (The unclosed-fence mechanism itself IS new and additive; also note '§5' is docs/engine/PLAN.md §5, not the START-HERE plan's §5, which is 'How MDMAX enhances markdown' and contains no container spec.)
new_defects: UNDISCLOSED DEPENDENCY, and it is load-bearing twice over: the +0.892% headline requires truncating sha256 to 16 hex characters (64 bits) — visible in the researcher's own C6 evidence line 'sha256: ec3d5a26a764f1d7' and reproduced by me. With a full 64-hex sha256 the same packer costs +1.092%, i.e. 23% more overhead. Worse, that same 64-bit digest is the ONLY tamper detector in the REJOIN CONTRACT and the only integrity backstop behind the INJECTION defense. corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… — 'sha_len=64: container=25,827,702 (+1.092%) manifest=179,478' vs 'sha_len=16: container=25,775,670 (+0.888%) manifest=127,446'.

SPEC GAP that breaks the head-index property: the manifest '{i, bytes, sha256, path}' as specified is NOT sufficient to compute physical byte offsets, because 26.6% of corpus files (288/1084) carry an unrecorded '\ No newline at end of file' sentinel of 28 bytes plus an inserted newline. My first seek-by-manifest attempt returned the WRONG BYTES ('correct=False') and only succeeded once I supplied the newline flag out of band. C8's whole 'index at the head, so it streams' argument needs an explicit offset or trailing-newline flag per entry. This is a one-field fix, but the spec as written does not have it.

MEMORY UNDERSTATED BY 7x at vault scale: C9 says a naive implementation is 'O(whole container) in RAM (516 MB)'. I measured peak RSS 3,832 MB packing the same 20x corpus — 7.4x the container size — because the item list, the join buffer, the str and the encoded bytes coexist. The researcher's conclusion (streaming pack and unpack is a hard requirement) is strengthened, but the budget number is wrong and would mis-size an implementation.

C4's '100% of the corpus' is already self-eroding and the report does not say so: the corpus's only four 4-backtick runs — the reason repomix's rule would emit 5 rather than 4 — sit inside frontmatter/docs/engine/PLAN.md itself (lines 652 and 1042, the ```` ```mermaid ```` idiom). Any vault that documents the container format acquires 4-backtick runs, and if any lands at column 0 the static '4' is wrong. The claim is a snapshot fact presented as a structural one; only the re-derived max+1 rule is structural.

The DESIGN's central write-surface conclusion rests on the one block of numbers I could not re-derive at all. '119/120 WRONG on merge_across', '120/120 on reorder', '47/120 unrecoverable on truncate', '303/400 at p=0.5', '78% within 10 lines' are reported with no seed, no destruction-model specification and no script. Given that the researcher itself reports the FIRST version of this same experiment produced the opposite conclusion (200/200 recovery) purely because the destruction model changed, the result is entirely a function of an unspecified model. Under this program's own evidence discipline these should be tagged as simulation and shipped with the generator, or the 'REFUSE AND LOCALISE, NEVER REPAIR' rule should be presented as a conservative default rather than an evidenced finding.

result.area: Adversarial verification of "Markdown as a codebase — what a compiler over a FOLDER enables that per-file tools cannot" (MDMAX-BUILD folder-compiler area)

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 1 — 'The pinned corpus reproduces exactly' and there are 9,077 wikilinks resolving 25.50% vs 624 markdown-syntax file links resolving 88.62%.
verdicts.reason: The CORPUS half is CONFIRMED to the byte: my own independent verifier (/private/tmp/claude-501/adv/verify.py) re-hashed every entry and printed 'CORPUS VERIFY: files_read=1084 sha_mismatch=0 missing=0 bytes=25548765', matching manifest total_files 1084 / total_bytes 25548765 exactly. The MARKDOWN-LINK half is CONFIRMED exactly: I independently count 624 markdown-syntax .md links, 2 of them fragment-bearing, and per-root md 16/86 = 18.6% and frontmatter 17/17 = 100.0% — three figures reproduced to the digit. But the WIKILINK half carries an UNDISCLOSED FILTER. The pinned corpus contains 13,026 wikilinks, not 9,077. The 9,077 is a body-only count with YAML frontmatter stripped, which the report never states. I proved the mechanism rather than guessing it: stripping YAML frontmatter yields 9,176 (1.1% from their 9,077) AND reproduces all four of their top-ghost counts EXACTLY and in the same order — sgnk-snapshot 24, _COMMUNITY_Test 22, sgnk-design 20, concept-llm-as-judge 14 — whereas the unstripped census gives concept-llm-as-judge 28. On that same frontmatter-stripped basis I measure resolution at 29.53% (2,710/9,176), not 25.50%.
verdicts.correction: The pinned corpus contains 13,026 wikilinks. The reported 9,077 excludes 3,850 wikilinks (29.6% of the total) that live inside YAML frontmatter, carried by the keys entities: (2,283), related: (1,407), relationships: (89) and up: (49). State the filter. On the report's own basis wikilink resolution is 29.53%, not 25.50%; including frontmatter links (which resolve at only 13.95%) the all-in rate is 24.93%. The qualitative finding — the two syntaxes have opposite resolution behaviour — survives, but the gap is 58 points (29.53% vs 87.50% under strict path resolution), not 63.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 2 — 71.48% of wikilinks are GHOSTs pointing at a note that exists nowhere on disk in any of the three roots; measured against full on-disk trees of md 10,976 files, knowledge 1,008, frontmatter 1,289.
verdicts.reason: The BUCKET STRUCTURE is confirmed and the two small buckets reproduce almost exactly: on the frontmatter-stripped basis I get ON_DISK_BUT_EXCLUDED_BY_CORPUS_POLICY 33 (0.36%) against their 30 (0.33%), and EXISTS_IN_ANOTHER_ROOT 248 (2.70%) against their 244 (2.69%). Their four buckets also sum exactly to their denominator (2315+30+244+6488 = 9077), so there is no arithmetic error. But the headline GHOST rate is 67.40% (6,185/9,176) in my reproduction, not 71.48% — a 4-point overstatement in the direction that flatters the claim. Separately, the stated on-disk denominators do not reproduce at all. With all three git HEADs matching the manifest pins exactly (md 02c22ec4, knowledge 464eb666, frontmatter 798ebbf3) I count every *.md case-insensitively with NO exclusions whatsoever and get md 5,573 / knowledge 428 / frontmatter 1,460 against their claimed 10,976 / 1,008 / 1,289. Untracked node_modules drift plausibly explains md and frontmatter; knowledge has no node_modules and is off by 2.4x.
verdicts.correction: Report 67.40% GHOST, or state the resolution policy that produces 71.48%. Re-derive the on-disk tree sizes at write time or drop them — they are presented as measurements and none of the three reproduces. The load-bearing conclusion (unresolved wikilinks outnumber resolved roughly 2:1 by design, so a soft tier is correct) survives at 2.28:1 rather than 2.8:1.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 3 — Docusaurus ships hard-fail on a broken file link and warn on a broken anchor as shipped defaults; @docusaurus/core has 1,513,550 weekly downloads.
verdicts.reason: Primary-read, verified by direct curl to raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/docusaurus/main/packages/docusaurus/src/server/configValidation.ts. Lines 180-182 are verbatim as quoted, including the trailing comment: `onBrokenLinks: 'throw',` / `onBrokenAnchors: 'warn', // TODO Docusaurus v4: change to throw` / `onBrokenMarkdownLinks: undefined,`. The stated line numbers are exact. npm: api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/@docusaurus/core returns {"downloads":1513550,"start":"2026-07-24","end":"2026-07-30"} — the figure is exact and current. This is the best-evidenced claim in the area.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 4 — Headings cannot be symbols: 71.3% of heading instances carry a non-globally-unique slug, 8.9% of files contain a within-file duplicate, github-slugger disambiguates positionally, and the corpus holds 534 positionally-determined anchors.
verdicts.reason: Own re-measurement with marked 16.4.2 + github-slugger 2.0.0 over the pinned corpus (/private/tmp/claude-501/adv/head.mjs) reproduces this closely and reproduces the headline percentage exactly. Mine: 29,102 headings (theirs 29,082), 12,373 distinct slugs (12,361), within-file duplicate slug instances 538 in 95 files = 8.8% (534 in 96 = 8.9%), positional anchors where actual != base 538 (534), and heading instances whose slug is not globally unique 20,751 = 71.3% — the same 71.3% to the decimal. All four named collisions match to the digit: connections 382, tldr 367, key-ideas 315, capabilities 197. The github-slugger mechanism quote is verbatim at lines 39-41 of the local node_modules/github-slugger/index.js. Every residual delta is under 0.9% and attributable to heading-walk differences.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 5 — Naive \n\n concatenation silently loses 809 of 291,278 block tokens (0.28%); a fence-state-aware separator makes the join exactly structure-preserving, delta 0; pairwise 4 of 1,076 adjacent pairs contaminated, cause histogram {odd_fence_count_in_A: 4}, offending files md/Brain/20-projects/{proj-advox-frontend,proj-gearup,proj-knowledge,proj-skills-registry}.md.
verdicts.reason: The shippable result — which is the point of the claim — reproduces exactly. My independent run (/private/tmp/claude-501/adv/cat2.mjs) gives: naive join loses block tokens and 'identical structure' is FALSE; the fence-aware separator gives delta 0 and 'identical structure' TRUE; pairwise 4 contaminated pairs with causes {"odd_fence_count_in_A":4}; and the offending A-files are EXACTLY the four named, in the same order. That is a four-way exact match on the mechanism, the fix, the fix's completeness, and the root cause. I am not killing this on the two arithmetic wrappers because the engineering conclusion is unaffected, but they are logged as defects below: the pair (809, 291,278) is counter-dependent and did not reproduce under any token definition I could construct (top-level blocks excluding 'space' give 250 lost of 107,212 = 0.23%; a raw top-level count including 'space' shows the join GAINING 609), and 1,084 files yield 1,083 adjacent pairs, not 1,076.
verdicts.correction: State the token definition, and report the loss as 'block-token structure is not preserved' with the counter named. The pair denominator is 1,083.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 6 — The prior census's '21 transclusions in md' is 100% false positives; real transclusions in the pinned corpus are ZERO, as are Quarto/Jekyll/MkDocs/MyST includes.
verdicts.reason: Own re-measurement (/private/tmp/claude-501/adv/trans.py) plus direct inspection. `grep -ro '!\[\[' --include='*.md'` over the whole md repo returns exactly 20 hits in exactly 7 files, ALL under docs/ — matching their stated 20-in-7-under-docs to the digit. include_quarto, include_jekyll, include_mkdocs_snippet and include_myst_rst are all 0, exact. After code-span and fence masking 3 embed occurrences survive corpus-wide (they said 2) and I read each: every one is prose describing the syntax, e.g. md/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-25-sgnk-md-roadmap.md:81 'embeds/transclusion `![[...]]`' inside a roadmap table. I also confirmed the prior claim exists in wf-mdmax-capability-2026-08-01.result.json verbatim: 'transclusions 21 ... TRUE VALUE FLOW (transclusion) 21 (0.13%)'. Caveat worth stating but not disqualifying: that prior census ran over '1,989 .md, 50,480,470 bytes' — a different, larger selection than the pinned 1,084 / 25,548,765 — so 'false positive' is strictly a cross-corpus comparison; it survives only because the raw population in the entire md tree is just 20 and all 20 are prose.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 7 — Reference resolution is monadic but that does not rule out a topological scheduler; stratifying {parse(f)} ∪ {symbols} ∪ {render(f)} makes the task applicative. Quotes from snowleopard/build.
verdicts.reason: Primary-read verified by curl. src/Build/Task/Applicative.hs carries verbatim 'Dependencies of applicative tasks are known statically, before their execution.' and `dependencies task = getConst $ task (\k -> Const [k])`. src/Build/Task/Monad.hs carries verbatim 'Dependencies of monadic tasks can only be discovered dynamically, i.e. during their execution.' src/Build/System.hs line 48 is verbatim `make = topological modTimeRebuilder` and line 69 verbatim `shake = suspending vtRebuilder`. The stratification argument is sound: with that key space all three dependency sets are statically enumerable, which is exactly what Const can extract. One quote is mis-tagged as verbatim — see defects.

verdicts.claim: WEAKER FALSIFIER, self-reported — '392 [text](#heading) intra-document anchors exist and 348 (88.78%) resolve, so a compiler with no heading symbols would break 348 working links.' Carried into the DESIGN as 'heading anchors remain first-class'.
verdicts.reason: The denominator 392 is exact — I count 392 intra-document anchors independently, twice, with two different extractors. The resolution figure is not reproducible and is almost entirely an artifact of an undeclared slug algorithm. Using marked 16.4.2 + github-slugger 2.0.0 — the very algorithm Claim 4 declares canonical and reads out of local node_modules to argue headings are positionally unstable — I get 86 of 392 resolving = 21.94%, a 4x overstatement. Sweeping four algorithms over the same 392 links: github-slugger 86 (21.94%), a loose [^a-z0-9]+ slug 116 (29.59%), a dash-collapsing slug 388 (98.98%). Their 348 (88.78%) matches none of them and sits between two. The mechanism is visible in the misses: md/Zephyrus/ecosystem.md links to `#2-the-studio-people-structure` while its heading is `## 2. The Studio — people & structure`, which github-slugger renders `2-the-studio--people--structure` (the em-dash and ampersand each leave a doubled hyphen) — it resolves only under a matcher that collapses runs of dashes. So the report uses github-slugger where it supports 'headings are unstable' and a looser matcher where it supports 'headings must be in the symbol table', without saying so.
verdicts.correction: Drop '348 resolve'. The defensible and more useful finding is: intra-document anchor health swings 77 percentage points (21.94% -> 98.98%) on a one-line difference in the slug algorithm, so MDMAX must choose and publish an anchor algorithm, and that single choice is worth more link health than any other decision in the linker. Note also that the corpus is Obsidian-authored and Obsidian matches heading links by text, not by GitHub slug — which is why the loose matchers score high — so the compiler's choice also determines whether these links keep working for their existing authors.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — 'Headings are NOT exported symbols by default... A heading becomes an exported symbol ONLY when it carries an explicit author-given id.'
verdicts.reason: The design's sole escape hatch for heading symbols is an author-given heading id, but the design never names a carrier for it, and every candidate collides with a settled finding this run was told not to contradict. Explicit heading ids in markdown are markdown-it-attrs / kramdown `{#id}` syntax, which is (a) not CommonMark and therefore a dialect needing its own parser, tensioning D6 ('No dialect needing its own parser'), and (b) named in this program's own settled findings as the carrier that 'degrades to VISIBLE JUNK'. The report accepts both of those findings elsewhere and does not reconcile them here. The same gap applies to the --inline mother-markdown 'breakpoint marker': the settled 24-renderer measurement says only the link reference definition and the [//]: # idiom are invisible in 24/24, and only the unknown-language fence reaches both raw-file and sanitized-HTML consumers — the design says the separator 'carries the breakpoint marker' without picking one of them.
verdicts.correction: Name the carrier for both the heading id and the breakpoint marker, and check each against the 24-renderer table before the design is treated as settled. This is a hole, not a contradiction — but it sits on the one construct the design needs to make heading symbols safe.

None of the three reproduces; knowledge is off by 2.4x with no node_modules to explain it.

'809 of 291,278 block tokens (0.28%)' — neither numerator nor denominator reproduces under any token definition I could construct. new_defects: UNDISCLOSED FILTER, the most important defect here: the wikilink census strips YAML frontmatter without saying so. This is not cosmetic. The 3,850 excluded links are the corpus's single largest population of STRUCTURED, DECLARED edges — related: (1,407) and up: (49) are hand-authored file references, and entities: (2,283) is graphify output naming concepts rather than files. That is precisely the 'a document NAMES a capability' shape D8/D9 are about, and the two-tier HARD/SOFT design has no third tier for it. I pre-registered the opposite hypothesis and it failed honestly: frontmatter wikilinks resolve at 13.95% (md 2.9%, knowledge 25.2%), WORSE than body links, so including them lowers the headline rather than raising it and the SOFT classification is if anything better supported. But the denominator is wrong, the population is undocumented, and a reader cannot tell that a third of the corpus's wikilinks were set aside.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE SLUG MODEL, across two claims in the same report: Claim 4 reads github-slugger out of local node_modules to establish that heading anchors are positionally unstable, while the falsifier scores intra-document anchors with a materially looser matcher to establish that 348 of them work. Under github-slugger the number is 86. Under a dash-collapsing slug it is 388. One report cannot use both silently. The finding this should have produced is stronger than the one it did: anchor health swings 77 percentage points on the slug algorithm, which makes 'pick and publish the anchor algorithm' the highest-leverage single decision in the linker — and it interacts with the corpus being Obsidian-authored, where links are matched by heading TEXT rather than by any slug at all.

The design's heading-id escape hatch has no carrier and collides with two settled findings. 'A heading becomes an exported symbol ONLY when it carries an explicit author-given id' requires {#id} attribute syntax, which is not CommonMark (tensioning D6, 'no dialect needing its own parser') and which this program's own 24-renderer measurement classes as degrading to VISIBLE JUNK. The same gap applies to the --inline 'breakpoint marker', which is never bound to one of the two carriers the same measurement found invisible in 24/24 (link reference definition, [//]: # idiom) or to the unknown-language fence.

'which no existing tool does' (the hard/soft link split) is contestable by the report's own primary source and was not searched. facebook/docusaurus configValidation.ts already ships tiered defaults across link classes: onBrokenLinks 'throw', onBrokenAnchors 'warn', and in the markdown.hooks block at lines 124-125 onBrokenMarkdownLinks 'warn' against onBrokenMarkdownImages 'throw'. That is four link classes with two different severities in one shipped config. The novelty claim should be narrowed to the specific wikilink-vs-path-link split or dropped.

Cross-corpus comparison in Claim 6's 'correction to the record': the prior '21 transclusions' was measured over '1,989 .md, 50,480,470 bytes' and is being called 100% false positives on the basis of a count over 1,084 files / 25,548,765 bytes — roughly half the byte volume, with Mirrors/ and Paste/ excluded by policy. The conclusion survives because the raw ![[ population in the ENTIRE md tree is only 20 and all 20 are prose, but the comparison as written is not like-for-like and the report should say so rather than say '100%'.

Pattern worth naming for the build gate: every one of the six numeric non-reproductions above moves in the direction that flatters the area's thesis (lower wikilink resolution, higher ghost rate, more surviving intra-doc anchors, larger token loss). None moves against it. That is the same reward-function signature the previous 18-area run was flagged for, at much smaller amplitude — the structural conclusions here are sound and independently reproducible, which the previous run's were not, but the numeric discipline has the same tilt. Recommend the build team take this area's DESIGN as load-bearing and re-derive every percentage in it before any of them is quoted downstream.

verdicts.correction: Either re-measure OKF frontmatter conformance over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4 and publish the script, or delete the sentence. The §13.5 'target, not host' recommendation stands on the runtime-deferral and 52-dl/wk evidence alone and does not need this number.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN item 2 risk register: 'invisibility of the link reference definition is now a DEFAULT (`strip_references` enabled), not a property of the format, so a downstream renderer can opt into showing it.'
verdicts.reason: My own replication contradicts the framing: with `strip_references` DISABLED and the tokens fully exposed, markdown-it 15's rendered output was byte-identical to the default ('RENDER IDENTICAL: true'). Exposing the token does not make the definition visible; it changes the token stream, not the HTML. Invisibility of link reference definitions remains a CommonMark property (they produce no output by spec), not a markdown-it default. The residual concern -- that a custom renderer could now write a rule to emit those tokens -- is legitimate but is an inference about hypothetical downstream consumers, presented inside a claim tagged own-measurement.
verdicts.correction: Reframe as: the token is now addressable, so a downstream renderer COULD choose to emit it; markdown-it 15 itself does not, and rendered output is byte-identical with the rule on or off (measured). Keep the recommended regression test -- it is the right test and my run is effectively a passing instance of it.

verdicts.claim: Meta-assessment: did the researcher genuinely look for its own pre-registered falsifier?
verdicts.reason: Yes, and unusually so -- this is the strongest good-faith signal in the report. The falsifier had two limbs and limb (b) FIRED, at real cost to the researcher's own headline. I reproduced the decisive test myself: stable 0.45.4 contains 0 files matching 'Add Comment', 'Send to AI', or 'orphaned'; beta 0.46.0-beta.32 contains all three, plus the minified anchor shape `exact:i,prefix:a,suffix:o`. That finding forced the headline down from 'shipped' to 'reached beta, absent from stable' -- a researcher optimizing for impact would have skipped the tarball download and claimed a shipped competitor. Limb (a) was also genuinely executed (I re-verified both file hashes and the content-addressed header). The second falsifier, reading all 37,544 bytes of SPEC.md for range/block identity, I re-ran by grep and it did not fire. The report also satisfies the two-negatives requirement honestly: Claims 6 and 8 both cut against the program's preferred story. Two minor evidence-precision slips: the 'verbatim' minified string `status:"orphaned"` is not literally present (the shipped minified form uses backticks, `{status:`orphaned`}`), and `rewritten` was listed as a beta marker though it appears in 5 files of BOTH tarballs and so does not discriminate.

survived: HEADLINE, in full. Both halves re-derived independently and reproduced exactly: inkeep/OpenKnowledge 3,239 stars / GPL-3.0 / 14,790 dl-wk / anchoring merged 2026-07-30T23:39:04Z / beta-only at 0.46.0-beta.32 published 2026-08-01T02:38:33.569Z / absent from stable 0.45.4; OKF v0.2 with no block identity, no range anchoring, no splice guarantee, no runtime, 52 dl-wk.
Claim 1 — OKF SPEC.md sha256:5a3311d2...f948 and 37,544 bytes confirmed byte-exact; §5.1 join-key passage verbatim; grep of the full spec confirms sources[].id is the only keyed identity.

Claim 2 — OKF is NOT acquiring a runtime. All four quotes verbatim (§10, §12 deferred, §1 non-goals, README line 64 'without any bespoke runtime'). Correctly targets the live sentence at docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:458.

Claim 3 — all adoption numbers reproduced exactly: okf 52/wk, hermes-okf 31/wk, topic:okf 181, topic:open-knowledge-format 103, description 275, awesome-okf 41 stars, `pip install myokf-cli` at README:23, myokf-cli and myokf both HTTP 404.

Claim 4 — both date corrections confirmed to the second via the commits API (2026-07-24T16:45:43Z / 16:45:07Z; 2026-06-12T05:02:31Z) and HN (2026-06-13, 87 points). Correctly targets docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:182.

Claim 6 — anchor.ts sha256:9f65280c...7acc and 261 lines exact; content-addressed header verbatim; Hypothesis-32 and Semiont citations present; `grep -ril inkeep docs/` = 0 confirms the prior art was genuinely missed by the program.
Claim 7 — bracket recovery with MAX_REWRITE_GROWTH=4 / REWRITE_GROWTH_FLOOR=64 and refusal-on-ambiguity confirmed in source (minor file misattribution of one sub-quote only).

Claim 8's MECHANISM — nearest-position tiebreak confirmed, and stronger than stated: it exists in BOTH anchor-search.ts:187 and anchor.ts:170. MDMAX's genuine differentiators (fuzzy S3 tier vs verbatim 'No fuzzy matching'; published correct/false/refusal rates vs none) hold.
Claim 9 — thread-store.ts header and the changeset's single-player closing line both verbatim; convergent validation of D2 confirmed.

Claim 10 — FULLY REPLICATED by me from a fresh tarball: 0 tokens default, 2 after disable, token JSON character-identical, render byte-identical, CHANGELOG 15.0.0/2026-07-30 verbatim, 27,323,922 dl/wk exact, docs/ grep = 0.
The pre-registered falsifier was genuinely executed and genuinely fired, costing the researcher its most impressive framing. I reproduced the decisive tarball test.
DESIGN items 1 and 2 as engineering direction, and the clean-room warning, which is correct and necessary given the GPL-3.0 source.
killed: Claim 5's number '127 open' issues — IMPOSSIBLE, not merely unreproduced. GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog has 93 open issues and 97 issues in its ENTIRE HISTORY, so 127 exceeds the all-time ceiling and cannot be an issue count under any filter. Reproducible OKF/SPEC-restricted values are 73 / 65 / 58. Exceeding 97 requires silently including PULL REQUESTS (is:open+OKF = 117, is:open all = 160). DESIGN item 3 restates it as '127 open spec issues ... the only part of OKF anyone is actually asking for', inheriting the inflation. Error is in the flattering direction. The qualitative claim and all three cited issue titles survive intact.

DESIGN item 3's '73.616% conformant' — an uncited corpus number in violation of the brief's rule 3, and untraceable: grep for '73\.616' across the whole repository returns ZERO hits, and none of the report's ten claims measures it. Three-decimal precision implying a measurement that does not exist anywhere in the record.

Claim 8's quantitative transfer — 'which MDMAX measured at 22.20% false' applied to OpenKnowledge's fallback. MDMAX's 22.20% measures content-hash-plus-nearest-position with NO context tier; OpenKnowledge's tiebreak fires only on the residue surviving exact-match plus bestByContext, with context widened at create time until the triple is unique. The structurally comparable row in MDMAX's own table is 'rigid context fingerprint' at 0.25% false — ~89x lower. An inference presented as a measurement; DESIGN item 1(b) inherits it.

DESIGN item 2's risk-register line that invisibility 'is now a DEFAULT ... not a property of the format' — my own replication shows render is byte-identical with strip_references enabled or disabled, so exposing the token does not make the definition visible. Legitimate as a forward-looking inference, but not what the measurement shows.
Claim 7's file attribution for `rewritten?: boolean` — the EVIDENCE block is headed anchor-search.ts, where the symbol occurs 0 times; it is in packages/server/src/comments/anchor.ts (2 occurrences).
new_defects: The report quotes GPL-3.0 source verbatim and at length (anchor.ts, anchor-search.ts, thread-store.ts) while DESIGN item 1 simultaneously mandates 'specify from the published behaviour, never from their source'. The research record itself now contains the source the clean-room instruction forbids using. Before any implementation, the team needs a written provenance boundary: which artifacts implementers may read, and a behaviour-only spec derived by someone who has not read anchor.ts. Flagging as a process risk, not a research error.

The minified string `status:"orphaned"` presented as a verbatim tarball finding is not literally present — the shipped bundle uses template literals, `{status:`orphaned`}`. The underlying substance (present in beta, absent in stable) is confirmed by my own grep, but the quoted form would not reproduce for anyone re-running it.

`rewritten` is listed among the beta-only markers, but it appears in 5 files of BOTH the 0.45.4 and 0.46.0-beta.32 tarballs and therefore does not discriminate stable from beta. The three genuinely discriminating markers are 'Add Comment', 'Send to AI', and 'orphaned'.

OpenKnowledge's two anchoring paths behave DIFFERENTLY on the tied case and the report does not distinguish them: anchor.ts (server) returns {status:'orphaned'} when nearest is still tied (line 186), while anchor-search.ts (app) returns best[0] when the position hint is undefined (line 191) — i.e. it guesses. If the team benchmarks against 'OpenKnowledge behaviour', it must specify WHICH path; they are not the same policy.

Unmeasured dependency risk in DESIGN item 2: markdown-it 15.0.0 is a MAJOR version with breaking changes I observed in the CHANGELOG (linkify-it => v6, 'No fuzzy links by default', 'No auth part check by default', Unicode punctuation terminating links). Pinning markdown-it@^15 is recommended without any assessment of these breaks against the certificate matrix, whose 24-config measurements were taken on an earlier line.

result.area: Adversarial verification of "The strongest case that MDMAX should not be built" — the claim that four of six MDMAX capabilities have executed working substitutes

verdicts.claim: C1 — 6,233 doc lines vs 365 src/test lines in 5ff90a4^..HEAD = a 17.1:1 doc-to-code ratio, and none of the 365 lines is engine work
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The bucketing reproduces byte-for-byte: `git diff --numstat 5ff90a4^..HEAD` gives docs +6233 -0, src/test +365 -26, other +0 -0; 16 commits; the five named files are exact; the seven engine-term greps over src/ return 0/0/0/0/0/0/0. But the RATIO is inflated in BOTH directions. Denominator: `git diff --numstat` prints `-	-` for test/preview/html-policy-xss.test.ts because git classified it binary — I ran `git show HEAD:test/preview/html-policy-xss.test.ts | wc -lc` = 327 lines / 16,643 bytes of ordinary TypeScript, silently dropped from the 365. Numerator: 1,494 of the 6,233 'documentation' lines are executable code committed in the same window — build-dossier.py 464, dossier.html 874, dossier.css 132, measure-overflow.mjs 24 (`git diff --numstat 5ff90a4^..HEAD -- docs | grep -v '\.md'`); markdown-only additions are 4,739.
verdicts.correction: On the researcher's own path bucketing, corrected only for the binary omission: 6233/692 = 9.0:1, not 17.1:1 — a 47% overstatement. Counting code as code: 4,739 prose lines vs 2,186 code lines = 2.17:1. The load-bearing qualitative point survives untouched (no MDMAX engine code exists), and the plan already says it about itself — docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §9.8: 'a 439 KB PDF about an engine with zero lines of code.'

verdicts.claim: C2 — 13 of 20 commits (not the plan's 12) are 100% docs paths; only 8 src+test files added since the app was cloned
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Per-commit classification over `git log -20` reproduces the researcher's list exactly: 798ebbf 3/3, 88a92f4 3/3, 8c0a426 5/5, 9055884 1/1, 525ad98 1/1, c565be9 1/1, f60eac0 1/1, c847f62 1/1, 575768e 1/1, ae81971 1/1, 57411a1 1/1, 33d1b3c 1/1, 5ff90a4 22/22 = 13 commits at 100%. `git ls-tree -r --name-only 0c1b427 | grep -cE '^(src|test)/'` = 309; at HEAD = 317; `git diff --name-status 0c1b427..HEAD -- src test | grep -c '^A'` = 8. docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:479 does read '12 of 20 commits are docs'. The correction runs against the plan and is correct.

verdicts.claim: C3 — KILL GATE K1 FIRES: a 30-line LCS diff resolves 86.658% with 77.297pp provably unambiguous vs content-hash-alone's 77.297%, strictly dominating and absorbing the entire ambiguity class S2 exists for
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The MEASUREMENT reproduces. My independent run — corpus_id sha256:3a010b16…, all 494 consecutive commit pairs touching a pinned-corpus file across all three roots, 31,149 anchorable block-versions under the plan's own §4.1 gate — gives LCS 85.036% matched, 76.346% on text unique in the old document, 8.690% on duplicate text; hash-alone-unique 76.352%. Their 86.658/77.297/9.361 on 394 pairs is the same result. I also checked the derivation they used for 'hash-alone': lcs_missed_but_hash_unique = 2 of 31,149, so the substitution is sound. But the CONCLUSION does not follow, on two counts. (a) K1's text is '`diff3-assisted` matches or beats CONTENT-DERIVED RE-ANCHORING on consecutive pairs' — content-derived re-anchoring is the full S1+S2+S3 scheme the plan books at 99.627% (§4.1 table), not the hash-alone row. 86.658% < 99.627%, and their own similarity gap-fill (90.17%; I get 88.789%) is still 9 points short — and a similarity gap-fill IS S3, the mechanism the claim says is unnecessary. K1 has not fired on the evidence presented. (b) 'absorbs the entire ambiguity class' conflates guessing with resolving: LCS makes a silent ORDER-based tiebreak on duplicate text, and the plan measured exactly that trade at 0.00% → 22.20% false. My own context proxy: of 2,707 duplicate-text LCS matches, 111 (4.10%) have NEITHER neighbouring block matching — 0.356% of all anchorable block-versions, ~7× the plan's claimed 0.050% false rate.
verdicts.correction: The finding is also not new: §9.3 already states 'the 294-revision-pair corpus was built from git history — the diff was in hand for all 41,642 block-versions and was never used as a baseline' and pre-registers diff3-assisted as benchmark arm 7. The insight is the plan's; the measurement is the researcher's, and it is good.
