Also note K1's own 'then' clause hands the invention the arbitrary-interval case — which the researcher's F2 admits they did not measure. Firing K1 therefore licenses a re-scope, not a cut.

verdicts.claim: C4 — token-count stratification shows all residual anchoring risk lives in blocks of ≤9 tokens: 47.0% of 3–5-token matches on duplicate text, 0.34% at 10–19, 0 of 13,426 at 20+
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Reproduces on my independent 494-pair run, corpus_id sha256:3a010b16…: by_token_bucket {matched, at-risk} = 3-5 [5329, 2360] = 44.28%; 6-9 [3899, 337] = 8.64%; 10-19 [3298, 10] = 0.30%; 20+ [13962, 0] = 0.00%. 2,697 of 2,707 at-risk block-versions (99.63%) are ≤9 tokens. The monotone collapse and the exact zero at 20+ both hold. This is the most valuable thing in the submission.
verdicts.correction: One scope note, not a defect: this is not the stratification §11/line 405 asks for. That asks for correct/false/refusal stratified by token count; what exists is matched/at-risk, because neither run has ground truth for 'false'. The 47.0% figure is an ambiguity rate, not an error rate.

verdicts.claim: C5 — splice-only writing is four lines over mdast offsets, byte-identical on 1,080/1,080 pinned-corpus files under identity round-trip and edit-then-restore
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The corpus selection is exactly right — I verified all 1,084 manifest sha256 digests match on disk, 25,548,765 bytes, 1,080 non-empty — and my run reproduces 1080/1080. But the test is a MATHEMATICAL TAUTOLOGY and cannot fail. `src.slice(0,s) + src.slice(s,e) + src.slice(e) === src` is true for ANY s ≤ e. I ran it with deliberately wrong offsets (2,7), absurd offsets (0,1) and a degenerate range (11,11): all four return true. A test that cannot go red proves nothing about whether mdast offsets are correct — LR#68 exactly. Second problem: `spliceBlock(src, node, newText)` is NOT safe as a four-line API. When I spliced a non-syntax-preserving replacement into each block and reparsed, the document's top-level block structure was disturbed in 994 of 1,080 files (a heading replaced by a bare word merges with its neighbour; a fence replaced by a word swallows the following blocks).
verdicts.correction: I re-ran a version that CAN fail — substitute one alphabetic character inside the block, reparse, require the block count preserved AND every other block's source text unchanged — on an explicit subset of corpus_id sha256:3a010b16… (every 3rd non-empty file ≤30KB, first 12 blocks each): 299/299 files, 2,832 splices, 0 disturbed. So the CONCLUSION is right and mdast offsets are correct. But the stated evidence is vacuous, and the API needs a reparse-and-verify guard, which is engine work.

verdicts.claim: C6 — the budgeted-projection ratio is overstated 4–10×: a headings-only index tier is 14.9× corpus-wide, not the plan's 61–152×, a number appearing exactly once with no derivation
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement + primary-read] Tier mismatch. I reproduce their number precisely (headings-only = 14.93× corpus-wide, median 11.66 per file, 1,710,778 index bytes vs their 1,712,207; and their single-file reproduction of docs/engine/PLAN.md at 409 nodes / 78 headings / 106,298 B / 4,474 B / 23.76× is exact). But the plan's INDEX tier is one line PER DOCUMENT, not per heading. The derivation is stated in docs/engine/research/wf-mdmax-capability-2026-08-01.result.json → /synthesis/1/ranked/0/evidence: 'full/index: MD-hand 90.37x (123 files, 2,346,224 B), knowledge 61.12x (236 files, 3,501,530 B), frontmatter/docs 66.60x (46 files, 766,848 B)'. Dividing bytes by ratio by file count gives 211.1, 242.8 and 250.3 bytes per DOCUMENT — consistent across three differently-sized corpora, and matching its `ships_as` spec: 'one index line per document carrying path + title + one-sentence description + SIZE'. On the pinned corpus (25,548,765 B / 1,080 files = 23,656 B per file), a 211–250 B/doc index yields 94.6×–112.1× — inside the claimed 61–152×. The researcher's own 14.93% figure is the OUTLINE tier, and the same evidence field states the outline band as 14.82–35.49×; 14.93 sits at its floor. They independently reproduced the outline tier and reported it as a refutation of the index tier.
verdicts.correction: 'Appears exactly once with no derivation' is also false: it is in PLAN.md:146, wf-mdmax-capability-2026-08-01.result.json, .raw.json and .journal.jsonl, with five named corpora and byte totals. BUT the researcher surfaced a real defect that caused their own error: PLAN.md:146 puts two incompatible definitions of 'index' in one sentence — a heading-based single-file example (77 headings, 4,171 B, 25.5×) immediately followed by a document-based five-corpus range (61–152×). That sentence should be split.

verdicts.claim: C7 — pain #13 (round-trip-sacred frontmatter) is already solved by yaml's parseDocument/set/toString, a two-call swap, not a compiler
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Both halves of their worked example reproduce exactly. gray-matter round trip is not byte-identical: it drops both `#` comments, unquotes "My Note", rewrites `date: 2026-08-01` → `2026-08-01T00:00:00.000Z`, `empty:` → `empty: null`, and quotes `'n': 3`. yaml's Document API preserves comments, key order, quoting and leaves the body byte-identical. Versions confirmed installed: gray-matter 4.0.3, yaml 2.9.0, both direct deps in the committed package.json. But I then ran it against the real corpus. On corpus_id sha256:3a010b16…, 907 files carry a genuine `---` frontmatter block, and a NO-EDIT yaml parseDocument→toString round trip is byte-identical on only 119 of them — 13.12%. 618 drift (610 of those purely flow-sequence spacing, `tags: [daily]` → `tags: [ daily ]`), and 170 (18.7%) do not parse at all: `related: [[video-…]], [[video-…]]` is Obsidian's convention and invalid YAML (UNEXPECTED_TOKEN), as is any plain scalar containing `@file` (BAD_SCALAR_START).
verdicts.correction: yaml is strictly better than gray-matter (13.12% vs 3.64% exact, and gray-matter throws on 171 of 907) so the DIRECTION is right and the swap is worth making. But 'already solved… a two-call swap' is not established: 86.9% of real frontmatter blocks would still be reformatted on save, and 18.7% cannot be round-tripped by either library. Solving pain #13 requires splicing the changed scalar's own range inside the frontmatter block — which is the engine work the claim says is unnecessary.

verdicts.claim: C8 — the founders' demand research ranks the compiler's flagship benefit 13th of 14 and the program defers its own #1 whitespace to serve its own #13 pain
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Every verbatim quote is exact. Row 13 reads '| 13 | Markdown/frontmatter mangling | Churns the purist early adopters | Obsidian's properties UI destroys YAML comments/order; plugin exists just to undo it |'. Rows 1–12 are in precisely the order given. 'Top 3 whitespace combinations nobody ships: 1. Real-time collab + plain markdown files + git history' is verbatim. docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:79 'Deliberately deferred: backend (Firestore vs anything else), auth mechanism, pricing numbers, mobile, real-time multiplayer' is verbatim. But the central move — equating 'the compiler's flagship benefit' with pain #13 — is the researcher's own mapping, and the plan maps it elsewhere explicitly. docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:39: 'Google Docs' real moat is not typing. It is the review loop — a comment that stays attached to the sentence it was about, a suggestion you can accept, a history you can diff. Every one of those needs a durable name…'. That is pain #6 — 'Real-time collab impossible in markdown-land | Kills adoption (teams) | The one thing switchers concede to Google Docs'.
verdicts.correction: An inference presented as a finding, and it inverts the conclusion: mapped to the plan's own stated purpose, MDMAX serves a 'Kills adoption (teams)' theme ranked 6th, not a 'Churns the purist early adopters' theme ranked 13th.

verdicts.claim: C9 — in 550,131 bytes of demand research, real-time collaboration appears in 138 string leaves vs 20 for commenting and 2 for provenance, a 6.9:1 gap, and F3 is therefore REFUTED
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Every raw count reproduces EXACTLY — 210,828 B / 1,853 leaves and 339,303 B / 1,951 leaves; realtime 51+87=138; commenting 3+17=20; provenance 0+2=2; 'block id' 0/0, 'block ref' 1/0, 'splice' 0/2, 'conformance' 0/1. The 6.9:1 RATIO is an instrument artifact. The collaboration side used a broad three-alternative stem, `real[- ]time|multiplayer|collaborat` — `collaborat` alone matches 114 of the 138. The commenting side used a narrow multi-word-phrase whitelist requiring literals like 'leave a comment' or 'suggestion mode'. On a symmetric instrument, de-confounded by dropping URL leaves (Reddit permalinks all contain '/comments/' — 144 of them) and stripping 'N pts / N comments' score metadata: review-loop terms (`comment|annotat|suggestion mode|track change|redlin`) = 169 leaves; collaboration terms (same regex as theirs) = 95. That is 1.78:1 in favour of the review loop — the OPPOSITE DIRECTION.
verdicts.correction: This inverts their own pre-registered falsifier. F3 was 'the founders' demand corpus evidences commenting/compiler capability at rough parity with real-time collaboration.' At 169 vs 95 it is better than parity. F3 FIRED and was declared REFUTED by an asymmetric instrument. The provenance finding (2 leaves) survives intact and is the strongest part of C9.

verdicts.claim: C10 — OKF v0.2 makes provenance/trust/lifecycle/staleness first-class in plain markdown+YAML, which is MDMAX §4.5 outright plus §6's detectable-staleness promise, shipped seven weeks before this gate
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] I fetched the spec directly: `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/main/okf/SPEC.md` → HTTP 200, 37,544 bytes, exactly as stated. The §1 quote is verbatim at line 44: 'OKF v0.2 makes provenance, trust, lifecycle, and attestation first-class while keeping the format minimally opinionated.' §5.1 `sources` carries resource/id/author/usage_count/last_modified as claimed; §5.2 generated/verified, §5.3 tiers unverified/machine-confirmed/human-reviewed, §5.4 status, §5.5 stale_after, §10 attested computations all confirmed by direct read. GitHub search for '"open knowledge format"' returns total_count 287 and scaccogatto/okf-skills at 206 stars created 2026-06-14 — both confirmed. But 'that is MDMAX §4.5 outright' is wrong. §4.5's stated need is per-SPAN provenance: 'Where did this span come from — which source, which page, which method, at what confidence… A table recovered by a model at 0.71 confidence and a verbatim text-layer extraction are indistinguishable downstream.' A case-insensitive grep for span|character offset|byte range|per-paragraph|inline annotation across all 37,544 bytes returns 0. And the spec explicitly REFUSES confidence, line 314: 'It does not store a credibility score: a score is subjective, unportable across consumers, and goes stale.'
verdicts.correction: OKF ships document/concept-level provenance with in-body claim citation by source id. That is the half of §4.5 nobody needed an engine for. The half that needs one — span, page, method, confidence — is absent by design. Separately: the 8,134 stars / 688 forks / created 2026-05-04 and the two SPEC.md commit SHAs are NOT verified by me; api.github.com returned HTTP 403 rate-limit on the repo and commits endpoints.

verdicts.claim: Meta — did the researcher genuinely hunt its own pre-registered falsifiers?
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Two of three, genuinely and well. F2's self-incriminating '20.476 days' reproduces to three decimals as the md-root median inter-revision gap in my own independent pair enumeration (md n=357 median=20.476; all three roots pooled n=499 median=1.602, p25=0.006 d). They reported the pessimistic slice against their own headline rather than the flattering pooled one. The arXiv 1512.06195 citation is verbatim-correct from the primary source, which I fetched: 'containing 20,953 highlighted text annotations… about 22% of highlighted text annotations can no longer be attached to their live Web pages.' Narrowing the headline to 'consecutive-revision and in-app' on the strength of a fired falsifier is exactly the discipline the gate asks for.
verdicts.correction: F3 is the exception and it matters, because F3 is the falsifier that guards the whole 'subordinate library, not a compiler' recommendation. It was tested with an instrument whose asymmetric breadth guaranteed the flattering answer, and under a symmetric instrument it fires. Two hunted honestly, one instrumented to lose.

survived: C2 in full — 13 of 20 commits are 100% docs paths (my per-commit classification matches theirs commit-for-commit), 309→317 src+test files, exactly 8 added since the clone. The plan's §9.8 '12 of 20' is wrong and the correction runs against the plan.

C4 in full — the token-count stratification reproduces on my independent 494-pair, 31,149-block run: 3-5 tokens 44.28% at-risk, 6-9 8.64%, 10-19 0.30%, 20+ 0.00% (0 of 13,962). 99.63% of all at-risk block-versions are ≤9 tokens. Monotone collapse and the exact zero at 20+ both hold. This is the most valuable artifact in the submission.

The LCS anchoring MEASUREMENT itself (not the K1 conclusion drawn from it) — 85.036% resolved / 76.346pp on unique text, against hash-alone-unique 76.352%. LCS does dominate hash-alone on resolution rate, and I confirmed the substitution they used for the hash-alone baseline is sound (only 2 of 31,149 blocks are hash-unique but LCS-missed).

Corpus integrity — all 1,084 manifest sha256 digests match on disk, 25,548,765 bytes, 1,080 non-empty. Their file selection IS the pinned corpus, and the 1,080-vs-1,084 gap is exactly the four zero-byte files.

gray-matter's lossiness, exactly as described — comments dropped, quoting stripped, dates coerced to ISO timestamps, `empty:` rewritten to `empty: null`; and worse than described, it throws on 171 of 907 real frontmatter blocks in the pinned corpus.

Every OKF fact reachable from primary source — SPEC.md HTTP 200 / 37,544 bytes, the §1 first-class quote verbatim at line 44, all of §5.1–§5.5 and §10, GitHub search total_count 287, okf-skills 206 stars.
arXiv 1512.06195 verbatim — 20,953 highlighted-text annotations, ~22% no longer attachable — cited honestly against their own headline.
Every verbatim quote from docs/FRONTMATTER-PRODUCT-PLAN.md and docs/mdmax/PLAN.md, including the full ranked pain table, the whitespace list and the deferral line.
The splice CONCLUSION, on my own re-test — 299/299 files and 2,832 syntax-preserving splices with structure and all sibling blocks intact. mdast offsets are correct.
C1's load-bearing half — 0 hits for all seven engine terms across src/, and no MDMAX engine code exists anywhere in the repo.
killed: C6 REFUTED — tier mismatch. The plan's INDEX tier is one line per DOCUMENT (211.1 / 242.8 / 250.3 bytes per file, derived by me from its own stated ratios × byte totals ÷ file counts across three corpora), not one line per HEADING (1,585 B/file, what was measured). On the pinned corpus a 211–250 B/doc index yields 94.6–112.1×, INSIDE the 61–152× band. Their 14.93× is the OUTLINE tier, whose stated band in the same evidence field is 14.82–35.49× — they reproduced it and mislabelled it a refutation. 'Appears exactly once with no derivation' is also false: 4 files carry it and the derivation names five corpora with file counts and byte totals.

C9's 6.9:1 ratio REFUTED — an artifact of a broad 3-alternative stem regex on the collaboration side against a narrow multi-word-phrase whitelist on the commenting side. Symmetric, URL- and score-metadata-de-confounded: review loop 169 leaves vs collaboration 95, i.e. 1.78:1 the OTHER WAY. This inverts their own pre-registered falsifier F3, which fires rather than being refuted.

C3's headline 'KILL GATE K1 FIRES' — K1 requires beating content-derived re-anchoring (the full S1+S2+S3 scheme at 99.627%), not the hash-alone row. 86.658% (mine: 85.036%) and even the gap-filled 90.17% (mine: 88.789%) fall 9–13 points short. And the gap-fill IS S3, the mechanism being argued away.

C3's 'absorbs the entire ambiguity class' — LCS order-guesses the duplicate class rather than resolving or refusing it. My context proxy: 111 of 2,707 duplicate-text matches (4.10%) have neither neighbouring block matching — 0.356% of all anchorable block-versions, ~7× the plan's claimed 0.050% false rate. The plan measured exactly this trade at 0.00% → 22.20% false.
C5's evidence — the identity round-trip is a tautology that returns true for deliberately wrong offsets, absurd offsets and a degenerate range. It cannot go red, so it certifies nothing (LR#68).

C7's 'already solved… a two-call swap' — yaml's no-edit round trip is byte-identical on only 119 of 907 real frontmatter blocks (13.12%) in the pinned corpus; 618 drift, 170 (18.7%) do not parse at all under yaml 2.9.0.
C10's 'that is MDMAX §4.5 outright' — 0 occurrences of span / character offset / byte range / per-paragraph / inline annotation in 37,544 bytes, and the spec explicitly declines to store confidence.
C8's mapping of the compiler to pain #13 — the plan maps it to the review loop at PLAN.md:39, which is pain #6, 'Kills adoption (teams)'.

C1's 17.1:1 ratio — 327 lines of real TypeScript were dropped from the denominator because git classified html-policy-xss.test.ts as binary, and 1,494 of the 6,233 'documentation' lines are executable build code. Corrected on their own bucketing: 9.0:1.
new_defects: REPO STATE, needs a human: the working-tree package.json has been clobbered from the committed 98 lines to `{"type":"module"}` — `git diff --stat package.json` = 1 insertion, 97 deletions. Every npm script (build, dev, test, typecheck, lint, verify, tauri:*) is gone in the working tree. This is almost certainly a research agent's edit to let it run .mjs files from the repo root. I did not touch it (RULE 4). `git checkout -- package.json` restores it; src/modules/vault/infrastructure/search-index.ts also carries an uncommitted 11+/4- change that should be inspected before any restore.

docs/mdmax/PLAN.md:146 puts two incompatible definitions of 'index' in one sentence — a heading-based single-file example (77 headings, 4,171 B, 25.5×) followed immediately by a document-based five-corpus range (61–152×). This is what produced the verifier's false kill and will produce the next one. Split the sentence and name each tier's unit.

18.7% of the pinned corpus's frontmatter (170 of 907 blocks) is not valid YAML under yaml@2.9.0 — Obsidian's `related: [[a]], [[b]]` convention throws UNEXPECTED_TOKEN and plain scalars containing `@file` throw BAD_SCALAR_START. Any provenance-in-frontmatter design (including the OKF §5 read-back recommendation) inherits this failure surface on the product's own primary corpus.

A four-line `spliceBlock(src, node, newText)` is unsafe without a guard: with non-syntax-preserving replacement text it disturbs top-level block structure in 994 of 1,080 pinned-corpus files. The safe version reparses and asserts block count plus sibling-text invariance — small, but it is engine work, and it is the kind of thing D7 exists to make explicit.

The 99.627% / 0.050% / 0.323% headline remains re-derived by NOBODY — not by the plan (§9.4 says so in writing, and §11 W2 flags it), not by this researcher, and not by me. Kill gate K2 is therefore still untested, and both sides of this debate are arguing about a number neither has reproduced. That, not the diff baseline, is the highest-value next measurement.

Neither run has ground truth for 'false'. Every anchoring number on both sides — 86.658%, 85.036%, 99.627% — is a resolution or match rate, not a correctness rate. Until someone hand-audits a sample, K1, K2 and K3 cannot be adjudicated, only argued.

result.area: Adversarial verification of "Technical foolproofing — what makes a markdown compiler unbreakable" (MDMAX final research gate)

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 1 — mdast-util-from-markdown is quadratic on a FLAT bullet list: 1,129/5,554/20,626/196,096 ms at 20k/50k/100k/200k items (6.09 MB), micromark 392/842/1,821/3,835 (k=1.08), Lezer 61/133/241/460; mdast 51.1x slower at 200k; 'k≈1.9 at 25k–100k, 9.5x per 2x above 100k'.
verdicts.reason: I regenerated the corpus and got BYTE-IDENTICAL files (588890 / 1488890 / 2988890 / 6088890), so the generator is fully reproducible, and the 20k–100k regime reproduces tightly: mdast 1101.3 / 5675.3 / 22504.7 ms (k=1.789 then 1.987), micromark 379.2 / 854.9 / 1806.7 (k=0.887 then 1.080), Lezer 57.6 / 135.7 / 246.8. The paragraph control at matched byte counts is linear for mdast (287.5 / 592.2 / 1157.2 ms, k=0.789 then 0.966), so the finding IS list-specific and content-independent. But the flagship 200k numbers do not reproduce: mdast 359,959.2 ms (not 196,096), gap 72.4x (not 51.1x), 100k→200k ratio 15.99x → k=4.00 (not 9.51x → k=3.25). I ruled out GC as the cause — rerunning at --max-old-space-size=12288 gave 337,172.9 ms, only 6% faster than the 4,288 MB default — so the cost is algorithmic, but at k=3.2–4.0 it is NOT 'quadratic', and the two independent runs of the same code disagree by 1.8x. micromark is also not linear across the full range: my 100k→200k is 1806.7→4971.3 ms, k=1.46, not 1.08. Harness: $TMPDIR/av/run1.mjs, node v24.6.0 darwin arm64.
verdicts.correction: The load-bearing conclusion — 'do not build an mdast tree; consume micromark events or the Lezer tree' — survives decisively (mdast is 19.4x slower than micromark at the SAME 2.99 MB on lists vs paragraphs). But state the regime, not a scaling law: mdast is super-linear on list items with a measured exponent of 1.79–1.99 between 20k and 100k, degrading to k≈3.2–4.0 above 100k with a machine-dependent absolute cost of 196–360 s at 200k. Drop the word 'quadratic' from the headline and drop the single-machine '9.5x per 2x' and '51.1x' figures, or band them.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 2 — WIKILINK_RE in src/modules/vault/infrastructure/markdown-parser.ts:12 is exactly quadratic on unclosed '[[' AND 'runs synchronously on the browser main thread for every file in the vault snapshot'.
verdicts.reason: The quadratic half CONFIRMS: I timed the verbatim regex and got 577.4 ms / 2,282.5 ms / 9,258.1 ms at 20,000 / 40,000 / 80,000 '[[' (40/80/160 KB), successive ratios 3.953x and 4.056x on 2x input ⇒ k = 1.983 and 2.020 — within 8% of the brief on absolutes and identical in exponent. The realistic variant is worse than the brief says: 40,000 lines of '- see [[Note N' (749 KB) takes 11,012.9 ms. The LOCATION half is REFUTED. parseMarkdown is imported in exactly two places (src/container/dependency-container.ts:11 and src/modules/vault/infrastructure/search-index.ts:15); both are server-only composition — dependency-container imports repoEnv/githubFetch, search-index imports getZipball/getHeadSha. I enumerated every 'use client' file in src and NONE imports dependency-container, markdown-parser, or search-index. SnapshotProvider.tsx is a client component but only fetches /api/vault/snapshot. next.config.ts has no `output: 'export'`, so the API routes are real server handlers.
verdicts.correction: The regex defect is real and I confirm it, but it blocks the shared Node event loop inside /api/vault/snapshot, /api/vault/folder, /api/share and the search index — it does not freeze the user's tab. That makes it a single-request server DoS affecting every concurrent user, not a client-side jank bug. State it that way; the fix (index scan instead of backtracking regex) is unchanged, but the worker-isolation prescription now has to be about the server process, not the browser main thread.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 3 — SHIPPED DEFECT: a 336-byte YAML alias bomb freezes the browser tab for ~12 s, because SnapshotProvider.tsx:78 does localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(snapshot)) and ParsedNote carries frontmatter: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> verbatim.
verdicts.reason: The primitives reproduce: my 337-byte 9-level alias bomb parses in gray-matter in 1.7 ms, structuredClone in 0.0 ms, JSON.stringify throws RangeError: Invalid string length after 4,612.2 ms at 1,082 MB RSS, and eemeli/yaml refuses it with 'ReferenceError: Excessive alias count indicates a resource exhaustion attack'. The SHIPPED-DEFECT chain does not. The frontmatter object never reaches any JSON.stringify. `grep -rn '\.frontmatter' src` returns exactly ONE hit outside the parser: get-snapshot.ts:199, `const slugRaw = (note.frontmatter as Record<string, unknown>)['public_slug']`, read as a string. The snapshot DTO that SnapshotProvider stringifies is VaultSnapshot = {sha, generatedAt, tree, notes: NoteMeta[]} and NoteMeta (src/modules/vault/application/dto.ts:35-43) is {path, title, tags[], outbound[], backlinks[], excludeFromGraph, publicSlug?} — no frontmatter field. The projection at get-snapshot.ts:196-209 discards it. Second independent reason: even if it were carried, src/app/api/vault/snapshot/route.ts does `JSON.stringify(snapshot)` on the SERVER before the client ever sees bytes, and JSON has no aliases, so a client object with shared references cannot exist.
verdicts.correction: This is an inference presented as a measurement — ParsedNote was conflated with VaultSnapshot. Re-file it as a latent hazard: gray-matter/js-yaml accepts an alias bomb that eemeli/yaml refuses, and any future code path that serialises a parsed frontmatter object inherits a 4.6–12 s freeze plus a RangeError. The prescriptions (switch to eemeli/yaml, add a node-count guard) stay justified on the parser-choice evidence alone; the 'browser tab freezes today' framing does not.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 4 — share-writer.ts calls matter.stringify(parsed.content, data), changing the frontmatter block on 695 of 737 files (94.3%), 33 byte-identical, 8 trailing-newline-only, body changed on 0 of 737; modal damage is a double-to-single quote flip. D7 violation in production.
verdicts.reason: Exact reproduction over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4 (I re-hashed all 1,084 files first: 1084/1084 sha256 match, 0 missing). My run: {sRun:737, sIdentical:33, sTrailingNlOnly:8, sBodyChanged:0, sFmChanged:695}. 695/737 = 94.30%. Modal damage confirmed as the quoting flip, e.g. md/Courses/WithArin Claude Code/WithArin Claude Code.md `up: "[[Home]]"` → `up: '[[Home]]'`. Source confirmed verbatim at src/modules/share/infrastructure/share-writer.ts:26 `const next = matter.stringify(parsed.content, data);` — and the file's own doc comment at line 3 claims it works by 'splicing the key into the YAML frontmatter', which it does not. This is a genuine D7 (splice-only writing) violation.
verdicts.correction: Two nits, neither fatal. (a) The stated triple does not sum: 33+8+695 = 736, not sRun=737. The missing file is md/pj.md, where matter.stringify itself THROWS — the researcher's harness evidently had no guard there and dropped the row silently. (b) '695 of 737 files with frontmatter' mislabels the denominator: 907 corpus files have a frontmatter block; 737 is the subset whose YAML parses. Against all files with frontmatter the rate is 695/907 = 76.6%.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 5 — Two shipped YAML parsers return different TYPES for the same field on 84.8% of real files: js-yaml and eemeli/yaml both parse 737 of 907 frontmatter blocks, agree on which 737, and disagree in 625 of them across 973 field occurrences, every divergence being YAML-1.1 !!timestamp Date vs YAML-1.2 string.
verdicts.reason: Reproduced to the digit over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4: {filesWithFrontmatterBlock:907, jsOk:737, eeOk:737, bothParsed:737, onlyJsAccepts:0, onlyEeAccepts:0, filesWithValueDiff:625, occurrences:973, kinds:[['Date() vs string()',973]]} — exactly one divergence class, no others, as claimed. 625/737 = 84.80%. Example md/Daily/2026-05-26.md :: title: Date(Tue May 26 2026 05:30:00 GMT+0530) vs string(2026-05-26). The two-parser topology also checks out in source: gray-matter/js-yaml at markdown-parser.ts:112 (server, vault index) and eemeli/yaml at src/modules/preview/presentation/frontmatter.ts:17 via `parseDocument`, consumed on the browser main thread by PropertiesPanel.tsx:55 `useMemo(() => parseFrontmatter(content), [content])`.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 6 — Obsidian wikilinks in YAML frontmatter break YAML on 170 of 1,084 pinned-corpus files (15.68%); both parsers reject identically (0 asymmetric); reason histogram 148 / 10 / 6 / 6; markdown-parser degrades but share-writer has no try/catch so Share is broken on 15.68% of the corpus.
verdicts.reason: Reproduced exactly over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4: jsErr=170, eeErr=170, onlyJsAccepts=0, onlyEeAccepts=0, bothThrow=170. 170/1084 = 15.68%. My reason histogram sums to exactly the claimed shape: 'end of the stream or a document separator is expected' 148, 'missed comma between flow collection entries' 10, 'can not read a block mapping entry' 6, 'incomplete explicit mapping pair' 6 → 170. Degradation asymmetry confirmed in source: markdown-parser.ts:110-119 wraps `matter(raw)` in try/catch with the comment 'A single bad note must NEVER crash the whole vault snapshot'; share-writer.ts:19 calls `matter(file.content)` bare.
verdicts.correction: One refinement on blast radius: the throw is caught one level up by the generic handler in src/app/api/share/route.ts, which returns HTTP 502 {error:'upstream_failure'}. So Share fails on those files with a misleading upstream error rather than an unhandled crash — still broken, but the user-visible symptom is a wrong status code, not a 500 or a process kill.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 7 — worker.terminate() interrupts a synchronous non-yielding parse (max overshoot 5.4 ms on a 250 ms budget across 9 shapes), BUT resourceLimits.maxOldGenerationSizeMb:32 did NOT stop a worker reaching heapUsed 3,382 MB / rss 4,030 MB parsing an 11.9 MB file TO COMPLETION (105x over the declared cap), so memory containment is pattern-dependent and must not be relied on.
verdicts.reason: The TIME half confirms: an infinite `for(;;){}` worker was reclaimed at 253.9 ms wall on a 250 ms budget (overshoot 3.9 ms) and at 1,002.9 ms on a 1,000 ms budget; micromark on the 6.09 MB flat list was reclaimed at 254.1 ms. The MEMORY half fails on the researcher's own shape. I built a 12,000,030-byte / 400,001-paragraph file and ran mdast-util-from-markdown in a worker with resourceLimits:{maxOldGenerationSizeMb:32}: the limit FIRED at 85.6 ms, exit code 1, and the parent's 'error' handler received `Error: Worker terminated due to reaching memory limit: JS heap out of memory`. The worker never completed and never approached 3,382 MB. It also fired on micromark + the 6.09 MB flat list at 78.2 ms with the same error. A worker cannot hold 3,382 MB under an effective 32 MB old-generation cap; the reported `limits` field in that evidence was almost certainly echoed from workerData rather than from an applied limit — self-confirming instrumentation.
verdicts.correction: The researcher's own follow-on observation is the one that survives: at resourceLimits 256 MB my run hard-aborted the whole PROCESS with rc=134 and a V8 `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory` trace, killing the parent. So the correct statement is the inverse of the one made: the cap fires reliably when it is TIGHT (32 MB → clean catchable ERR), and becomes an uncatchable process abort when it is LOOSE (256 MB). The design's byte/line/list-marker PRECHECK is still the right call and the parent must still expect all four outcomes — but the stated justification ('the guard silently does nothing') is refuted, and the constant chosen for maxOldGenerationSizeMb is now the thing that decides whether you get an exception or a SIGABRT. That is a design parameter, not a best-effort footnote.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 8 — THE BRIEF'S CRASH ATTRIBUTION IS BACKWARDS. Bisected: marked 16.4.2 parses 1,907 nested '>' in 10.6 ms and fails at 1,908 with 'SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression' (it builds a regex proportional to blockquote depth) — a regex-size limit, not a stack overflow; micromark parsed depth 200,000 in 28,328 ms with no crash.
verdicts.reason: The DIRECTION confirms and I endorse it: micromark never crashed at any depth I tested (1,000 / 5,000 / 20,480 / 50,000 → 7.5 / 24.7 / 250.0 / 2,166.5 ms, all OK), Lezer likewise (2.3 / 2.7 / 7.7 / 21.6 ms), and marked does throw — so 'remark CRASHES THE PROCESS on 20 KB of nested blockquotes' is indeed wrong and the researcher is right to say so. The BISECT SPECIFICS do not reproduce. Running marked in a FRESH process per depth (to remove bisect order/JIT contamination) for both natural shapes: '>'.repeat(d)+' x' and '> '.repeat(d)+'x', depth 1907 → OK (11.4 / 14.2 ms) and depth 1908 → OK (10.6 / 13.0 ms). First failure is at depth ~2733 for both shapes, and the error is `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` — a stack overflow, precisely the class the claim says it is NOT. My own single-process bisect gave 2734, so the discrepancy is not order effects on my side.
verdicts.correction: The mechanism 'it builds a regex proportional to blockquote depth' is an inference from an error string, and I could not reproduce the error string it rests on. Restate as: marked 16.4.2 throws a catchable RangeError (stack overflow) at blockquote depth ~2,733 on this build; micromark and Lezer do not throw at 50,000. Also worth adding as its own finding: micromark's depth cost is k=2.42 between depth 20,480 and 50,000 (250.0 → 2,166.5 ms), so 'micromark is linear' is measured on flat lists only and does not hold for nesting.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 9 — THE BRIEF UNDERSTATES THE BRACKET BOMB BY 3–4x: on the exact 80,002-byte CVE-2023-22484 shape micromark takes 34,209.7 ms and mdast 26,488.0 ms, not the 8.6 s in the brief; Lezer 1,110.2, marked 19.0; nested-bracket exponent k=1.77.
verdicts.reason: The MEASUREMENTS reproduce well — on 40,000 '[' + 'a' + 40,000 ']' I get micromark 38,540.4 ms, mdast 25,700.5 ms, marked 17.4 ms, Lezer 1,042.5 ms; and the micromark scaling 3.2 / 9.9 / 37.2 / 123.8 / 516.5 ms at n=500..8000 fits k=1.90 over 2000–8000 against the researcher's 1.77, same class. But the CLAIM being made is a comparative one — 'the brief understates by 3–4x' — and it is arrived at by comparing this machine's wall-clock to another machine's wall-clock, which is not a valid inference; my own micromark number is 12.7% above the researcher's on identical bytes, and my mdast number is 3.0% below, on the same hardware and node build. Nothing here can distinguish 'the brief measured a different machine' from 'the brief measured a different shape'. Also, the described construction (40,000 '[' + 'a' + 40,000 ']') yields 80,001 bytes, not the 80,002 stated.
verdicts.correction: Report the absolute measurement with its hardware and stop there: on node v24.6.0 / darwin arm64, an 80 KB nested-bracket document costs micromark ~34–39 s and mdast ~26 s while Lezer costs ~1.0–1.1 s and marked does not implement the construct. That is a devastating enough number on its own and it does not need the cross-machine ratio, which cannot survive scrutiny.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 10 — THE OFFSET MODEL: bytes and UTF-16 units diverge on 93.4% of the corpus, not 4.5%; only 71 of 1,084 files (6.55%) have bytes==UTF-16==code points==graphemes; the engine PLAN's '103 of 2,314 files (4.5%)' understates the real boundary risk 21x.
verdicts.reason: Every raw number reproduces to the digit over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4: {n:1084, allFourEqual:71, b_ne_u16:1013, u16_ne_cp:38, cp_ne_gr:42, maxSkewBytesU16:533366 in md/_Archive/Satinath Content JSON (raw source).md, totals {bytes:25548765, utf16:24699622, codepoints:24699360, graphemes:24573891}}; skew 849,143 = 3.324%. But the INTERPRETATION is a category substitution, and my own instrumentation shows why: I additionally counted files containing at least one non-ASCII character and got 1,013 — EXACTLY equal to b_ne_u16. So 'bytes != UTF-16 units' is not a discovered hazard, it is the definition of 'this file is not pure ASCII'. For the UTF-16-native offset model the design itself chooses in §3, the boundary that can be split is a surrogate pair, i.e. non-BMP — which on this corpus is 38/1084 = 3.51%, LOWER than the PLAN's 4.5%, not 21x higher. The '21x' divides a 93.45% rate over 1,084 files by a 4.5% rate over a different 2,314-file selection, so it is both a different phenomenon and a different denominator.
verdicts.correction: Keep the numbers, drop the multiplier and the 'PLAN understates' framing. The honest statement is: 93.45% of files need a byte↔UTF-16 conversion at any byte boundary (true of any non-ASCII corpus); 3.51% carry non-BMP characters where a UTF-16 offset can split a surrogate pair; 3.87% have code-point!=grapheme boundaries. The design prescriptions — one unit, one OffsetMap, branded U16Offset/ByteOffset/GraphemeIndex, assertBoundary — are all independently justified by the 3.51% and 3.87% figures and by the 533,366-unit worst-case skew. They do not need the 93.4% headline, which will not survive a reviewer who notices it is just 'contains a non-ASCII byte'.

verdicts.claim: META — Did the researcher genuinely look for its own pre-registered falsifier, or write one it knew it would not find?
verdicts.reason: Genuinely looked, and this is the strongest part of the submission. Clause (1) was a real risk to the headline and I re-ran it: mdast on paragraphs at matched byte counts (588890/1488890/2988890) is linear at k=0.789 then 0.966 while the same bytes as list items give k=1.789 then 1.987 — the control could have killed the finding and did not. Clause (2) was run across four sizes. Clause (3) produced a result AGAINST the brief the researcher was handed ('remark CRASHES THE PROCESS') and was reported as a refutation of its own tasking rather than buried, and the researcher volunteered the one thing it could not falsify (the rc=134 SIGABRT), which I independently reproduced at resourceLimits 256 MB. I also tried to manufacture a kill on the incidental 'stripCode is the only ReDoS in that file' claim and FAILED: 16,000 unmatched fences (229 KB) strip in 0.3 ms and 80,000 unmatched backticks (240 KB) in 0.8 ms — both linear, so that claim stands.
verdicts.correction: The falsifier's scope is the weakness, not its sincerity. All three clauses interrogate TIMING, and every defect I killed is a REACHABILITY or MECHANISM error — does the alias bomb reach JSON.stringify (no), does the regex run in the browser (no), was resourceLimits actually applied (yes, and it fired), does marked fail at 1,908 with a SyntaxError (no). A fourth pre-registered clause of the form 'for each shipped defect, trace the value from parse to the failing call and show the type that carries it' would have caught three of the four. Recommend that clause be mandatory for any claim tagged SHIPPED DEFECT.

survived: The core prescription: do not build an mdast tree. mdast-util-from-markdown is super-linear on flat list items (my k=1.789 at 20k→50k, 1.987 at 50k→100k) while a paragraph control at identical byte counts is linear (k=0.789, 0.966) — 19.4x slower on the same 2.99 MB. Lezer is the cheapest at every size. Content-independent and list-specific, exactly as claimed.

The 20k–100k timing table, reproduced within ~10% on every cell: mdast 1101.3/5675.3/22504.7 vs claimed 1129/5554/20626; micromark 379.2/854.9/1806.7 vs 392/842/1821; Lezer 57.6/135.7/246.8 vs 61/133/241. The generator reproduces byte-identical files (588890/1488890/2988890/6088890).

CLAIM 2's regex quadratic. WIKILINK_RE timed verbatim: 577.4 / 2,282.5 / 9,258.1 ms at 20k/40k/80k '[[', ratios 3.953x and 4.056x on 2x input ⇒ k=1.983 and 2.020. The realistic half-typed-vault variant is WORSE than reported: 11,012.9 ms on 749 KB.

CLAIM 4 in full, over corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4: {sRun:737, sIdentical:33, sTrailingNlOnly:8, sBodyChanged:0, sFmChanged:695} = 94.30%, modal damage a double→single quote flip. share-writer.ts:26 is a genuine D7 violation and its own doc comment falsely says 'splicing'.

CLAIM 5 to the digit: 907 frontmatter blocks, 737 parsed by both, 0 asymmetric acceptances, 625 files with a value divergence across 973 occurrences, EXACTLY one class (js-yaml Date vs eemeli string). 625/737 = 84.80%.
CLAIM 6 to the digit: 170/1084 = 15.68%, both parsers reject identically, reason histogram 148/10/6/6 summing to 170.

CLAIM 7's time guard: worker.terminate() reclaimed an infinite for(;;) spin at 253.9 ms on a 250 ms budget and micromark on 6.09 MB at 254.1 ms. terminate() does interrupt synchronous non-yielding JS. This is the load-bearing fact of the isolation design and it holds.

CLAIM 8's direction: micromark never crashed at blockquote depth 50,000 (2,166.5 ms) and Lezer took 21.6 ms; marked throws. The brief's 'remark CRASHES THE PROCESS on 20 KB of nested blockquotes' is correctly refuted.
CLAIM 9's absolute measurements on the 80 KB bracket bomb: micromark 38,540.4 ms, mdast 25,700.5, marked 17.4, Lezer 1,042.5 — same class as reported on every parser.
CLAIM 10's raw corpus arithmetic, every figure exact: 71 / 1013 / 38 / 42 / 533366 and totals 25548765 / 24699622 / 24699360 / 24573891.

DESIGN §5's surprising corpus fact: link reference definitions occur 0 times. I parsed all 1,084 files with mdast — 0 definition nodes, 0 linkReference nodes, 0 imageReference nodes, 0 parse errors. The argument for adopting Lezer's TreeFragment.applyChanges rather than writing an invalidation rule stands.

The incidental claim that stripCode is linear and WIKILINK_RE is the only ReDoS in markdown-parser.ts. I attacked it and failed: 16,000 unmatched fences (229 KB) = 0.3 ms; 80,000 unmatched backticks (240 KB) = 0.8 ms.

Corpus integrity: all 1,084 pinned files re-hashed, 1084/1084 sha256 match, 0 missing, corpus_id confirmed as sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4 with total_files 1084 / total_bytes 25548765.
killed: CLAIM 3's shipped-defect attribution. The YAML alias bomb cannot reach JSON.stringify: NoteMeta (dto.ts:35-43) carries no frontmatter field, and `grep -rn '.frontmatter' src` returns exactly one consumer — get-snapshot.ts:199 reading ['public_slug'] as a string. Independently, route.ts stringifies on the SERVER first and JSON has no aliases, so the client object cannot contain shared references. 'A 336-byte file freezes the browser tab for ~12 seconds' is an inference presented as a measurement.

CLAIM 7's memory half. resourceLimits:{maxOldGenerationSizeMb:32} DID fire on the researcher's own shape — mdast on a 12,000,030-byte / 400,001-paragraph file terminated at 85.6 ms with a catchable parent 'error': `Error: Worker terminated due to reaching memory limit: JS heap out of memory`. It never reached 3,382 MB. The reported `limits` field was echoed, not applied.

CLAIM 8's bisect. In fresh processes, marked 16.4.2 parses depth 1907 AND 1908 successfully (11.4 / 10.6 ms) on both natural blockquote shapes; first failure is ~2,733 with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` — a stack overflow, the exact class the claim says it is not. 'It builds a regex proportional to blockquote depth' is an inference from an error string I could not reproduce.

CLAIM 2's location. parseMarkdown is server-only: imported at dependency-container.ts:11 and search-index.ts:15, both server composition; zero 'use client' files in src import it; next.config.ts has no static export. It blocks the Node event loop, not the browser main thread.

CLAIM 1's headline numbers above 100k. mdast at 200k reproduces as 359,959.2 ms not 196,096 (1.84x), gap 72.4x not 51.1x, per-2x ratio 15.99x (k=4.00) not 9.51x (k=3.25). A 12,288 MB heap rerun gave 337,172.9 ms — only 6% faster — so it is not GC, but at k=3.2–4.0 it is not 'quadratic' either, and two runs of identical code disagree by 1.8x.

CLAIM 10's '21x understatement of boundary risk'. b_ne_u16 (1013) is EXACTLY equal to my independently-counted 'files containing at least one non-ASCII character' (1013) — it is a tautology, not a hazard. The surrogate-splitting risk the design actually guards is non-BMP at 38/1084 = 3.51%, LOWER than the PLAN's 4.5%. The multiplier divides two different phenomena over two different denominators (1,084 vs 2,314 files).

CLAIM 9's comparative framing. 'The brief understates by 3–4x' compares this machine's wall-clock to another machine's; my own micromark figure is 12.7% above the researcher's on identical bytes and identical hardware. Cross-machine timing ratios cannot support the claim. Also the described construction gives 80,001 bytes, not 80,002.
new_defects: UNREPORTED SHIPPED DEFECT, more severe than CLAIM 4: gray-matter's stringify re-parses its string argument. node_modules/gray-matter/index.js:161 reads `matter.stringify = function(file, data, options) { if (typeof file === 'string') file = matter(file, options); ... }`. share-writer.ts:26 passes `parsed.content` — a raw string — so the BODY is re-parsed as if it had its own frontmatter. On md/pj.md this THROWS a YAMLException from inside matter.stringify (surfacing as a 502 on Share), and for any body beginning with a '---' delimited block it will silently consume that block as frontmatter and DROP it. This accounts for the missing file in the researcher's own 33+8+695=736 vs sRun=737. It converts CLAIM 4 from 'cosmetic quoting churn' into 'possible silent body truncation', which is the one thing D4/D7 exist to prevent.

micromark is NOT linear outside the flat-list case, contradicting the design's central parser-choice argument. On nested blockquotes my measurements give k=2.42 between depth 20,480 and 50,000 (250.0 → 2,166.5 ms). On the flat list itself, my 100k→200k point is k=1.46 (1,806.7 → 4,971.3 ms), not the k=1.08 quoted. 'Consume micromark's event stream' inherits a super-linear depth cost that the k=1.08 headline hides; only Lezer stayed near-linear on every shape I tested (452.4 ms at 200k items, 21.6 ms at depth 50,000, 1,042.5 ms on the bracket bomb).

The resourceLimits finding inverts into a design parameter nobody has chosen. A TIGHT cap (32 MB) produces a clean catchable ERR in the parent at 78–86 ms; a LOOSE cap (256 MB) produced rc=134 and a V8 `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed` that killed the whole process including the parent. The design says resourceLimits 'is still SET ... and costs nothing' — on this evidence a badly-chosen value is the difference between an exception and a SIGABRT, so the constant must be specified and regression-tested, not documented as best-effort.

Rule-3 violations in the DESIGN block: three corpus-derived numbers carry no corpus_id and no stated alternative selection — 'the real corpus's worst is "how to use:" at 2,324', 'real-corpus average is 186', and Tier B's '997/1,080 identical (92.31%)'. The last also uses a denominator of 1,080, four files short of the pinned 1,084, with no explanation; 997/1084 would be 91.97%. These are exactly the uncited-corpus-number defect the evidence discipline names.

The design's Tier A/D conformance figures ('micromark is already 652/652', 'marked scores 531/652 (81.4%)', '121 known divergences') are stated as measurements but no CommonMark 0.31.2 spec suite is present in this repo and I could not verify them locally. The arithmetic is internally consistent (531/652 = 81.44%, 652-531 = 121) but the numbers themselves are unverified here and should be tagged secondary until the suite is vendored.

result.area: Is there actually a new era of markdown, or is that a story we are telling ourselves
result.headline: There is a real regime change, but it is in markdown's CONSUMER and in a brand-new tooling category, not in volume and not in the format: the render-what-a-model-emitted stack grew ~3x the npm baseline (react-markdown 11,786,121 -> 103,114,261/mo, streamdown 0 -> 14,477,148/mo since 2025-08-14, remend 0 -> 16,192,091/mo since 2025-12-03) and AGENTS.md went 0% to 26.51% of the 300 most-starred GitHub repos in 15 months, while generic markdown parsers grew only 1.44x faster than the whole npm registry, markdown's share of repository file trees FELL 12.68% -> 10.41% (2024-08 -> 2026-06, 12 repos), and CommonMark has shipped zero new conformance examples in any released version since 2021-06-19 with spec commits declining every single year since 2019.
result.falsifier: PRE-REGISTERED, four falsifiers, written before the conclusion. (F1) If markdown's share of repository file trees ROSE materially 2024-08 -> 2026-06, "not volume" is wrong. Looked: pooled across 12 cloned repos it FELL 12.68% -> 10.41%; absolute .md count went x0.97 while total files went x1.18; share fell in 7 of 12. Did not fire. (F2) If generic markdown parsers outgrew the npm baseline by more than 2x, "not volume" is wrong. Looked: markdown-parser median x4.05 vs 14-package control median x2.81 = 1.44x excess. Did not fire. (F3) If the format itself showed renewed activity, "not the format" is wrong. Looked: CommonMark released examples 652 (0.30, 2021-06-19) -> 652 (0.31.2, 2024-01-28); last release 2.5 years ago; commits/yr 48/15/14/15/13/11/7/6 from 2019 to 2026; cmark-gfm's last release is 0.29.0.gfm.13 on 2023-07-21, still pinned to CommonMark 0.29 (2019). Did not fire. (F4) If a NEW class of model-specific markdown package grew far faster than everything else, then "just volume growth, no new era" would be wrong. IT FIRED. streamdown x179.60 in ten months, remend from nonexistent to 16.2M downloads/month in seven. My first-draft headline was "there is no new era, only npm-wide inflation." F4 killed it and I rewrote the headline to the regime-change-in-consumer form above. That rewrite is the honest record of this area.

findings.claim: A markdown tooling category that did not exist 12 months ago is now at 14-16 million downloads per month, and every member of it exists because the AUTHOR of the markdown is a model. This is the single strongest evidence for a regime change and it is not volume growth.
findings.evidence: api.npmjs.org/downloads/point, fetched 2026-08-01. streamdown: 2025-08 = 80,606 -> 2026-06 = 14,477,148 (x179.60); npm registry.npmjs.org/streamdown gives created=2025-08-14. remend: 2024-08 = 0 -> 2026-06 = 16,192,091; created=2025-12-03. rehype-harden 2026-06 = 16,052,832. harden-react-markdown created=2025-07-31.

findings.claim: The purpose of that new category, in its own words, is that markdown produced by a model is a DIFFERENT PARSING PROBLEM from markdown produced by a person — arriving incomplete, token by token, with unterminated blocks.
findings.evidence: registry.npmjs.org/streamdown, README verbatim: "Formatting Markdown is easy, but when you tokenize and stream it, new challenges arise. Streamdown is built specifically to handle the unique requirements of streaming Markdown content from AI models, providing seamless formatting even with incomplete or unterminated Markdown blocks." package description: "A drop-in replacement for react-markdown, designed for AI-powered streaming." remend description: "Self-healing markdown. Intelligently parses and styles incomplete Markdown blocks."

findings.claim: Generic markdown parsers grew only 1.44x faster than the npm registry baseline. Most of the apparent markdown explosion is npm-wide inflation, not markdown.
findings.evidence: api.npmjs.org/downloads/point, 2024-08-01:2024-08-31 vs 2026-06-01:2026-06-30. 8 markdown parsers (marked, markdown-it, remark-parse, unified, mdast-util-from-markdown, showdown, commonmark, markdown-it-attrs) median x4.05. 14-package non-markdown control (lodash, chalk, js-yaml, xml2js, handlebars, ejs, semver, dotenv, express, axios, typescript, react, webpack, eslint) median x2.81. Excess = 4.05/2.81 = 1.44x. Same 1.44x over 2022-08 -> 2026-06.

findings.claim: The growth is concentrated exactly where model output is rendered, and legacy markdown renderers with no AI-stack position are SHRINKING. That pattern is a consumer shift, not a volume shift.
findings.evidence: 2024-08 -> 2026-06 npm point downloads: react-markdown 11,786,121 -> 103,114,261 (x8.75); rehype-raw 5,759,306 -> 52,886,938 (x9.18); remark-gfm 14,035,123 -> 110,967,795 (x7.91); shiki 8,103,106 -> 64,247,830 (x7.93). Against control median x2.81 that is ~3x excess. Meanwhile markdown-to-jsx 22,908,372 -> 18,185,739 = x0.79, an absolute DECLINE; showdown x1.85 and commonmark x1.73, both BELOW the npm baseline.

findings.claim: Agent-instruction markdown went from nonexistent to a quarter of the most-starred repositories on GitHub in about 15 months. This is the clearest convention birth on the record.
findings.evidence: HEAD root-tree census via api.github.com/repos/{r}/git/trees/HEAD over the 300 highest-starred GitHub repos (stars:>30000, fetched 2026-08-01), 215 measured: AGENTS.md 57/215 = 26.51%; CLAUDE.md 51/215 = 23.72%; .claude/ 27/215 = 12.56%; skills/ 16/215 = 7.44%; README.md 201/215 = 93.49%. Earliest AGENTS.md creation date in the sample is 2025-05.

findings.claim: That adoption curve is already FLATTENING, not accelerating. Monthly new AGENTS.md files in the sample halved after March 2026.
findings.evidence: First-commit month of the AGENTS.md path per repo (api.github.com/repos/{r}/commits?path=AGENTS.md, oldest page via Link rel=last), 49 dated of 57: 2025-05 +2, 2025-09 +4, 2025-10 +4, 2025-11 +5, 2026-01 +5, 2026-02 +7, 2026-03 +7, then 2026-04 +4, 2026-05 +2, 2026-06 +3, 2026-07 +3. Peak +7/month in Feb-Mar 2026; last four months average +3.0/month.

findings.claim: llms.txt is measurably dead in the population that matters, and so is .cursorrules. Convention births mostly do not survive; the settled llms.txt cautionary note is if anything understated.
findings.evidence: Same 215-repo census, 2026-08-01: llms.txt 1/215 = 0.47%; .cursorrules 2/215 = 0.93%; GEMINI.md 5/215 = 2.33%; AGENT.md 0/215 = 0.00%; .windsurfrules 0/215. For contrast CONTRIBUTING.md, a 15-year-old convention, is 106/215 = 49.30%. AnswerDotAI/llms-txt (created 2024-09-01, 2,541 stars) has ~100 commits total across 23 months with zero-commit months in 2025-07/08/09 and 2026-02/03.

findings.claim: Markdown is now the single most-read file type inside an AI agent's tool loop — ahead of every programming language — in a workspace that is majority TypeScript/React.
findings.evidence: Scan of all 13,947 .jsonl transcripts under ~/.claude/projects (290,674 tool_use lines), 2026-08-01. Of 36,840 Read tool calls: .md 8,661 = 23.51% (rank 1), .png 20.82%, .tsx 16.51%, .ts 11.09%, .py 6.01%. Of 19,391 Write/Edit/MultiEdit calls: .tsx 25.47%, .md 4,791 = 24.71% (rank 2). NOTE: this is NOT the pinned corpus; it is an explicitly different selection — one workspace's complete Claude Code transcript set.

findings.claim: Nearly half of all markdown an agent reads is markdown an agent itself wrote. The machine-to-machine loop is not a projection, it is already 44% of traffic.
findings.evidence: Same transcript set (~/.claude/projects, 13,947 files, 2026-08-01): 1,563 distinct .md paths read (8,663 read calls); 1,258 distinct .md paths written (4,791 write calls); 659 paths in BOTH = 42.2% of read paths and 52.4% of written paths. Read calls landing on an agent-written file: 3,832 / 8,663 = 44.2%.

findings.claim: Within the pinned corpus, essentially all NEW markdown is created inside an agent session. 94.3% of files created in June 2026 and 92.4% of July 2026.
findings.evidence: corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. SELECTION: the 991 of 1,084 corpus files that are git-tracked at each root's pinned head (md 691/756, knowledge 249/272, frontmatter 51/56). Creating commit (git log --diff-filter=A --root --no-renames) carries an AI marker (message contains 'claude' / 'Generated with' / the Claude Code robot trailer): 578/991 = 58.3% overall; by creation month 2026-05 69/450 = 15.3% (the human legacy vault import), 2026-06 448/475 = 94.3%, 2026-07 61/66 = 92.4%. Per root: knowledge 248/249, frontmatter 51/51, md 279/691.

findings.claim: NEGATIVE-ADJACENT CORRECTION: markdown's share of repository file trees did not grow. It fell. The 'markdown volume explosion' framing is not supported at the repo level.
findings.evidence: 12 repos cloned --filter=blob:none --bare (tailwindcss, express, flask, requests, axios, prettier, astro, fastapi, vite, svelte, transformers, langchain), git ls-tree -r at rev-list -1 --before=DATE. 2024-08-01 -> 2026-06-01: pooled .md+.mdx 4,357 -> 4,228 (x0.97) while all files 34,360 -> 40,617 (x1.18); pooled share 12.68% -> 10.41%; median per-repo share 8.25% -> 5.08%; share fell in 7 of 12 repos. Over 2020-08 -> 2026-06 (n=10) pooled share 12.40% -> 12.08%, up in 5 down in 5.

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO A SETTLED FINDING. 'CommonMark has had zero net new conformance examples since 2021' is right in spirit and wrong in detail, and the precise version matters because the plan cites a count from it.
findings.evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec/{tag}/spec.txt: 0.29 date '2019-04-06' = 649 examples; 0.30 date '2021-06-19' = 652; 0.31.2 date '2024-01-28' = 652; master HEAD today still reads version '0.31.2' date '2024-01-28' but carries 655 examples. So: zero net new in any RELEASED version since 2021-06-19, and +3 sitting unreleased on master for 2.5 years. docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.2 cites '443 of 655 CommonMark spec examples' — that is master, not a release, and should be labelled as such.

findings.claim: GitHub's own markdown flavour has not been released in three years and is still pinned to a 2019 CommonMark base. If markdown's job had genuinely changed, the reference implementation would show it.
findings.evidence: api.github.com/repos/github/cmark-gfm/releases: latest tag 0.29.0.gfm.13, published_at 2023-07-21. Preceding: 0.29.0.gfm.12 (2023-07-13), 0.29.0.gfm.11 (2023-04-06). The tag name pins CommonMark 0.29, whose spec.txt date is '2019-04-06'. Repo not archived (archived: false), open_issues_count 135, last commits 2026-07-13 'Merge pull request #383 ... cmake-version' and 2025-12-19 'Update cmake minimum requirement.' — build-system housekeeping, not spec work.

findings.claim: The most-used markdown parser in the JS ecosystem has not shipped a release in 34 months while its usage went up 4.5x. Consumption changed; tooling did not move at all.
findings.evidence: registry.npmjs.org/remark-parse: latest version 11.0.0 published 2023-09-18, total_versions 31, releases per year 2019:3 2020:7 2021:2 2023:2 and nothing in 2024, 2025 or 2026. Downloads 2024-08 = 36,005,792 -> 2026-06 = 161,511,318 = x4.49. Same shape at markdown-it: zero releases in all of 2025, and a 31-month gap between 14.0.0 (2023-12) and 15.0.0 (2026-07-30). Only marked is genuinely active (18.0.7 @ 2026-07-21, 13 releases in 2026).

findings.claim: The share of an agent's file reads that are markdown roughly quadrupled across three months, and the trend survives removing every markdown-research project from the sample.
findings.evidence: Transcript scan bucketed by record timestamp. All 13,947 transcripts: .md share of Read calls 6.17% (2026-05, n=2,106) -> 16.94% (2026-06, n=9,859) -> 27.53% (2026-07, n=24,844); of Write/Edit calls 6.08% -> 20.81% -> 30.17%. Confound-controlled by dropping every project directory matching frontmatter/md/knowledge/.claude/zephyrus/scratchpad (11,475 transcripts kept): 6.06% -> 17.04% -> 24.71% reads, 5.43% -> 22.22% -> 30.01% writes. CAVEAT: three months is not the 24-36 month window the brief asked for, and this is one workspace.

findings.claim: METHOD DEFECT FOUND AND DISCARDED: the GitHub REST code-search API cannot be used as an adoption proxy and any finding built on it is invalid. Flagging because it is the obvious tool for this question.
findings.evidence: api.github.com/search/code?q=path:README.md returned {"total_count":1152,"incomplete_results":false}. There are more than 100 million README.md files on GitHub. The same endpoint returned path:AGENTS.md 131, path:CLAUDE.md 98, path:SKILL.md 99, path:llms.txt 72 — all with incomplete_results:false. The endpoint also rate-limits at 10 requests/minute. I discarded every one of these numbers and rebuilt the census from git trees instead.

findings.claim: OKF has a real, dated, seven-week-old third-party ecosystem but I could not locate a canonical Google-owned spec repository, and every top implementation is Claude Code tooling rather than a runtime.
findings.evidence: api.github.com/search/repositories?q=open-knowledge-format+in:name returns total_count 23, every one created on or after 2026-06-14. Highest-starred OKF repos overall: scaccogatto/okf-skills (created 2026-06-14, 206 stars, "The OKF toolkit for Claude Code"), serradura/okf-gem (2026-07-11, 115), OWOX/models (2026-06-26, 85), 0dust/OKFy (2026-06-14, 62). Four guessed canonical paths all returned HTTP 404: google/open-knowledge-format, googleapis/open-knowledge-format, GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format, open-knowledge-format/spec.

findings.claim: The streaming-markdown category has already forked across frameworks, which is what a category looks like rather than one lucky package. And nothing in the same search space serves block identity or collaborative comments.
findings.evidence: registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search?text=incomplete+markdown+streaming returns, in the top 8: remend, streamdown, markstream-vue ("Vue/Nuxt streaming Markdown renderer for AI chat, LLM token stream"), svelte-streamdown, vue-stream-markdown ("Streaming markdown output, Useful for text streams like LLM output"). The same endpoint for text=markdown+block+anchor+id and text=collaborative+markdown+comments returns zero markdown-anchoring or markdown-commenting packages in the top 8 — only babel block-scoping plugins, strip-json-comments and CKEditor 5.

findings.claim: The two halves imply DIFFERENT PRODUCTS and the plan is currently built for the half that is not growing. frontmatter's thesis is the human review loop; the measured growth is the machine loop, and the plan has no coverage of it.
findings.evidence: grep -rniE 'stream(ing|down)|incomplete (markdown|block)|unterminated|partial (markdown|parse)' over docs/mdmax/PLAN.md, docs/engine/PLAN.md, docs/engine/README.md returns 3 hits, all about MD4C parser architecture speed ('MD4C (streaming callbacks)', 'MD4C (streaming) | 1.174 s | reference floor'). Zero hits for incomplete/unterminated/partial markdown. Against that: 44.2% of measured agent markdown reads land on agent-written files, and streamdown+remend together are ~30.7M downloads/month.

negatives: THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE — markdown's share of repository file trees FELL, not rose. Across 12 major repos cloned locally and measured with git ls-tree at pinned commits, pooled .md+.mdx share went 12.68% -> 10.41% between 2024-08-01 and 2026-06-01; the absolute markdown file count went DOWN (4,357 -> 4,228, x0.97) while total files went UP (x1.18); per-repo share fell in 7 of 12. Over the full 2020-08 -> 2026-06 window the pooled share is essentially flat (12.40% -> 12.08%, up in 5 repos, down in 5). If there were a markdown volume explosion, repositories are where it would show, and it does not. The dominant signal is repository restructuring (langchain 6.03% -> 0.97%, svelte 12.49% -> 1.54%, prettier 14.10% -> 4.98% as docs sites moved out), which is noise, not a trend.

SECOND STRONGEST — the format and its reference implementations got QUIETER during the supposed new era, not busier. CommonMark: 649 examples at 0.29 (2019-04-06), 652 at 0.30 (2021-06-19), 652 at 0.31.2 (2024-01-28) — zero net new released conformance examples in five years and no release at all in 2.5 years; the three 0.31.x releases all landed on the same day (2024-01-28), a version-bump train rather than sustained work; commits to the spec repo per year run 48 (2019), 15, 14, 15, 13, 11, 7 (2025), 6 (2026 partial) — monotonically declining through exactly the window in question, with the most recent spec.txt change being the copy-edit 'Removed uses of "may not."' (2026-02-24). GitHub's cmark-gfm has not cut a release since 0.29.0.gfm.13 on 2023-07-21 and is still pinned to CommonMark 0.29 from 2019. remark-parse has shipped nothing since 11.0.0 on 2023-09-18 while its downloads rose 4.49x. A format whose job had genuinely changed would show it in the spec. This one shows the opposite.

THIRD — the entire consumer-shift measurement is n=1 and three months long. The 23.51%-of-reads and 44.2%-machine-loop numbers come from ONE person's 13,947 Claude Code transcripts, in a workspace whose owner spent June and July 2026 building a markdown compiler. The time series only spans 2026-05 to 2026-08, which cannot support any claim about the 24-36 month window the brief asked about. The confound control (dropping frontmatter/md/knowledge/.claude/zephyrus projects, 11,475 transcripts kept) preserves the trend (6.06% -> 17.04% -> 24.71%) but cannot remove the fact that this person's own work shifted toward documentation over those months.

FOURTH — 'AI-marked' in the corpus authorship measurement means the creating commit mentions Claude, not that a model wrote the prose. A human typing every word inside a Claude Code session gets the same trailer. So 94.3% for June 2026 is an upper bound on machine authorship in the strict sense and a lower bound in the loose sense (agent-written files committed by hand are missed). It measures 'created during an agent session', which is the honest reading and a weaker claim than 'machine-authored'.

FIFTH — convention births mostly die, and the sample proves it against the same measuring stick that produced the AGENTS.md number. In 215 top-starred repos: llms.txt 0.47%, .cursorrules 0.93%, AGENT.md 0.00%, .windsurfrules 0.00%, GEMINI.md 2.33%. AGENTS.md at 26.51% is currently the exception, and its own monthly add rate has already halved from +7/month (Feb-Mar 2026) to +3.0/month (Apr-Jul 2026). Betting the product on 'agent conventions keep growing' is betting on a curve that is visibly bending over.
unclaimed: A markdown document model that accepts INCOMPLETE input as a first-class state — a prefix with an unterminated fence, a half-written table row, a dangling link — and produces stable block identities that do not renumber when the next token arrives. The rendering layer solves this (streamdown 14,477,148/mo, remend 16,192,091/mo, plus markstream-vue, svelte-streamdown, vue-stream-markdown); no EDITOR or document model does. Searches run: registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search for 'incomplete markdown streaming' (top 8 are all renderers), 'streaming markdown editor' (zero markdown editors in top 8), 'markdown block anchor id' (zero markdown-anchoring packages in top 8). Also grepped docs/mdmax/PLAN.md + docs/engine/PLAN.md + docs/engine/README.md for stream|incomplete|unterminated|partial: 3 hits, all about MD4C parser throughput.

A provenance field on a markdown block: who wrote this paragraph — a person, a model, or a person editing a model's draft. 94.3% of markdown created in the pinned corpus in June 2026 was created inside an agent session, and the first question any review loop asks is authorship, yet nothing carries it. Searches run: npm search 'collaborative markdown comments' (returns strip-json-comments, comment-json, CKEditor 5 — nothing markdown-native); root-tree census of 215 top repos found no provenance convention file of any kind alongside AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md.

A measurement of the machine-write-to-machine-read share of a markdown corpus. I had to build it from raw transcripts because no tool reports it; 44.2% of agent markdown reads land on agent-written files, and nobody in the surveyed literature or tooling publishes this ratio. Search basis: the 18-area capability result and the 25-agent findings file in docs/engine/research/ contain no such metric, and npm has no package in this space under the four queries above.

A degradation target class for MODELS alongside renderers. The plan's degradation certificate models (product, surface) renderer pairs; it does not model 'this construct survives into a model's context window at cost X'. Nobody does — the 24-renderer matrix in docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.3 has no model column, and the llms.txt ecosystem (1/215 adoption) is the only attempt at model-facing packaging and it failed.
result.design: "There is a new era" should ship as ONE addition to MDMAX and one deletion from the story, not as a strategy pivot. WHAT SHIPS: a prefix mode on the MDMAX parser and resolver — `mdmax parse --prefix` accepts a byte prefix of a document, returns a partial AST in which every complete block carries its normal content-derived block id and the trailing incomplete region is a single explicitly-typed OPEN node (open_fence, open_table, open_list, open_paragraph) carrying the raw bytes. Contract: for any document D and any two prefixes k < k', every block id assigned at k that is not inside the OPEN region at k is byte-identical at k'. That is the §4.1 anchoring guarantee applied to the time axis instead of the edit axis, and it costs almost nothing because the S1 exact-hash-over-normalized-text stage already gives it. CARRIER: no file change whatsoever — this is a library and CLI mode, D6/D8/D9 untouched, and it is the one capability where the market has already proven demand at ~30.7M downloads/month across streamdown+remend and has served it only at the presentation layer. DEGRADATION: if a consumer ignores prefix mode entirely they get today's behaviour, a parse error or a mangled trailing block; the OPEN node is additive. CLI SURFACE: `mdmax parse --prefix --ids` on stdin, streaming NDJSON of {block_id, kind, byte_range, stable:true|false}, so an editor can render token-by-token while keeping comment anchors pinned to the blocks that have already settled. SECOND, SMALLER THING: add one reserved field to the `fm:` namespace for block provenance (human | model | mixed) as a VALUE, per D8, not a node type. WHAT GETS DELETED FROM THE STORY: any claim that markdown volume is exploding. It is not — repository share fell 12.68% to 10.41% and generic parsers beat the npm baseline by only 1.44x. The pitch is "markdown's reader changed", and the evidence for that is strong and specific; the pitch is not "there is more markdown", and that claim will not survive a hostile investor with an npm terminal.
result.measurement: THE EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES IT: block-id churn under token-by-token arrival. CORPUS: the pinned corpus, corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4, restricted to the 991 git-tracked files, plus a second arm of 500 real assistant markdown responses extracted from ~/.claude/projects transcripts (explicitly a different, stated selection — the transcripts are model-authored markdown, which is the actual input distribution). TASK: for each document, replay it as prefixes at every 32-byte boundary; at each prefix run the resolver and record the id assigned to every settled block. VERIFIERS, all rules-based and deterministic (LR#25, cheapest applicable verifier): (V1) churn rate = fraction of (prefix, block) pairs where a block that was settled at prefix k has a different id at prefix k+1 — this must be 0 by the contract, so any nonzero value is a defect, not a score; (V2) OPEN-region size = bytes classified OPEN divided by total bytes, measured at every prefix, reported as a distribution not a mean; (V3) settle latency = number of prefixes between a block's first appearance and its id becoming final. BASELINES, three, all implementable in an afternoon: block-index ids, byte-offset ids, and remend's actual behaviour (npm i remend, feed the same prefixes, diff its emitted DOM). n: 991 documents x ~mean 3,200 prefixes each, roughly 3.2 million (prefix, document) observations — large enough that a 0.1% churn rate is visible. PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, written now so they can be wrong: (P1) block-index ids churn on more than 50% of prefixes, because every new block shifts every subsequent index — this is the same failure mode as the 55.50% false rate already measured for block-index anchoring in docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.1. (P2) content-hash ids churn on exactly zero settled blocks and the churn is confined to the trailing OPEN region. (P3) the OPEN region exceeds 20% of the document for fewer than 5% of prefixes, EXCEPT inside code fences, where it will be near 100% until the closing fence arrives — and if that exception turns out to dominate the transcript arm, the whole prefix mode is worth much less than it looks, because model output is fence-heavy. P3 is the prediction most likely to embarrass the design and it is the reason the transcript arm exists. Every number reported must be produced by the script, tagged with the corpus_id or the explicit alternative selection, and run at least three times (LR#63).
result.kill_condition: Kill the prefix/streaming direction if EITHER of two things is true. (1) Pre-registered prediction P3 fails badly on the transcript arm: if more than 30% of prefixes over real model-authored markdown sit inside an unterminated code fence, then "stable ids for settled blocks" buys almost nothing, because the interesting content is the part that has not settled — and the correct answer is to let streamdown/remend own the presentation layer and for MDMAX to never touch streaming. (2) Churn measured on the diff path is already zero in practice: if in frontmatter a previous version of the document essentially always exists (which docs/mdmax/PLAN.md §4.1 already concedes — "content-derived re-anchoring is the fallback and the verifier, not the primary mechanism"), and the CodeMirror ChangeSet plus offline-sync before/after covers the streaming case too, then prefix mode is solving a problem the harness already solved and it should not be built. Kill the ERA CLAIM itself — the framing, not the code — if a rerun of the npm control in six months shows the model-facing stack (react-markdown, remark-gfm, rehype-raw, streamdown, remend) falling back to within 1.5x of the 14-package npm baseline. That would mean the 2025-2026 spike was AI-application churn rather than a durable consumer shift, and the honest response is to stop saying "new era" out loud. Concretely: the excess-growth ratio is 3.1x today (react-markdown x8.75 / control median x2.81); if it drops below 1.5x, the story is dead.
result.unverified: COULD NOT VERIFY — the sandbox blocks every host outside a small allowlist (github.com, api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, registry.npmjs.org, api.npmjs.org, pypi.org, and a few vendor APIs). Curl to agents.md, llmstxt.org and directory.llmstxt.cloud hung until the 2-minute tool timeout. Consequences, each stated at its true tier: (1) The llms.txt figure in the brief — "28% of 137,000 domains published one and 97% received ZERO requests" — is SEARCH-ONLY to me. I could not reach the source and did not re-derive it. My independent substitute is own-measurement: llms.txt exists in 1 of 215 top-starred GitHub repos (0.47%). Do not treat the 28%/97% pair as verified by this run. (2) AGENTS.md's own claimed adoption count (whatever agents.md publishes) is UNREAD. Everything I report about AGENTS.md is my own tree census, n=215, one snapshot plus per-file creation dates. (3) Hugging Face dataset cards — NOT MEASURED at all; huggingface.co is not on the allowlist and I found no proxy worth reporting. The brief asked for it and I do not have it. (4) OKF SPEC.md v0.2 — NOT READ. I found no canonical Google repository at four guessed paths (all HTTP 404) and did not want to attribute a spec to a third-party mirror. What I have is search-only-plus-API: 23 repos named open-knowledge-format, all created on or after 2026-06-14, top implementation 206 stars. The brief's instruction "READ SPEC.md rather than a blog post" is UNFULFILLED for this area. (5) PyPI download trends — NOT MEASURED; pypi.org's JSON API carries no download counts and pypistats.org is not on the allowlist, so the entire Python side of the parser story is missing and my 1.44x excess-growth figure is JavaScript-only. (6) The AGENTS.md creation curve uses the first commit touching the CURRENT path; a repo that renamed the file would date to the rename, biasing the curve late. 8 of 57 AGENTS.md files had no resolvable date and are excluded. (7) An intermediate census over the first 43 repos of the alphabetically-sorted top-300 list gave AGENTS.md 5/35 = 14.29%, which conflicts with the full-sample 57/215 = 26.51%; the partial slice was alphabetically biased toward award-lists and tutorial repos and I discarded it rather than reporting the flattering or the unflattering half. (8) INFERENCE, not measurement: the claim that frontmatter's product thesis targets the non-growing half. The grep showing zero streaming coverage in the plan is primary; the strategic reading of it is mine.

result.area: Is there actually a new era of markdown, or is that a story we are telling ourselves

verdicts.claim: Claim 2 — the new packages exist because model-authored markdown is a different parsing problem (streamdown/remend README + descriptions)
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Fetched registry.npmjs.org/streamdown readme 2026-08-01. Verbatim, character-for-character as quoted: 'Formatting Markdown is easy, but when you tokenize and stream it, new challenges arise. Streamdown is built specifically to handle the unique requirements of streaming Markdown content from AI models, providing seamless formatting even with incomplete or unterminated Markdown blocks.' package description 'A drop-in replacement for react-markdown, designed for AI-powered streaming.' and remend 'Self-healing markdown. Intelligently parses and styles incomplete Markdown blocks.' both exact. No paraphrase, no embellishment.

verdicts.claim: Claim 3 — generic markdown parsers grew only 1.44x faster than the npm baseline; most apparent markdown growth is npm-wide inflation
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Re-fetched all 22 packages from api.npmjs.org/downloads/point for 2024-08-01:2024-08-31 and 2026-06-01:2026-06-30. Every one of the 22 raw download figures reproduces to the digit. Recomputed: 8-parser median = 4.0495, 14-package control median = 2.8145, excess = 1.4388. Rounds to 4.05 / 2.81 / 1.44 exactly as stated. Note the contamination runs in the researcher's disfavour: marked, unified and remark-parse are all direct streamdown dependencies, so the 4.05 is inflated by the AI stack and the true generic-parser excess is lower, making this claim conservative.

verdicts.claim: Claim 8 — markdown is the single most-read file type inside an agent tool loop, ahead of every programming language
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Independent scan of ~/.claude/projects (13,968 .jsonl now vs their 13,947; this session adds files). Read calls with a path = 36,846: .md 8,663 = 23.51% rank 1, .png 20.82%, .tsx 16.51%, .ts 11.10%, .py 6.01% — matches to the decimal. Write/Edit/MultiEdit = 19,416: .tsx 25.44%, .md 4,791 = 24.68% rank 2. Correctly flagged as a different selection from the pinned corpus, as the brief requires. Two immaterial blemishes: claim 8 prints 8,661 md read calls where claim 9 prints 8,663 for the same dataset (8,663 is correct), and '290,674 tool_use lines' does not reproduce — I count 205,142 tool_use blocks. Neither figure enters any ratio.

verdicts.claim: Claim 10 — 94.3% of corpus files created 2026-06 and 92.4% of 2026-07 were created inside an agent session
