verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Verified corpus-manifest.json carries corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4, matching the brief. Re-derived at the three pinned heads (02c22ec4/464eb666/798ebbf3): git-tracked selection 991 of 1,084 — md 691/756, knowledge 249/272, frontmatter 51/56 — every structural number exact. AI-marked creating commit: mine 577/991 = 58.2% vs their 578/991 = 58.3%; per root mine md 278 / knowledge 248 / frontmatter 51 vs theirs 279/248/51. By month mine 2026-05 68/448, 2026-06 448/476, 2026-07 61/67 vs theirs 69/450, 448/475, 61/66. Replicates to within one file out of 991. Their internal arithmetic also reconciles (450+475+66=991, 69+448+61=578).

verdicts.claim: Claim 5 — AGENTS.md went 0% to ~26.5% of the 300 most-starred GitHub repos in about 15 months
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Re-ran the census 2026-08-01: search stars:>30000 sorted by stars, 300 repos, root tree via api.github.com/repos/{r}/git/trees/HEAD. All 300 fetched with zero errors. Full 300: AGENTS.md 92 = 30.67%, CLAUDE.md 76 = 25.33%, .claude 45 = 15.00%, README.md 278 = 92.67%. Apples-to-apples on the top 215 by star rank: AGENTS.md 69/215 = 32.09%. Earliest month 2025-05, so 15 months is right. Their 26.51% is CONSERVATIVE — the real figure is ~30-32%. Their 215-of-300 sample loss is unexplained (I lost none) and biased the headline down, which is the honest direction.

verdicts.claim: Claim 7 — llms.txt and .cursorrules are measurably dead in the top-repo population
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Same full-300 census: llms.txt 1/300 = 0.33%, .cursorrules 2/300 = 0.67%, GEMINI.md 7/300 = 2.33%, AGENT.md 0/300 = 0.00%, .windsurfrules 0/300 = 0.00%, against CONTRIBUTING.md 168/300 = 56.00%. Same picture, same conclusion, slightly different denominator. The settled llms.txt cautionary note survives.

verdicts.claim: Falsifier F3 — the format itself shows no renewed activity (CommonMark shipped zero new conformance examples since 2021-06-19)
verdicts.reason: [primary-read + own-measurement] Pulled spec.txt at tags 0.29/0.30/0.31.0/0.31.2 and counted the 32-backtick example fences: 0.29 = 649 examples, 0.30 = 652 (date field '2021-06-19'), 0.31.0 = 652, 0.31.2 = 652 (date '2024-01-28'). Zero new examples across two releases and 2.5 years — decisive. Bare-cloned the repo: commits/yr 2019=48, 2020=15, 2021=14, 2022=15, 2023=13, 2024=11, 2025=7, 2026=6 — matches '48/15/14/15/13/11/7/6' digit for digit. github/cmark-gfm latest release 0.29.0.gfm.13 published 2023-07-21T15:22:23Z, exact.
verdicts.correction: The adjective 'spec commits declining every single year since 2019' is contradicted by the researcher's own table: 2021=14 rises to 2022=15. And 2026's 6 covers 7 months, annualising to ~10, above 2025's full-year 7 — a rate-vs-absolute comparison. The conclusion is untouched; only the word 'every' is wrong.

verdicts.claim: Claim 6 — AGENTS.md adoption is already flattening; monthly new files halved after March 2026
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Re-derived first-commit month for every AGENTS.md via commits?path=AGENTS.md with the oldest page from Link rel=last. 92 of 92 dated, zero failures. Full 300: 2026-02 11, 03 12, 04 9, 05 10, 06 5, 07 4 — last four average 7.0 against a March peak of 12, a 39% dip driven entirely by the final two months. Apples-to-apples on the top 215: 69 repos (not 57), months 04-07 = 6,5,5,3, average 4.75 (not 4,2,3,3 / 3.0). Their 2026-05 figure of +2 is the sharpest miss: I measure 5 on the same 215 and 10 on the full 300. April and May sit at or near peak in both of my samples, so 'halved after March 2026' does not hold. Their own enumeration also sums to 46 while the text states 49 dated of 57 — a 3-file internal arithmetic defect. What survives is a two-month dip on n=4 and n=3, which at Poisson noise of roughly +/-3 on a ~8/month base is not a trend.
verdicts.correction: Adoption in the top-starred population is running at roughly 5-10 new AGENTS.md per month with a March 2026 peak of 12 and no established downtrend. Do not tell the team the curve is flattening on two months of data.

verdicts.claim: Headline leg — markdown's share of repository file trees FELL 12.68% to 10.41% (2024-08 to 2026-06, 12 repos), therefore 'not volume'
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Unreproducible as published: the 12 repos are never named and no corpus_id is cited, which the brief's rule 3 makes a defect on its face. I ran an independent, fully specified test — 12 named major OSS repos, commit nearest 2024-08-01 and nearest 2026-06-30 via commits?until=, full recursive trees, 2 skipped as truncated. Result reverses the direction: pooled md share ROSE 2.39% (4,460/186,903) to 2.74% (6,556/239,656); md files x1.47 against total files x1.28; median per-repo share rose 1.15% to 1.90%; share fell in only 3 of 10. Per-repo 2026-06: react 27.50%, next.js 4.08%, tensorflow 3.35%, pytorch 2.34%, kubernetes 1.91%, node 1.37%, go 0.28%, django 0.13%, home-assistant 0.09%. Their 12.68% baseline is roughly five times higher than any real code repository I measured, so their 12 repos cannot be code repos — the selection cannot carry a general claim about 'repository file trees'.
verdicts.correction: On named major repositories markdown is OUTGROWING the rest of the tree (x1.47 vs x1.28). The DESIGN section instructs the team to delete 'any claim that markdown volume is exploding' on the strength of this number — that instruction would delete a claim my measurement supports. Either name the 12 repos and pin them to a corpus_id, or drop the repo-share leg entirely and rest 'not volume' on claim 3 alone, which does hold.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — the market has proven demand at ~30.7M downloads/month across streamdown+remend
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] streamdown 2.5.0's dependency list contains an exact pin, "remend": "1.3.0", alongside "rehype-harden": "^1.1.8". Worse, both packages ship from the SAME repository: registry metadata gives streamdown repository git+https://github.com/vercel/streamdown.git directory packages/streamdown, and remend the identical URL with directory packages/remend. Adding a package to its own pinned dependency from the same monorepo double counts one install base. The monthly series proves the pull-through: 2026-04 streamdown 10,809,649, remend 9,723,249, rehype-harden 10,315,499; 2026-02 3,791,087 / 2,920,598 / 3,461,931 — the dependencies track the parent within ~10%.
verdicts.correction: The defensible figure is ~16M downloads/month for one dependency closure, not 30.7M across two independent packages. Do not put 30.7M in front of an investor with an npm terminal.

verdicts.claim: Claim 1 — a markdown tooling category that did not exist 12 months ago is now at 14-16M downloads/month, and every member exists because the author is a model
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement + primary-read] Every raw number reproduces exactly: streamdown 2025-08 = 80,606 to 2026-06 = 14,477,148 (x179.60, created 2025-08-14T23:59:03.091Z), remend 0 to 16,192,091 (created 2025-12-03T07:13:55.547Z), rehype-harden 16,052,832, harden-react-markdown created 2025-07-31T02:53:44.948Z. The observation that a model-output-shaped package class appeared from nothing is real and is the strongest thing in the area. But 'category' and 'every member' imply independent convergent adoption by many actors, and all four are Vercel: streamdown and remend from github.com/vercel/streamdown (author hayden.bleasel@vercel.com), rehype-harden from github.com/vercel-labs/markdown-sanitizers (maintainer cramforce), harden-react-markdown from github.com/vercel/harden-react-markdown (cramforce). The README even states 'Streamdown powers the [AI Elements Message]'.
verdicts.correction: This is one vendor's stack propagating through a dependency chain, not a category. State it as 'Vercel shipped a model-output markdown stack that went 0 to ~16M downloads/month in ten months' — still striking, and it survives scrutiny. The current wording invites the reply that you counted one product four times.

verdicts.claim: Claim 9 — nearly half (44.2%) of all markdown an agent reads is markdown an agent itself wrote
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Arithmetic is flawless — I reproduce 1,563 distinct md read paths, 8,663 read calls, 1,258 distinct written, 4,791 write calls, 659 in both, 42.2% of read paths, 52.4% of written, 3,832/8,663 = 44.2%, every figure exact. The defect is the definition: the write set unions Write with Edit/MultiEdit, and Claude Code REQUIRES a Read before any Edit, so the harness manufactures read-then-write pairs on files the agent never authored. Splitting them: paths reaching a genuine Write (creation) account for 552 paths and 3,120 read calls = 36.0%; paths only ever Edited add 107 paths and 712 read calls = 8.2%, and those 712 reads are compelled by the tool's precondition, not evidence of a machine-to-machine loop.
verdicts.correction: 36.0%, 'just over a third', is the defensible figure for markdown an agent actually created. Still a strong result — it just is not 'nearly half'.

verdicts.claim: Claim 4 — growth is concentrated exactly where model output is rendered, ~3x excess over the control
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Ratios reproduce exactly: react-markdown x8.749, rehype-raw x9.183, remark-gfm x7.906, shiki x7.929, markdown-to-jsx x0.794, showdown x1.850, commonmark x1.735; AI-stack median 8.339 / control median 2.8145 = 2.96, so '~3x' is arithmetically right. Three problems with the inference. (a) Wrong denominator: react itself sits in their own control at x5.745, so react-markdown's excess over its actual host ecosystem is 8.749/5.745 = 1.52x, not 3.11x — the control median is dragged down by legacy packages (chalk x1.41, xml2js x1.75, webpack x1.89). (b) Not independent: rehype-raw and remark-gfm are both direct streamdown dependencies, so they are not separate confirmations of the same phenomenon. (c) shiki is a syntax highlighter, not a markdown renderer.
verdicts.correction: The clean, load-bearing evidence here is markdown-to-jsx's absolute decline (22,908,372 to 18,185,739 = x0.79) against react-markdown's x8.75 — same job, same ecosystem, opposite direction, and neither is a streamdown dependency. Lead with that pair and drop the four-package '3x' framing.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — prefix parsing is a capability the market has served 'only at the presentation layer'
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Parser-layer incremental and streaming markdown predates streamdown by years. @lezer/markdown, npm created 2021-08-11, describes itself verbatim as 'Incremental Markdown parser that consumes and emits Lezer trees' and is what CodeMirror 6 runs on. tree-sitter-markdown has existed since 2019-09-30 and tree-sitter is incremental by construction. micromark — the CommonMark reference implementation underneath remark/unified — ships a documented duplex streaming API, 'import {stream} from micromark/stream'. The proposal's genuinely novel part is narrower than stated: content-derived block IDs that stay byte-identical across prefixes, plus explicitly-typed OPEN nodes. That narrower claim I could not refute.
verdicts.correction: Reframe as 'existing incremental parsers reuse nodes but expose no stable cross-prefix block identity for anchoring' and cite @lezer/markdown and micromark/stream as prior art. Also surface micromark's own verbatim warning, which bears directly on the contract: 'Some of the work to parse markdown can be done streaming, but in the end buffering is required.'

survived: Claim 2 — model-emitted markdown is a distinct parsing problem, in the vendors' own words. Verbatim primary-read, exact.

Claim 3 — generic parsers beat the npm control by only 1.44x. Reproduced to four significant figures (4.0495 / 2.8145 / 1.4388), and conservative, since three of the eight 'generic' parsers are streamdown dependencies.
Claim 8 — markdown is the #1 file type an agent reads (23.51%, ahead of .tsx and .ts) and #2 written. Replicated to the decimal on an independent scan.
Claim 10 — 94.1-94.3% of June 2026 and 91-92.4% of July 2026 corpus files were created in an agent session. Replicated to within 1 file of 991, corpus_id verified against the manifest.
Claim 5 — AGENTS.md from nothing to a quarter-plus of the most-starred repos in 15 months. Confirmed and understated: 30.67% on the full 300, 32.09% on the top 215.
Claim 7 — llms.txt (0.33%) and .cursorrules (0.67%) are dead; AGENT.md and .windsurfrules are at zero. Confirmed on a larger sample.

Falsifier F3 — the format is frozen. 652 conformance examples at 0.30 (2021-06-19) and still 652 at 0.31.2 (2024-01-28); cmark-gfm's last release 0.29.0.gfm.13, 2023-07-21. The single most decisive fact in the area.
The headline's core direction — the regime change is in markdown's CONSUMER, not in the format. Both supporting legs of that specific sentence hold.
killed: Claim 6 — 'adoption is already FLATTENING'. The monthly series does not reproduce on either sample. Their +2 for 2026-05 measures 5 on the same top-215 and 10 on the full 300; April and May sit at or near the March peak. Their own enumeration sums to 46 against a stated 49.

Headline leg — 'markdown's share of repository file trees FELL 12.68% to 10.41%'. Unreproducible as published (12 unnamed repos, no corpus_id) and directionally reversed on a fully specified 10-repo test: pooled share ROSE 2.39% to 2.74%, md files x1.47 vs total files x1.28, share fell in only 3 of 10.

DESIGN — '~30.7M downloads/month across streamdown+remend'. remend is a pinned dependency of streamdown and ships from the same Vercel monorepo. The sum double counts one install base; ~16M is the honest figure.
DESIGN — the capability 'has served it only at the presentation layer'. Refuted by @lezer/markdown (incremental, 2021), tree-sitter-markdown (2019) and micromark's documented stream API.
'CommonMark spec commits declining every single year since 2019' — refuted by the researcher's own table (2021=14 to 2022=15) and by comparing a 7-month 2026 against full years.
new_defects: THE BIG ONE — the 'new category' is one vendor. All four packages in claim 1 are Vercel-published: streamdown and remend from github.com/vercel/streamdown (packages/streamdown, packages/remend), rehype-harden from vercel-labs/markdown-sanitizers, harden-react-markdown from vercel/harden-react-markdown. streamdown 2.5.0 pins remend 1.3.0 and rehype-harden ^1.1.8 as direct dependencies, and the monthly series shows the deps tracking the parent within ~10% (2026-04: 10.81M / 9.72M / 10.32M). The area's strongest claim is one product counted up to four times.

DESIGN CONTRACT HAZARD, own-measurement — a link reference definition arriving later mutates a settled, NON-trailing block, which the OPEN-node quarantine does not cover. Prefix 'See [foo]. Para two. Para three. ' renders block 1 as '

See [foo].

'; appending ' [foo]: /url ' makes it '

See foo.

'. Block 1 has two paragraphs after it, so it is not in the trailing region. The stated ID contract survives (a hash over normalized text is unchanged), but the proposed NDJSON 'stable:true' flag would be WRONG: an editor painting token-by-token must repaint a block it was told had settled. Sharpest irony available — the offending construct is the link reference definition, which this program's own settled findings name as one of only two carriers invisible in 24/24 renderers. Fix: either mark blocks containing unresolved link references 'stable:false', or define stability as ID-stability only and say so explicitly in the contract.
micromark's README states the fundamental limit verbatim and it belongs in the design doc: 'Some of the work to parse markdown can be done streaming, but in the end buffering is required.'
Claim 8 reports 8,661 md read calls; claim 9 reports 8,663 for the identical dataset. 8,663 is correct.
'290,674 tool_use lines' does not reproduce — I count 205,142 tool_use blocks across 13,968 transcripts. Immaterial to every ratio, but it is an uncited number.

The 215-of-300 census sample loss is never explained. All 300 root trees fetch cleanly with no errors, and the loss pushed AGENTS.md down (57/215 vs my 69/215) — so it is unexplained, not merely conservative.

Their 12.68% markdown share baseline is ~5x higher than any real code repository I measured (max 20.51%, median 1.15%). Whatever those 12 repos are, they are not representative code repositories, and the number is presented as a general fact about 'repository file trees'.

FALSIFIER-HONESTY JUDGMENT: the researcher genuinely looked. F4 demonstrably fired and rewrote the headline — the report states the first draft was 'there is no new era, only npm-wide inflation', and the surviving headline is the more conservative one. F2 and F3 reproduce exactly on independent re-derivation, which is strong evidence they were actually executed rather than asserted. This is materially better process than the prior run's 100% flattering-direction defect rate. The failure is construction, not effort: F1's population was never specified, making it the one falsifier that could not be checked by anyone — and it is the one that turns out to be directionally wrong.

result.note:
SCOPE. 29 kills were handed to me; I audited 21 to primary sources and left 8 unaudited rather than guess: moat's 'only durable moat is S5 multi-tenancy', 'and by C2PA before that', and 'DESIGN item 1 expiry field IS the moat'; market-and-gift's 'eleven canonical free artifacts' and 'Claim 6's 2 of 15 disagree'; and aios-transfer's 'markdown fails MOST', 'file_modified=26', and 'both failure modes'. All eight turn on the ORIGINAL claim text or on a transcript-mining selection rule that is not on disk in this repo (the current run's results are not written yet; only the previous 18-area run at docs/engine/research/wf-mdmax-capability-2026-08-01.result.json is). Auditing them without the researcher's population definition would be reconstructing a denominator by guesswork — the exact defect several of these kills correctly identify. The 4/21 rate is therefore a rate over what was checkable, not over all 29.

HOW TO USE 19%. Roughly one kill in five is itself wrong. That is far better than the 100% headline defect rate the verification layer was built to fix, so the layer is doing real work and should be kept — but it is nowhere near clean enough for a kill to be executed unaudited. The concrete governance implication: nothing should be DELETED on a kill alone. On this sample, executing all 21 kills unaudited would have destroyed four correct findings, including a corpus denominator that reproduces to within 0.003%.

THE FAILURE SIGNATURE, AND IT HAS A DIRECTION. All four overturns are the same species: a verifier constructing a denominator or a definition, finding it does not match, and reporting a defect instead of reporting that it could not reproduce the researcher's definition. 31,630 vs 31,631 — four definitions tried, not the plainest one. 4 uses vs 5 matches — a grammar production counted as a use and a byte-identical mirror counted twice. 80 days — one endpoint assumed, the exact-matching alternative untested. 4,800/day — one snapshot inspected, its own daily-committed history not. Note the asymmetry: the researchers' defects ran flattering; the verifiers' defects run damning. Both are reward functions. A verifier scored on kills found will manufacture kills exactly the way a researcher scored on findings will manufacture findings, and the manufacturing looks identical — a number stated without the derivation attached.

MANDATORY NEGATIVES AGAINST MY OWN DIRECTION. (1) My job biases me toward overturning, and 17 of 21 kills survived contact with the primary source — several of them (OKF's grep -ic confidence = 0 over exactly 37,544 bytes; the 188/69 union summing to 542 out of 409; the six-directory heredoc probe; the ArchieCur matrix being exactly 14x17) reproduced to the unit on first attempt. The verification layer is largely accurate, and an auditor who came back with a high overturn rate would be the third reward function in this chain. (2) Two of my four overturns are softer than the other two. The '80 days' overturn depends on an endpoint I cannot read from the original claim; if C8 said 'in 80 days of development' with the last commit as the endpoint, the kill is right and my overturn is wrong. The '+4,800/day' overturn concedes the procedural point entirely — the figure WAS uncited, and 'derivable-in-principle' is not the same as 'was derived'. The two I would defend hardest are the 31,631 and the [[note#^id]] recount, both of which I reproduced from the pinned corpus with multiple independent tools.

PRE-REGISTERED FALSIFIER. Before starting I fixed what would prove my headline wrong: if the four overturns each turned out to rest on a definition the researcher demonstrably did NOT use, the false-kill rate would collapse toward 0 and the verification layer would deserve unconditional trust. I went looking. For the ATX count I ran six regex variants x two fence policies plus three grep formulations and found 31,631 under every strict-start variant — the researcher's number is not reachable only under a contrived definition, it is reachable under the default one. For the block-ref count I checked the two FEATURE-GAP-REPORT.md files' sha256 specifically to try to prove the verifier right about their distinctness, and they are identical. The falsifier did not fire on those two. It remains live on the other two.

CORPUS DISCIPLINE. Every corpus number above is against corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4. I re-resolved all 1,084 manifest paths against the live working trees before using it: 0 missing, 0 sha256 mismatches, 25,548,765 bytes total. The corpus is fully reproducible today and is the one asset in this program I would trust without re-derivation.

RULE 4. No commits, no pushes, no installs, no writes outside $TMPDIR (the regression-gate probe ran with SGNK_REGRESSION_GATES redirected into $TMPDIR so the live ~/.sgnk/state gates file was never touched; verify-ladder ran only against a synthetic tree in $TMPDIR, never against the repo, to avoid py_compile writing __pycache__). One `rm -rf` on a $TMPDIR path I had just created tripped the bash-guard warn hook; the directory did not exist and nothing was removed. I avoided rm thereafter.

BONUS DEFECT, OUTSIDE THE KILL SET. ~/.sgnk/bin/sgnk-regression-gate.sh line 70: `before=\"$(grep -c . \"$GATES\" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)\"` returns the two-line string '0\\n0' when the gates file exists but is empty, because `grep -c .` prints 0 AND exits 1, so the `|| echo 0` fires as well. Line 70's `[ \"$after\" -le \"$before\" ]` then errors with `[: 0 0: integer expression expected` and the guard is inoperative. This is the write-landed check added specifically for LR#67 — the check built to catch false greens fails open on the empty-file case. It is a live bug in a tool the AIOS transfer plan depends on, and none of the kills or claims mention it.

The failure boundary is a pure function of --stack-size, and the verifier ran with a larger stack than the researcher. On Node v24.6.0 at the DEFAULT stack (984 KB): depth 1907 THROWs RangeError deterministically 5 runs of 5; a full bisect gives last-OK 1901 / first-THROW 1902 for the tight ('>>>...> x') and spaced ('> > > ... x') shapes, and 2338/2339 for the multi-line staircase. Then the smoking gun: `node --stack-size=2000` parses depth 1907 in 10.8 ms and --stack-size=4000 in 10.2 ms - matching the verifier's own reported 11.4/10.6 ms almost exactly. So the verifier compared a large-stack run against a default-stack run and called the researcher's bisect wrong; the researcher's ~1907 is within 0.3% of the default-stack boundary I measure. This is the brief's named failure mode - wrong denominator - applied to a stack budget. IMPORTANT: only the BISECT half falls. The same kill's mechanism half is CONFIRMED and must be kept - every failure I observed at every depth and shape is `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, and the fact that it is tunable by --stack-size proves it is stack depth, not a depth-proportional regex. 'It builds a regex proportional to blockquote depth' remains an unreproduced inference.
result.note:
HEADLINE: the verification layer is sound. 28 of 29 kills survive independent re-derivation from primary sources; 1 is a false kill. 3.4% false-kill rate against the research layer's 100% headline defect rate means the verifiers should be trusted to GATE, and the previous instinct to delete twelve design sections on unaudited kills was the wrong risk to worry about - the wrong risk is the opposite one.

BUT TRUST THE VERDICTS, NOT THE NUMBERS. 5 of the 28 upheld kills carry arithmetic or attribution defects of their own, so verdict reliability is ~97% while number reliability is ~83%. Do not paste a verifier's replacement figure into the PLAN without re-deriving it: (1) custom-pointers C7 - the verifier's '10 distinct values' is unreproducible; I get 12 under all six regex x scope combinations AND under the eemeli-YAML ground truth. Its 195 and 365 are exact. (2) custom-pointers C5 - 'modifiable' is not in the securemodelines allowlist; only 'readonly' is. (3) product-gap C9 - the M128,24A104 path is a tooltip glyph beside feature names, not 'the Image storage row's Prime column'. (4) hold-more C10 - the replacement 4.6% is an n=30 point estimate quoted without a CI. (5) parsing-robustness CLAIM 1 / CLAIM 9 - the verifiers' own replacement timings are as unreproducible as the researchers'; I could reproduce neither party's absolute wall-clock (remark-parse is near-linear to 100k paragraphs, k 0.67-1.30, and the worst per-2x I could construct across six shapes is 3.1x).

ONE SYSTEMIC DISEASE EXPLAINS THE SINGLE FALSE KILL AND 3 OF THE 5 BLEMISHES: an equality-pinned assertion on an environment-dependent quantity. The CLAIM 8 false kill is exactly that - a marked blockquote depth boundary that moves from 1902 to >1907 the moment --stack-size changes, measured on two different stack budgets and reported as a contradiction. Same family as CLAIM 1 and CLAIM 9 (wall-clock across machines) and C10 (a sample estimate as a point value). This is Learned Rules #63 and #65 recurring inside the tool built to catch them. RECOMMENDATION: any verifier assertion about a timing, a stack depth, a heap figure, or a sampled rate must state the environment and assert a BAND, never an equality; and any such assertion must be run at least 3 times before it is allowed to kill anything.

TWO KILLS ARE RIGHT FOR THE WRONG REASON and should be re-worded before they go in the record, not deleted: custom-pointers C7 (correct thesis - the regex distorts counts, not the distinct-value count - reached via a wrong '10') and parsing-robustness CLAIM 8 (correct mechanism critique - stack overflow, not a depth-proportional regex - reached via a bisect that does not hold).

MY OWN FALSIFIER, PRE-REGISTERED: I said before starting that if the verifiers were reward-hacking for defects I would find their replacement numbers failing to reproduce more often than the claims they killed. That prediction was WRONG in the aggregate - 22 of 29 kills reproduced to the digit or near it against primary sources (npm download counts, GHSA payloads, W3C and Quarto spec text, Google Docs discovery, the pinned corpus, HackMD's live DOM, and live node runs). It was right in exactly one case, CLAIM 8, and that is the one I overturned.

METHOD AND LIMITS. Every corpus number above is against corpus_id sha256:3a010b1649899795d79274fc528dbece97fdabf4ff0f81cc02ab619c048c51a4, which I re-materialized from docs/engine/research/corpus-manifest.json: all 1,084 files resolved, 0 missing, 0 sha256 mismatches, so the vaults have not drifted since pinning. THE ONE LIMITATION THAT MATTERS: the original researcher texts are live workflow output and are NOT in the repo - I could not read them. I audited each kill against primary sources while taking the kill's own quotation of its target at face value. If a verifier misquoted the claim it was killing, I would not have detected it, and the areas where a kill hinges on the exact original wording (custom-pointers C1, C7; parsing-robustness CLAIM 9's 80,001-vs-80,002 byte detail, on which I make no finding) carry that residual risk. RULE 4 respected throughout: no commits, no pushes, no installs, no deletions, no outbound calls; every artifact I wrote lives under $TMPDIR/ka.
